item.title: High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target multiple industry sectors
item.description:
Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a high-volume phishing campaign using Microsoft 365 outage-themed lures to target organizations across multiple sectors worldwide.

The post High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target multiple industry sectors appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. Phishing attack overview
  2. Attack chain overview
  3. Mitigation and protection guidance
  4. References
  5. Learn More

On November 13, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. The threat actors used phishing emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications to lure recipients into clicking a malicious link. The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them. This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures.

Microsoft identified the threat actor’s use of specific sender domain names, randomized outage subjects, recipient-specific tracking links, and a common non-Microsoft destination to make the messages appear relevant while complicating simple pattern matching. We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext.

If credentials were entered, organizations should consider the risk of account compromise, mailbox access, business email compromise, internal phishing, inbox-rule manipulation, and access to cloud collaboration data. Microsoft Defender blocks malicious domains used in this campaign, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines phishing emails. We will continue to monitor this campaign and other related threats. Security teams can use Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR capabilities to investigate messages, URLs, clicks, and potential follow-on activity.

Phishing attack overview

Microsoft analyzed the email lures sent on November 13, 2026: the emails used the subject pattern “Outage – <random token>” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”

Example subject line:

  • Outage – aF7vG6

Example display names:

  • MSF Outage Notification
  • AMZ Service Health

One example email body referenced a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12 and claimed that four messages were held after the outage. The urgency of a 24-hour deletion deadline and the prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” call to action were intended to drive immediate interaction.

The activity used distinct sender domains, including: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. The messages also used email-delivery and link-tracking infrastructure to generate recipient-specific URLs. In multiple samples, click-tracking links led to reallifeaccounting[.]com or reallifeaccounting[.]com/themelist0.html.

The sample set was link-based: no QR codes or non-EML attachments were observed, and Microsoft did not identify evidence of executable, archive, document, or other malware payload delivery. The off-brand destination and Microsoft 365 impersonation support an assessment of likely credential phishing, but the available evidence did not include the final page source, credential fields, credential-submission telemetry, or post-compromise activity. Microsoft therefore has not attributed the campaign to a named threat actor or malware family.

Attack chain overview

  1. Delivery: A user receives an email from the moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com or newbooker[.]com sender-domain cluster. The subject contains “Outage -” followed by a randomized string of character tokens. The body of the message includes a fake email conversation positioned to be hidden from the recipient and appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion.
  2. Impersonation: The message poses as a Microsoft 365 service-health notification, uses a target-specific display-name prefix, and references Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Copilot.
  3. Social engineering: The lure claims that messages were held during an outage and will be deleted within 24 hours, creating urgency and fear of lost business email.
  4. User interaction: The recipient selects “RESTORE MESSAGES” or “TAKE ACTION”. A recipient-specific tracking URL records or routes the click.
  5. Redirect: The observed link chain leads to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html in some samples.
  6. Assessed threat actor objectives: Microsoft assesses that the activity was likely intended to capture credentials. Credential submission and subsequent account compromise were not directly observed in the supplied evidence.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Immediate actions

Messages in environments protected by Microsoft Defender for Office are currently blocked/quarantined, and we have not observed any indicators of compromise from this attack.

However, organizations can consider taking the following steps:

  • Search for and remove phishing messages. Search mail telemetry for the observed sender domains, display-name and subject patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domain. Quarantine matching messages and remove delivered copies in accordance with organizational response procedures.
  • Identify users who clicked campaign links. Identify users who selected campaign links. Review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to determine whether the destination was reached and whether credentials may have been entered.
  • Reset credentials and investigate potentially compromised accounts For any user who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations. Review the account for suspicious sign-ins, OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions, and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, or Teams.
  • Block or closely monitor campaign infrastructure. Block or closely scrutinize reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Avoid broadly blocking shared email-delivery infrastructure based only on this campaign; combine sender, content, URL, and behavioral signals to reduce collateral impact.
  • Remind users how to verify legitimate service-health communications. Remind users that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct them to non-Microsoft domains to recover held mail. Validate service issues through the Microsoft 365 admin center rather than through unsolicited email links.

Ongoing hardening

  • Require multifactor authentication and prioritize phishing-resistant methods, such as passkeys or security keys, where possible.
  • Review and enable Safe Links and Safe Attachments policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
  • Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) to help retroactively neutralize phishing, spam, or malware messages that were delivered before new threat intelligence became available.
  • Use Attack simulation training and ongoing awareness guidance to help users recognize outage-themed urgency, sender-domain mismatches, and requests to restore or release messages.
  • Encourage users to report suspicious messages through the organization’s established Outlook reporting workflow so security teams and Microsoft can investigate quickly.

Microsoft Security Copilot

Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run the following prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat:

  • Incident investigation: Summarize related alerts and incidents and identify the affected users and devices.
  • Microsoft User analysis: Review the activity of users who selected the campaign links. This includes sign-ins, MFA-method changes, inbox or forwarding rules, and OAuth grants.

Note that some promptbooks require access to plugins for Microsoft products such as Microsoft Defender XDR or Microsoft Sentinel.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics

High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 Outage lures to target multiple industry sectors.

Advanced hunting queries

These sample queries search for campaign characteristics in Microsoft Defender XDR. Review the results in the context of your environment and adjust the indicators only after validation. The queries do not set a time range; use the advanced hunting time selector for the period you want to investigate.

Find messages by sender domain or subject pattern

This query searches for the observed sender-domain clusters and the randomized outage subject pattern.

let campaignDomains = dynamic([
    "moments-notice.com",
    "em4493.moments-notice.com",
    "newbooker.com",
    "em.newbooker.com"
]);
EmailEvents
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (campaignDomains)
    or Subject matches regex
        @"(?i)^(?:\[external\]\s*|\*external\*\s*)?outage\s*-\s*[a-z0-9]{6}$"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
    SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName,
    Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc

Find messages containing campaign URLs

This query identifies message URLs that contain the observed destination, click-tracking hosts, or tracking-pixel pattern, and joins the results to message metadata.

let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([
    "reallifeaccounting.com",
    "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click",
    "url.newbooker.com/ls/click",
    "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3."
]);
EmailUrlInfo
| where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts)
| project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
        SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName,
        Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
    SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, Url, UrlDomain,
    UrlLocation, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc

Investigate user clicks on campaign URLs

This query searches click telemetry for the observed destination and tracking patterns so investigators can identify affected users and determine whether clicks were allowed.

let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([
    "reallifeaccounting.com",
    "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click",
    "url.newbooker.com/ls/click",
    "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3."
]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, Workload,
    NetworkMessageId, IPAddress, IsClickedThrough, UrlChain
| order by Timestamp desc

For users who interacted with campaign links, also investigate:

  • Unusual sign-ins
  • New devices or user agents
  • MFA-method changes
  • OAuth grants
  • Inbox or forwarding rules
  • Delegate permissions
  • Unusual access to mailbox or collaboration data

These behaviors were not observed in the source messages, they are post-click investigation targets for suspected Microsoft 365 credential phishing.

MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed

The activity exhibited the following techniques. Microsoft did not map credential capture, malware execution, command and control, or data exfiltration because the available evidence did not directly demonstrate those actions.

Initial Access

  • T1566.002 Phishing: Spearphishing Link | Messages contained a “RESTORE MESSAGES” link that used tracked redirect URLs and led to a non-Microsoft destination.

Defense Evasion

  • T1036 Masquerading | Messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service-health communications and used Microsoft product names and copyright language.

Execution

  • T1204.001 User Execution: Malicious Link | Recipients were urged to select a link within 24 hours to prevent the alleged deletion of held messages.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

item.title: 16th November – Threat Intelligence Report
item.description:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 16th November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.  TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES TSMC, a major Taiwanese semiconductor manufacturer, has confirmed a data breach at an unnamed cloud provider that exposed information about current and former employees. A hacker advertised 6.9 GB of allegedly stolen […]

The post 16th November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 16th November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin. 

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

  • TSMC, a major Taiwanese semiconductor manufacturer, has confirmed a data breach at an unnamed cloud provider that exposed information about current and former employees. A hacker advertised 6.9 GB of allegedly stolen employee data on a cybercrime forum. According to the company, TSMC’s own systems and customer data were unaffected.
  • Danish shipping and logistics giant Maersk confirmed unauthorized access and data theft from a legacy system inherited through an acquisition. The WhiteArmor extortion group claimed to have stolen approximately 100GB of information and demanded $5 million. Maersk stated that its other systems and customer operations remained unaffected.
  • Japan’s Osaka city government disclosed a data breach exposing more than one million email addresses after attackers compromised a third-party email distribution service. The November 2 attack affected nearly 400 customers of the provider, exposing approximately 77 million addresses and enabling the distribution of fraudulent emails.
  • ConnectWise, a US-based IT management software provider, disclosed attacks targeting its ScreenConnect remote access platform. Attackers compromised managed service provider environments and deployed malicious remote access tools on at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations. The campaign may have involved the abuse of third-party extensions.

AI THREATS

  • Researchers analyzed a suspected AI-assisted intrusion targeting a US retailer. After security tools blocked the attacker’s initial commands, the intruder switched to apparently AI-generated scripts. The attacker extracted credentials from SolarWinds Orion monitoring software configuration files and accessed another server within minutes, demonstrating rapid adaptation during the intrusion.
  • Researchers revealed an autonomous intrusion campaign in which attackers used DeepSeek and Zhipu GLM AI agents against at least 19 organizations during 25 operations. The campaign compromised 10 targets, including semiconductor, defense, and civil-society organizations, exposing credentials and sensitive information, including more than one million personal records.
  • Researchers uncovered an exposed server belonging to Silent Lynx, a cyberespionage group targeting Central Asian governments. The attackers used a DeepSeek-powered AI agent to automate reconnaissance, data collection, and evidence removal. Compromised systems included Tajikistan’s railway network and government document infrastructure containing thousands of sensitive files.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

  • Check Point Research has traced attacks exploiting PHP2Shell through the Mobile Access portals of unpatched Check Point Security Gateways. Attackers then exploited CVE-2026-123039 to escalate privileges, achieved persistence, and in some cases wiped a VMware ESXi host. The first wave of attacks targeted Israeli organizations before expanding worldwide, and the tooling shows similarities to China-linked malware.
  • Microsoft released November security updates fixing more than 1,000 vulnerabilities, including an actively exploited Outlook flaw, CVE-2026-124194, that can expose authentication data and enable user impersonation. The release also fixes 48 critical code-execution flaws, including CVE-2026-116928, which could let malicious email attachments run code without being opened.
  • Google patched CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity vulnerability affecting Chrome’s XML processing component that has been exploited in active attacks. The November security update addresses nine vulnerabilities across supported platforms, including Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android. The fixes address security weaknesses that could enable code execution or bypass existing protections.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (Google Chrome Use After Free (CVE-2026-125350))

  • Apache has fixed CVE-2026-119618, a critical vulnerability affecting HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when HTTP/2 is enabled. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely. Successful exploitation could compromise vulnerable servers. Version 2.4.71 addresses the issue.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

  • Check Point Research has identified cyberespionage campaigns linked to CopperDragon, a suspected digital quartermaster to China-nexus threat actors. The campaigns targeted government, military, telecom, and critical infrastructure organizations worldwide. Attackers compromised internet-facing systems and legitimate websites to distribute backdoors and steal sensitive information.
  • Check Point Research has published its October 2026 threat landscape. Organizations faced an average of 2,550 weekly attacks, down 9% from September but up 32% year over year, while one in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage. Ransomware reached a record of 1,063 reported
  • Check Point Research has summarized the activity of Shahid Kaveh, an IRGC-affiliated cyber unit that France blamed for the October sabotage of refrigeration controllers at around 700 retail sites, causing widespread food losses and fires. The unit operates the CyberAv3ngers persona.
  • Researchers analyzed Russia-linked Turla’s Cereal toolset, a cyberespionage platform discovered on compromised government Microsoft Exchange servers in Kazakhstan and Romania. The malware enables operators to extract emails, credentials, and system information. Romanian operations reportedly targeted communications involving NATO and European Union organizations.

The post 16th November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: Usable Security at Luxury Hotels
item.description:
Interesting case study from luxury hotels. Attackers used a fake booking request to gain access to a reservations inbox, where they copied genuine refund requests and got fraudulent ones approved.

This is a good illustration why “just don’t click on links” is bad advice. It can’t work when answering strangers’ emails is the job. Even worse, in this case the guest-first culture punishes hesitation. More interesting, the case study shows that splitting security between owner, operator, and brand leaves nobody accountable. And this is exactly the setting where blaming staff becomes the convenient answer...

item.title: SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions
item.description:
SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy unauthorized remote access and target technicians. Explore the attack chain, mitigations, and Microsoft Defender XDR hunting.

The post SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. ScreenConnect architecture and attack surfaces
  2. Attack chain overview
  3. Mitigation and protection guidance
  4. Indicators of compromise and supporting artifacts
  5. References
  6. Learn More

Beginning on November 11, 2026, ConnectWise reported an active campaign of a threat actor gaining unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect instances belonging to managed service providers (MSPs). Microsoft Threat Intelligence has confirmed ConnectWise’s reported activity and we have also observed threat actors abusing ScreenConnect, a legitimate remote-support application, to install unauthorized remote-access clients and deploy a malicious worm, SCKit, on ConnectWise customer managed endpoints.

Additionally, Microsoft analyzed the malicious worm’s behavior: deployment starts with commands issued through ScreenConnect to silently install an identical client connected to threat actor-controlled infrastructure. A batch launcher retrieves a PowerShell decoder that decrypts and extracts SCKit using device-specific key material. The toolkit establishes persistence through scheduled tasks and registry Run entries and deploys RelayTrap, a component designed to deliver a malicious payload to a connecting technician.

We have identified that the worm targets IT support technician workstations using the hijacked authenticated ScreenConnect Session and uses the victim’s management console to distribute payloads to other managed devices. The resulting access to either target enables threat actors to remotely administer affected endpoints, execute commands, and deploy further tools independently of the legitimate support instance.

Defenders should investigate technician workstations and downstream affected endpoints. Removing an unauthorized client alone does not remove the toolkit’s persistence or invalidate exposed web sessions. In this blog, we examine SCKit’s attack chain and payload components and provide mitigation guidance, indicators of compromise, and Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting queries to help organizations identify and disrupt this activity.

ScreenConnect architecture and attack surfaces

ScreenConnect, formerly ConnectWise Control, is a remote-support and access platform used by MSPs to administer customer devices, often alongside remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Its operating model has three parts:

  • Management instance. A cloud-hosted or on-premises ScreenConnect server provides the web console and manages sessions. Its relay service carries communication between the technician and endpoint clients.
  • Technician workstation. Support staff sign in to the console through a browser and launch a local host client for interactive support.
  • Customer endpoint. An installed guest, or access, client maintains unattended access and executes commands delivered through ScreenConnect.

An Access session provides persistent, unattended access through the installed client. A Support session is a temporary connection that an end user joins for assistance. ScreenConnect also supports remote commands from the web console without an interactive technician session. The endpoint client receives the command and runs it on the customer device; the technician workstation is not an intermediary for that execution.

Reported server-side entry through extensions

Extensions are add-ons installed on the ScreenConnect server to add features or integrate with other products, including ticketing and RMM tools. ConnectWise Automate was formerly named LabTech; Labtech Plus is a third-party extension, not the Automate product itself. The RMM+ extension family exposes remote-command APIs protected by a separately configured passphrase rather than the technician’s normal console sign-in.

ConnectWise’s advisory describes a reported authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32: when no access key was configured, the extension accepted an empty key. In that configuration, an unauthorized caller could submit commands to the server’s API for delivery to managed endpoints without a normal ScreenConnect user sign-in. ConnectWise is investigating extension abuse as an initial-access route; the entry method for the reported campaign remains under investigation.

A separate path from customer endpoints to technicians

SCKit is a malware toolkit that includes RelayTrap, a malicious replacement for the ScreenConnect client on an affected customer endpoint. RelayTrap is designed to deliver a payload to a technician’s workstation when they connect for support. ConnectWise states that the fix for CVE-2026-84869 blocks the toolkit’s attempted endpoint-to-technician spread. This client-side attack path is separate from the server-side access used to deploy SCKit.

Attack chain overview

The deployment sequence below runs on the customer endpoint. It establishes a separate remote-access connection and prepares the scripts and RelayTrap component that target a later technician

1. ScreenConnect commands install an additional client

The threat actor uses the MSP’s ScreenConnect management instance to direct the installed endpoint client to start cmd.exe. That local process invokes curl.exe to download an MSI over HTTP from an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect server. The command requests /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi with access-session parameters and a c=Exploited<N> marker (c=Exploited9 in the illustrated command), and saves the installer to C:\Windows\Temp\sc.msi.

Windows Installer then installs the package silently on that endpoint, without restarting it, using /i, /qn, and /norestart. The added client connects to an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect instance, creating a remote-access channel separate from the MSP’s approved instance. Securing access to the legitimate console does not remove this additional client or its connection.

2. A batch launcher retrieves the PowerShell decoder

Further commands on the customer endpoint stage the toolkit. A PowerShell command decodes a URL-safe Base64 string and writes the result to a batch file in Windows Temp. The batch sets BATPATH to its own location, downloads the decoder from ns[.]mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4, and starts it with -Mode full.

The decoder reads BATPATH, or falls back to SCKIT_SELF, to locate the launcher. Its hidden-relaunch branch creates a VBScript wrapper and runs it through wscript.exe to start the same batch without a visible window.

The scripts use the following p values at the same server path to request individual components:

3. The decoder decrypts and extracts the SCKit bundle

The decoder reads MachineGuid from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography and includes it as the m request parameter. The response provides a Base64-encoded body and two headers, X-Lab-Half and X-Lab-Salt.

To derive the decryption key, the decoder hashes the UTF-8 machine identifier with SHA-256, XORs that hash with 32 bytes decoded from X-Lab-Half, and appends the machine-identifier bytes to the recovered secret material. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 then derives a 32-byte key using the response salt and 4,096 iterations.

The decoder uses the first 16 bytes of the decoded response body as the initialization vector (IV). It decrypts the remaining bytes using AES-256-CBC with PKCS7 padding, decompresses the plaintext with GZip, and writes the resulting ZIP archive. The archive is then extracted to %TEMP%\SCKitBundle.

In full mode, the decoder prepares %TEMP%\SCKit\trapkit\payload and stages the watcher, installer, alert script, and RelayTrap.cs. It also copies its batch launcher into the payload directory for RelayTrap to distribute. The copied launcher retrieves the decoder and starts toolkit deployment.

The decoder also stages ToolboxRelayUploader.exe for console-based payload distribution and retrieves sqlite3.exe for browser-cookie queries if a suitable copy is absent. It includes two launch paths: full mode starts the distribution script without a separate configuration file and supplies a local script path; the other path stages a helper and lab-context.json and passes -SkipLocalExecution.

4. Additional component: PowerShell script loader

Alongside the bundle decoder, SCKit includes a separate loader for encrypted PowerShell scripts. Unlike the decoder, which retrieves and expands an archive, this component requests a script using p=1 with the machine identifier. It applies the same secret-recovery, PBKDF2, AES-CBC, and GZip operations, but uses a salt embedded in its source rather than one supplied in a response header.

After decompression, the loader converts the bytes to UTF-8 text and writes %TEMP%\k<32-hex>.ps1, using a newly generated random GUID for the filename. It starts a hidden PowerShell process to run the file with the forwarded arguments, then attempts to remove the script after the child process exits.

5. RelayTrap adds persistence and targets connecting technicians

On the customer endpoint, persistence keeps the toolkit available for a later support connection. The deployment places scripts under C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap. The RelayTrapLiteAlert value in the machine-wide CurrentVersion\Run key launches an alert script at user logon. A scheduled task starts the watcher with a payload filename and lists of client identifiers and relay hosts to exclude. The -PollSeconds 10 argument configures the watcher to poll every 10 seconds.

The watcher enumerates ScreenConnect client services and reads their executable paths and connection parameters. For each client, its build routine creates a directory under trapbins, copies libraries from that client’s installation, and uses the .NET C# compiler to build RelayTrap.exe. It checks for changes to the source or client libraries before rebuilding.

RelayTrap is designed to reuse the customer endpoint’s ScreenConnect connection details in place of its normal client. When a technician connects with a vulnerable host client, RelayTrap attempts to deliver the staged batch launcher through that session. The launcher retrieves the same decoder, extending the toolkit’s deployment design from the customer device to the technician workstation. Configured skip lists exclude specified client identifiers and relay hosts from processing.

ScreenConnect services are also configured for automatic startup. Registry writes target Microsoft Defender Antivirus path exclusions for staged MSI copies and CWInstall_…\Installer.ps1. The installer configuration lists sc[.]payproofkit[.]com and cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com as additional ScreenConnect MSI sources. A subsequent curl.exe command downloads another client installer from sc[.]payproofkit[.]com.

6. Browser access targets authenticated ScreenConnect sessions

SCKit also targets the technician’s browser, which is used to sign in to the management console. The browser-access code searches Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Opera GX profiles for cookies named .ASPXAUTH. Its database route identifies associated hosts and queries encrypted cookie values. It copies cookie databases and their supporting files, with a volume-shadow-copy fallback for locked databases. The decryption code uses the Chromium master key and the Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI) in the current user’s context, with AES-GCM routines for v10 and v11 cookie values.

The memory-scanning route first examines browser network-service processes identified by network.mojom.NetworkService in their command lines. An embedded C# scanner uses OpenProcess, VirtualQueryEx, and ReadProcessMemory to inspect readable committed memory regions for cookie strings and nearby host strings. If the initial scan finds no candidates, it scans other browser processes.

The console-distribution component is designed to combine an authentication cookie with the required anti-forgery and access tokens, enumerate accessible sessions, upload a payload using ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, and queue execution through the Shared Toolbox. The workflow also includes removing the uploaded Toolbox item after distribution.

This component targets the technician’s management-console access, rather than only the original customer device. The account’s permissions determine which additional sessions and devices the distribution workflow can reach.

7. Cleanup and redeployment

The toolkit’s cleanup script places a stop marker in the trap directory. It removes trap-related tasks, services, processes, Run entries, and files, and restores ScreenConnect client services unless client removal was requested. It then removes any remaining stop marker to allow a newly deployed watcher to run.

After running the cleanup script, the decoder’s cleanup mode starts the bundled dropper again unless -NoReArm is set. Cleanup therefore also serves as a path to redeploy the toolkit.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Secure ScreenConnect administration and technician clients

Address the server-side extension APIs and technician clients separately. Extension authentication and client-side file transfer are different attack surfaces; securing one does not remove the other or an existing endpoint installation.

  • Keep the identified extensions disabled. Follow the vendor advisory for Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link. Review their installation and configuration history alongside administrative access.
  • Update technician clients separately from the console. ConnectWise states that ScreenConnect client 26.6.5 and later block the toolkit’s attempted endpoint-to-technician transfer technique. The fix for CVE-2026-84869 was released on September 8, 2026. Verify each technician client’s installed version; a cloud-console update does not automatically update those clients. The vendor bulletin also describes temporary file-transfer restrictions while updates are pending.

Remove established access

  • Investigate through a separate channel. Use Microsoft Defender for Endpoint live response or another approved out-of-band method instead of ScreenConnect on a suspected affected device. Isolate affected endpoints and include connecting technician workstations in scope.
  • Preserve console and endpoint evidence. Retain extension, authentication, Run Command, and Toolbox records together with process, file, task, and registry history. Review Toolbox history for tools removed after use, and inspect queued commands and tools before reconnecting devices.
  • Revoke exposed sessions from a clean device. Invalidate affected ScreenConnect web sessions and associated identity-provider sessions, rotate exposed credentials, and review accounts and permissions. Password changes alone do not address every existing session.
  • Remove persistence and unapproved clients. Validate each client’s enrolled instance and relay destination before removing it. Remove malicious tasks, Run values, trap files, and unauthorized exclusions through approved response tooling. Do not use a cleanup script recovered from the kit as a remediation tool.
  • Verify the complete state before restoring connectivity. Confirm approved services and destinations, effective antivirus settings, and the absence of re-created tasks or scripts. Review tamper-protection events when investigating exclusion changes. Rebuild devices when integrity cannot be established.

Keep Microsoft Defender Antivirus, cloud-delivered protection, and tamper protection enabled. Verify that devices meet the requirements for protecting antivirus exclusions. Maintain an inventory of authorized remote-management instances and use application control to restrict unapproved software.

Microsoft Defender XDR detections

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following Microsoft Defender for Endpoint alert titles to investigate activity associated with this threat. Review related alerts together with device timelines and ScreenConnect audit records to trace command execution, persistence, browser-data access, and network connections.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics report to get the latest intelligence on SCKit and the abuse of ScreenConnect, including protection status, affected assets, and recommended actions for their environment.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics and Secure Now

Customers can access the threat analytics report: SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions

Customers can also access recommended controls and guidance on Secure Now.

Advanced hunting queries

Each query below runs independently and uses a 14-day lookback. Adjust the time range to the investigation window and available retention, and correlate results with approved administrative activity.

Connections to campaign infrastructure

Find connections to the listed domains and IP addresses. Review the full destination, initiating process, and approved remote-support infrastructure for each match.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (
    "ns.mo7sen.dev", "sc.payproofkit.com",
    "newnewnew.gotdns.org", "soxnewwork.homedns.org",
    "cdn007-digitaldownloads.com")
    or RemoteIP in ("185.99.255.28", "155.94.150.39")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ReportId

Toolkit command lines and cookie-query activity

Find command lines containing distinctive toolkit names, staging paths, installer markers, or cookie-query strings.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "/EadF.php"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "SCKit"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "RelayTrap"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "Panel-Lateral"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "ToolboxRelayUploader"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains ".ASPXAUTH"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "c=Exploited"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Known installer, archive, and uploader files

Find file events for the sc.msi package, staged ZIP, and uploader using their SHA-1 hashes. The query uses SHA-1 because SHA256 is usually unpopulated in DeviceFileEvents. Combine hash matches with command-line and persistence findings.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where SHA1 in~ (
    "0be01e7bd69cfdd222645d49bb5ad9961372fef2",
    "3f81c9c874a896c46e4bccea2fad2eaa3d9f2054",
    "13ce33b19daee3963f7e15d461b191c38f6bc0d3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
    SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Registry values referencing RelayTrap

Find writes to the RelayTrapLiteAlert value or values containing RelayTrap. Review the registry key, value data, and initiating process.

DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "RelayTrapLiteAlert"
    or RegistryValueData contains "RelayTrap"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RegistryKey,
    RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

RelayTrap scheduled-task events

Find scheduled-task events containing RelayTrap or TrapWatch. Inspect the task definition to identify its triggers, executable, and arguments.

DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType contains "ScheduledTask"
| where AdditionalFields contains "RelayTrap"
    or AdditionalFields contains "TrapWatch"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType,
    AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

Microsoft Defender Antivirus path-exclusion writes

Find Microsoft Defender Antivirus path-exclusion registry writes. Review changes naming Windows Temp, ConnectWiseControl_, CWInstall_, or RelayTrap, and verify their authorization and effective policy.

DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey contains @"\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RegistryKey,
    RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, ReportId

SCKit – Generated PowerShell Loader Artifacts

Identifies temporary PowerShell files matching the k<32-hex>.ps1 naming pattern generated by the SCKit loader, potentially revealing staged payloads independently of known file hashes or infrastructure.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^k[0-9a-f]{32}\.ps1$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName,
ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
InitiatingProcessFileName

Indicators of compromise and supporting artifacts

Network addresses are defanged. Use the installer hashes to locate the listed packages, then verify the client’s enrolled ScreenConnect instance and related activity. The toolkit also uses the legitimate SQLite utility; investigate its use alongside the browser-cookie queries described above.

Network infrastructure

File hashes

Hashes identify individual files. The watcher compiles RelayTrap against local client libraries, and embedded configuration changes script hashes. Use file and process behavior to investigate other builds. The table includes configuration, cleanup, and proof artifacts to support the investigation.

Client identifiers and behavioral artifacts

References

  • ConnectWise security investigation and partner guidance (advisory covering the RMM+ extension authentication flaw). ConnectWise (accessed 2026-11-13)
  • ScreenConnect security bulletin, 2026-09-08 (CVE-2026-84869 fix and client 26.6.5 guidance). ConnectWise (accessed 2026-11-13)
  • ScreenConnect extensions. ConnectWise (accessed 2026-11-13)
  • 6 tips for ConnectWise Control partners (remote commands from the web console). ConnectWise (accessed 2026-11-13)
  • Requirements for protecting antivirus exclusions with tamper protection. Microsoft Learn (accessed 2026-11-13)
  • Investigate entities on devices using live response. Microsoft Learn (accessed 2026-11-13)
  • Take response actions on a device. Microsoft Learn (accessed 2026-11-13)
  • Advanced hunting best practices in Microsoft Defender XDR. Microsoft Learn (accessed 2026-11-13)
  • DeviceFileEvents table (advanced hunting schema). Microsoft Learn (accessed 2026-11-13)

item.title: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
item.description: AI-orchestrated penetration testing platforms like ARTEX have become increasingly powerful tools enabling effective attacks on exposed infrastructure. Here we share Cloudflare’s observations and recommended countermeasures.
item.content:encoded:
Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks.

ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese.) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment.

We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars:

  • Fortify the front gate: Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with advanced rules such as rate limits.
  • Security station in the foyer: Anomaly detection on all web applications your customers access.
  • Identify phony visitors: Implement Bot Defense.
  • Remove the back door: Implement Identity-Gated Access for all high-risk external and internal web applications.
  • Inspect deliveries: Enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls.
  • Neighborhood watch: Implement Threat Intelligence to gain visibility into attacks.

What is an LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrator?

Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. These tools turn compromises into a hill-climbable problem, which agents are specifically good at.

The AI LLM pentesting tools that currently exist

We are currently tracking 50+ AI LLM agents. The table below shows the top five LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrators. Each is extremely popular (1k+ GitHub stars) and fully autonomous. The fully autonomous nature of these agents represents a doctrinal shift in offensive cyber capabilities:

  • Human skills are no longer the limit: A harness performs every step of the OODA loop by observing the environment, orienting itself to prioritize valuable and/or vulnerable targets, decide on an action, and act autonomously.
  • Speed increase: Having multiple parallel agents working towards a goal is a large shift compared to single operator or multiple operator augmented by AI.
  • Scale: A single operator can target multiple organizations at the same time, greatly increasing their blast radius.
  • Small mistakes are easily discovered: Autonomous frameworks relentlessly and systematically test exposed services, including their configurations.

Architecture

Planning model

Built-in capabilities/execution environment

Post-exploitation capabilities

ARTEX (and forks)

Planner and parallel agents

Graph of goals, leads, and findings is linked to separate asset graph of target

Directly on host or container with network/root access, can install/develop tools as needed

Nothing built-in, requires user instruction

LuaN1aoAgent

Supervisor agent, planner agent, and generic executor agents

Three graphs, with goals/tasks/blockers, evidence/hypothesises/exploits, and target/local

Container with network/user access, can develop tools as needed and install user packages

Built-in SSH and Chisel for tunneling and attempted reconnection after disruption

Decepticon

Orchestrator agent dispatching specialist sub-agents

Graph of objectives with prerequisites

Kali container running as root, can develop tools as needed

Dedicated post-access, Active Directory and cloud pivoting skills

Cairn

Dispatcher orchestrating work to existing AI harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi)

Graph of facts and leads; new nodes trigger dispatcher

Kali container with root access or directly on host, can develop tools as needed

Prompt guidance and Kali tools

PentestGPT-Agent

Supervisor agent and one generic executor agent

Task list with dependencies, goals, and evidence

Run on host, can develop tools as needed

Nothing built-in, requires user instruction

Observations from the world's largest network

As of November 12, ARTEX and its forks make up over 60% of currently known AI penetration testing orchestrators. The charts below help us understand how adoption of these tools has changed over the past six weeks. Since the removal of the original ARTEX repository on October 8, traffic has grown more than tenfold, and has increased more than 30x since October 1.

As demonstrated above, the takedown of ARTEX on October 8 (and widespread reporting of it) likely caused a hydra effect, where the removal of the original repository led to a massive increase in the number of forks and modifications which can be seen in the steep acceleration of unique instances around October 8.

Identity-chained LLM exploitation

Over the last eight weeks, our Cloudforce One team has been called into multiple incident response investigations involving ARTEX and ARTEX-derived LLM exploitation frameworks. We’ve seen firsthand how exposed credentials are being chained with LLM-based exploitation frameworks to gain the upper hand over defenders.
We observed multiple incidents in which a threat actor gained initial access to a hyperscaler environment and pivoted directly into the customer's Cloudflare environment. Root-cause analysis revealed a common credential hygiene failure. Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure. LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments.

ARTEX in action

As part of one incident response investigation, our team observed ARTEX gaining access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. Available evidence indicated that the compromise most likely originated through a third-party hyperscaler.

We observed that a large number of new Worker scripts had been created with distinct names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-*, and artex-do-*. The naming of each Worker script correlated to distinct behaviors and actions it was taking, and was often postfixed by an alphanumeric identifier. We observed activity in excess of 69 requests per minute across multiple unique parts of their Cloudflare infrastructure and 400 database dump requests in an hour. We also observed attempted persistence mechanisms and attempts to validate session tokens for other third-party applications. While we believe that much of this activity was lightly guided by the human operator, this is just one example of the speed and breadth that ARTEX and similar frameworks can achieve post-compromise.

Our recommendation: the Modern Security Model

Large Language Models increase the ability of a threat actor to rapidly iterate through the Cyber Kill Chain against a target. They do this by giving the actor the advantage of speed and validation. Each step of the Cyber Kill Chain can be validated and fed into the next stage of the attack. This level of orchestration is unparalleled and effectively vaporizes legacy cyber security models. A modern model must be used against these attacks.

To help explain this model further, let’s use the metaphor of protecting a house on an estate. Each section below outlines how to defend against the threat at each step.

Fortify the front gate: implement traffic control and a WAF with advanced rules

Before anyone even sets foot on your lawn, they have to reach the perimeter fence.

On an unprotected estate, an adversary can drive an endless fleet of decoy trucks straight into your driveway, completely blocking the entrance and smashing through the barriers (Layer 3/4 volumetric floods and direct IP probing).

With perimeter gate security in place, all incoming traffic is routed through massive, distributed outer gates miles away from the main house. Rogue delivery trucks are filtered out to the highway, rogue utility tunnels trying to wiretap your property are severed, and only legitimate foot traffic ever reaches your home address.

Network traffic control serves as an important role in stopping volumetric attacks.

A security station in the foyer: anomaly detection

Once visitors arrive at the main entry, they meet a strict security station at the foyer.

Automated prowlers don't just kick the door; they disguise themselves. They attempt weird ways to get in the door — stuffing paper into the lock, trying variations like //front-door//back-room/ to trick the mechanism into swinging open.

The security guard at the door enforces clear rules:

  • You cannot knock 500 times in five seconds.
  • You cannot disguise your path with trickery.
  • You cannot attempt to roll a massive flatbed cart through the front hall to haul away the house's internal blueprints (diagnostic heap dumps). Suspicious behavior is turned away immediately.
  • Implement security keys and hardware based FIDO keys.

Web Application Firewall (WAF) serves as a key defense mechanism in stopping application exploitation through rate limits and anomaly detection.

Identify phony visitors: implement Bot Defense

A sophisticated intruder rarely looks like a masked burglar; they disguise themselves as ordinary visitors. But automated agents, headless browser scrapers, and AI reconnaissance tools don't act like real people.

They don't blink, their posture is unnervingly rigid, their cadence is mechanical, and their "identification" is often a sloppy imitation of a real visitor badge.

Bot Defense and challenges act as behavioral specialists watching the crowd through one-way glass. It flags the unnatural cadence, catches the synthetic micro-behaviors, and quietly escorts the machines off the property before they can touch a single doorknob.

Remove the back door: implement Identity-Gated Access and micro-segmentation

Many homes historically were built with side doors or a cellar hatch (internal admin panels, /actuator diagnostic endpoints, and remote gateways). Even if locked, a prowler could stand on the sidewalk, shine a flashlight on the cellar door, and start picking the lock.

Zero Trust application access does something radical: it bricks up the doorway from the outside and restricts which rooms can be entered.

To anyone wandering the perimeter, the cellar door does not exist. There is no lock to pick, no handle to rattle, and no light on inside. The only way in is with an escort who checks your biometric badge, confirms your device has a clean bill of health, and steps you directly into the specific room you need — leaving the rest of the house out of view.

For those who do enter, you have to ensure they cannot breach rooms next to the room they enter. Micro-segmentation is a highly effective strategy at stopping lateral movement. It limits compromised credentials from breaching production, test, and development systems.

Inspect deliveries: enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls

You receive daily supply deliveries to your estate — groceries, mail, maintenance parts. In digital terms, this is your incoming API traffic, which must be inspected and verified.

Intruders often attempt to bypass controls by sending unvalidated payloads or forged delivery manifests meant for restricted internal systems.

The porch protocol mandates thorough inspection and schema validation for all traffic:

  • Every incoming request must undergo OpenAPI schema validation to ensure it strictly conforms to expected definitions and structures.
  • Drivers and couriers must present validated mutual TLS (mTLS) certificates to establish trusted, authenticated connections.
  • Any request failing inspection or missing valid credentials is rejected immediately at the boundary.
  • Default-Deny Posture: Every positive security implementation ends with an explicit deny-all rule at the bottom of the ruleset.

Neighborhood watch: implement threat intelligence to gain visibility into attacks

Even with ironclad walls, an isolated property can be vulnerable if a syndicate invents a brand-new infiltration technique across town.

Threat intelligence acts as your warning network with neighboring estates. When a rogue actor sets up a new command-and-control safehouse down the road or begins deploying dynamic tunneling vans in your district, you receive an early dossier. Your estate updates its watchlists, recalibrates its sensors, and slams the gate shut before the actor ever turns onto your street.

How to get real-time help

ARTEX and similar LLM-based frameworks pose a significant challenge to legacy cyber defense models. Even the historical defense-in-depth model — which emphasizes a classic network DMZ — falls short in today's complex architectures. Tomorrow's attacks will only advance as orchestration tools become the new normal.

Securing legacy equipment and on-premises devices requires an identity-gated approach that logically makes these devices impossible to reach on the Internet. Beyond identity, slowing or making lateral movement more noisy is the goal of micro-segmentation. This architecture emphasizes a containment-first approach to security, which is essential when users are consistently losing their keys. When combined, the elements of the Modern Security Model are the answer to this vexing problem.

If you are facing an active security incident and need the Cloudforce One team on the ground to help respond to the incident or require threat intelligence support, please contact us immediately. If you need help implementing the Modern Security Model outlined here, please contact our Solutions Engineering team.

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.

I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.

I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code.

AI will hack all sorts of social, economic and political systems. It will find vulnerabilities and exploit them. This is a difference in kind, not just degree. We’re not ready for it, and we need to think about the implications now.

First, I want to broaden the term “hacking.”

The tax code isn’t computer code, but it is code. It’s a series of algorithms with inputs and outputs. It has vulnerabilities, which we call loopholes, and exploits, which we call tax avoidance strategies. Black hat hackers exploit them for profit. We call them accountants and attorneys.

What is a hack? One definition: “Something that a system permits, but is unanticipated and unwanted by the designers.” It’s subjective and implies novelty and cleverness. A hack follows the rules of a system but subverts its goals or intent, just as a software hack follows the logic of code while doing something its authors neither anticipated nor wanted.

All systems of rules can be hacked, including professional sports, customer reward programs, financial systems and politics. Hacks even work against our cognitive functions. A curved hockey stick is a hack, and we know the name of the man who invented it. Mileage runs were a hack. The filibuster was originally a hack in Roman times. Gerrymandering is a hack. Hedge funds and private equity are full of them.

A system is just a set of rules or norms, and the rules aren’t always formal. Even the best-designed rules will be incomplete, inconsistent or ambiguous. As long as people want to subvert a system’s goals, there will be hacks.

AIs are becoming hackers. After decades of slow progress, they’ve gotten very good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in computer code. They do this largely autonomously, and they’re getting better scarily fast. But the implications extend far beyond software, to the tax code, financial regulations and all sorts of social, economic and political systems.

There are two distinct issues. First, someone might instruct an AI to hack one of these systems, feeding it the world’s tax codes or financial regulations to find profitable loopholes. Second, an AI might hack a system on its own, inadvertently. Both are dangerous, but the second is worse because we might never know it happened.

Now, reward hacking. AIs don’t solve problems the way people do. They stumble on solutions we never anticipated, and some subvert the intent of the system. They don’t share our context and don’t necessarily understand the implications, norms and values we take for granted.

Reward hacking is when an AI achieves a goal in a way its designers neither wanted nor intended.

Early pre-LLM examples are telling. In a two-person soccer simulation, an AI learned that kicking the ball out of bounds forced the opposing goalie to throw it in and leave the goal undefended. In a stacking simulation, an AI learned to flip a block upside down rather than stack it. In an evolution simulation where the goal was to cross a distant finish line, an AI made itself tall enough to fall over the line instead of growing longer legs or stronger muscles.

These are all hacks, the result of poorly specified goals or rewards. Today, they’d come from bad prompting.

The problem is universal. One researcher tried to teach a robot vacuum not to bump into things. Instead, it learned to drive backward, because there were no sensors in the back.

Any capable AI will find hacks wherever the rules have problems, inconsistencies or loopholes that still produce an acceptable solution. We see a hack because we understand context. The AI doesn’t, at least not in the same way.

This problem shows up often in myth.

In the story of King Midas, the god Dionysus grants him a wish: everything he touches turns to gold. Midas ends up starving when his food, drink and daughter all turn to gold. It’s a specification problem. He programmed the wrong goal.

In the Golem of Prague, a ghetto animates a clay statue to guard its residents. It guards them past all reason until they figure out how to turn it off. This is a guardrail problem. The villagers never limited the golem’s actions.

More generally, think of this as the genie problem. Genies are precise about the wording of wishes and can be maliciously pedantic when granting them. There’s no way to outsmart a genie. Whatever you wish for, he can grant it in a way you wish he hadn’t.

The reason is that in human language and thought, goals are always underspecified. We never include every caveat, exception and proviso, and we never close off every avenue for hacking. Any goal we specify will be incomplete. That’s largely fine in human interactions, because people understand context and usually act in good faith.

If I asked you to get me coffee, you’d pour a cup from the nearest coffee pot or walk to the corner shop. You wouldn’t bring me a pound of raw beans, buy a coffee plantation or snatch a cup from a stranger’s hands. I wouldn’t have to specify any of that. You’d just know.

Similarly, if I asked you to develop a technology that turns things to gold on touch, you wouldn’t build it to starve the person using it. You’d just know.

In 2015, Volkswagen was caught cheating on emissions tests. Human engineers programmed a regular computer to detect testing and behave differently during it. The cheat went undetected for years because it’s hard to tell what software is doing.

If I asked you to design engine control software that maximizes performance while passing emissions tests, you wouldn’t design it to cheat without realizing you were cheating. An AI would, because it will think “outside the box” when it has no concept of the box.

Unless programmers specify that the system must not behave differently during testing, an AI might come up with the same hack. The programmers would be satisfied, the accountants would be ecstatic, and no one would know until someone audited the code.

We can now constrain the goal to avoid that particular hack, but programmers won’t anticipate others. The lesson of the genie is that there will always be hacks programmers don’t anticipate.

We’re building AI genies: systems that take broad instructions and figure out how to carry them out, sometimes in ways we didn’t expect or intend. That’s the whole point of vibe coding. You underspecify what you want and let the AI work it out. Sometimes that produces genie behavior.

We can’t completely specify goals to an AI, and AIs can’t fully understand context. More precisely, current AIs have a shallow grasp of concepts. If we asked a current LLM to get me coffee, it would almost certainly do the right thing.

I worry about goals that aren’t well represented in training data, and about hacks that aren’t obvious, whose effects are subtle, like the Volkswagen hack.

Recommendation engines are an early example. They push people toward extreme content. No one programmed that. It emerged because that’s what people respond to. It didn’t take a bad actor. A basic automated system with feedback found the hack on its own.

We’re now seeing a second generation with today’s AI coding systems. AI researcher Simon Willison asked Fable to track down a stray scrollbar in a web app. When he returned, it had opened browsers, written its own screenshot tools, edited the framework’s internal templates to make the bug appear on cue and set up a local web server to collect measurements. It found the bug, but it also did many things he never asked for. Another researcher gave Fable a complex task, and it tried to hack its own memory limits because it needed more storage.

A new OpenAI model did something similar when it hacked into Hugging Face. It was being benchmarked on its ability to turn vulnerabilities into exploits. It decided the best way to reach its goal was to break out of its containment, access the internet and break into the Hugging Face network, because it thought the answers would be there.

Today’s LLMs are acting like genies, especially when powerful models are combined with sophisticated harnesses.

There are two kinds of genies. The Dionysus genie does the wrong thing. It understands your prompt literally but not correctly, and returns a mess you never intended. The Golem genie does the right thing but tramples everything in its path to get there. The paperclip maximizer is a Golem genie.

Consider some examples. Ask an AI to deal with spam calls, and a Dionysus genie might change your phone number. Ask it to book a particular flight, and a Golem genie might hack the airline database because the flight is full. Ask it to get a refund for an online purchase, and a Dionysus genie might draft a legal threat on fake letterhead and send it to the company. Ask it to buy tickets to a popular concert, and a Golem genie might discover the ticketing system is rate-limited and spin up thousands of cloud servers to hammer it. You’d know if some of these things happened, but you might never realize if others did. More detailed prompting won’t fix this. The lesson of the genie is that no amount of detail is good enough.

AI researchers aren’t surprised by any of this. Many are working on defenses against reward hacking and subtler forms of genie behavior. Some of this falls under “value alignment”: How do we teach AIs context? And how an AI satisfies a goal matters as much as whether it does. I want to build a benchmark to measure genie-like behavior, so we know where models stand and whether alignment is improving.

Think beyond LLMs and computer code. Consider specialized AIs built to find loopholes, and hacks of more general systems: the tax code, financial regulations and democratic procedures.

Financial systems are the most likely first target, because their rules are designed to be algorithmically tractable. High-frequency trading is itself a hack. Imagine giving an AI all of the world’s financial laws, plus all the news and financial data, and the goal of finding profitable loopholes. I suspect large investment banks are already doing this. The results will be novel tricks that are legal but unintended and unwanted, some of which might break the financial system.

Tax loopholes are the next likely target, for the same reasons. For a while, AIs will identify potential loopholes, and human hackers, namely attorneys and accountants, will decide which are feasible.

Further out, expect hacks of regulatory, legislative and procedural systems, and of the broader economy.

Hacking is as old as humanity. We’re creative problem solvers and loophole exploiters. We manipulate systems to serve our interests and strive for more influence, power and wealth.

Still, no human pursues their interests without constraint. Even sociopaths are limited by the complexity of society and their own contradictory impulses. They worry about their reputation and punishment, and they have limited time. These human qualities have limited hacking.

Hacking changed as everything became computerized. Computers are uniquely hackable because of their formalism and complexity. Today, nearly everything is a computer, from cars and appliances to phones. Our social, economic and political systems, including taxation, finance and elections, all involve computers.

Until recently, hacking was exclusively a human activity. Finding a novel hack required expertise, creativity, time and luck.

AI hacking will change everything again. AIs aren’t bound by the constraints that limit people. They’ll think like aliens, and they’ll change hacking’s speed, scale, scope and sophistication, sometimes at our direction and sometimes on their own.

Speed is the easiest to see. A creative process that takes a human months or years could be compressed into hours or seconds.

Scale is next. Once AI systems start discovering hacks, they can exploit them at a scale we’re not ready for. We already see this with AI-generated slop, which is rampant on social media. AI bots post around the clock, sometimes overwhelming real human discussion. It’s hard to know how much of social media is still people talking to people. What looks like boisterous political debate may be bots arguing with other bots, artificially shaping what we think and what we think others think.

Scope makes hacks more dangerous. AIs already make decisions that affect our lives, decisions we once thought belonged only to humans. As AI systems grow more capable, society will hand them more decisions, and more important ones. Hacks of these systems will do more damage.

Finally, AI hackers are more sophisticated. They can hold more variables in working memory and generate more complex hacks. What might happen if you fed an AI the entire U.S. tax code? Would it figure out, without being told, that it’s smart to incorporate in Delaware and register a ship in Panama? Consider the Double Dutch Irish Sandwich, the strategy Apple and Google used to avoid paying U.S. taxes. It involves U.S., Dutch and Irish law and an offshore tax haven. How many loopholes will an AI find that we don’t already know about? Dozens? Hundreds? Thousands? We have no idea.

These hacks will largely be perpetrated by the powerful against the rest of us. AI is fundamentally a power-enhancing technology, and so is hacking. The more power you already have, the more a hack gives you. If you or I found a tax hack, we might make a few thousand dollars. If a large investment bank found one, it and its clients could make billions.

Our societal systems for dealing with hacks were built when hackers were human, and they reflect the pace of human hacking. We have no system of governance that can handle hundreds, let alone thousands, of newly discovered tax loopholes. We won’t be able to recover from an AI finding unanticipated but legal hacks of financial systems, operating at AI speed, scale, scope and sophistication. Hacking becomes a problem society can no longer manage.

Now, defense. AIs that find software vulnerabilities help defenders as well as attackers. Vulnerabilities can be patched, removing them permanently, or turned into signatures that security systems use to detect and block attacks. In theory, AI could identify and patch every automatically discoverable vulnerability before a product ships. This is rapidly becoming routine in software development. We call it vulnops. We can imagine a future where accidental software vulnerabilities are a thing of the past.

Deliberate vulnerabilities are different. There will be an arms race. AI will craft increasingly obscure back doors, and AI will find them. It becomes a contest between the speed of creation and the speed of patching, and between obfuscation and reverse engineering.

The same logic applies to broader systems. Yes, AI hackers might find hundreds of vulnerabilities in the existing tax code. But the same technology can evaluate potential loopholes in any proposed tax law or ruling. A legislator, a watchdog group or a reporter could take the text of a bill and identify every exploitable loophole before it passes. The difference is that, unlike software, knowing about a tax loophole doesn’t mean it gets patched. In theory, though, we can fix them before the rich and powerful exploit them. So maybe defense will come out ahead here, too.

That requires resilient governing structures that can respond quickly. It won’t help if updating the tax code takes years, or if a legislative hack becomes so entrenched that it can’t be fixed politically. Maybe a lobbyist put it there on purpose. Maybe it was discovered after the law passed, and now lobbyists want to keep it. Microsoft can patch the vulnerabilities it finds. Patching is much harder when legislatures have to do it. We need society’s rules and laws to be as patchable as our computers.

This is a hard problem of modern governance, and it goes well beyond AI. It’s the problem of building governing structures for the speed and complexity of the information age.

The umbrella idea is trust. What do we need for AI systems to be truly trustworthy? Capability isn’t enough.

AIs won’t be trustworthy if the companies controlling them spy on us or subtly manipulate us. I call this the friend vs. tool problem. Will we have AI agents, or AI double agents?

AIs won’t be trustworthy if they’re insecure. How do we know they haven’t been manipulated? Almost all AIs operate in adversarial environments, so someone will benefit from hacking them. Unless we know they’re secure, we shouldn’t trust their output.

And AIs won’t be trustworthy if they act like genies. We need to know they’ll perform tasks the right way, not just perform the tasks we ask for.

I’ve written extensively about the need for “integrous” AI, including how to think about the problem, what a research agenda looks like and what good laws and policies look like. I predict integrity will be the key security problem of this decade, just as confidentiality was the key problem of the last one. This applies to both AI and the internet of things.

The big shift is agency, which I think of as Web 3.0. Computers now affect the physical world directly and with growing autonomy. Sensors go from data sources to attack surfaces, and actuators go from outputs to attack capabilities. An integrity failure no longer means bad spreadsheet data. It means the wrong dosage, the wrong valve position or the wrong braking distance.

Integrity isn’t one thing. I break it into input integrity, processing integrity, storage integrity and contextual integrity. Each is complex and important, and each deserves its own talk. I’ve written about them, and I hope you’ll read it.

Much of this isn’t really an AI problem. It’s not a technical problem so much as a capitalism problem or a democracy problem.

The failures of late-stage capitalism and democracy in the information age both stem from the rich and powerful getting too good at hacking our social, economic and political systems. This is the core argument of my 2021 book.

Seen this way, AI is exacerbating existing problems. Human inefficiency has largely kept those problems in check, and that won’t work much longer.

So consider this a call to action. Technically, we need to understand how AIs hack systems, build systems that are resilient to hacking and build AIs that won’t act as genies. Politically, we need to learn to govern and regulate at the speed of technology. Otherwise, market failures will overwhelm our ability to govern them.

I said hacking is as old as humanity and that AIs will overwhelm our ability to deal with it. The solutions aren’t specific to AI, but AI makes them more urgent. We need to understand them, and we need to implement them.
