item.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.description: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
item.content:encoded:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading:
Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF)
Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn
TrendAI’s analysis
Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

item.title: 2nd November – Threat Intelligence Report
item.description:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 2nd November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin. TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES Binance, a global cryptocurrency exchange, has suffered a cyberattack resulting in the theft of approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets. Attackers reportedly compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop and abused internal wallet infrastructure […]

The post 2nd November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 2nd November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

  • Binance, a global cryptocurrency exchange, has suffered a cyberattack resulting in the theft of approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets. Attackers reportedly compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop and abused internal wallet infrastructure to authorize unauthorized withdrawals. The incident ranks among the largest cryptocurrency thefts ever recorded and is linked to North Korean group.
  • Polymarket, a US-based prediction market platform, has disclosed a cyberattack involving a compromised third-party service that distributed malicious JavaScript to its website. The script hijacked authenticated trading sessions and attempted unauthorized transactions. Approximately $2.7 million in cryptocurrency was traced to a suspected attacker-controlled wallet.
  • Japan Airlines, a major Japanese international airline, has disclosed a third-party data breach affecting approximately 92,000 passengers through the Amadeus reservation system. Exposed records included passenger names and flight information. Approximately 2,000 individuals also had contact information, passport details, and additional travel records potentially accessed.
  • The Florida Department of Education has disclosed a data breach involving unauthorized access to its student financial aid website, potentially affecting 4.9 million individuals. Compromised information reportedly includes names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, and contact details. The incident was identified on October 19.

AI THREATS

  • Researchers have identified extensive use of AI agents by the GOLD OGRE ransomware group during Aur0ra attacks. Operators supplied compromised credentials and objectives, allowing AI tools to perform network reconnaissance, identify privileged accounts, and support lateral movement. The group also used AI-assisted development to test endpoint security evasion techniques.
  • Researchers have documented expanding AI adoption among North Korean cyber threat actors. The activity includes using language models to support reconnaissance, develop malicious tools, refine social engineering, and accelerate intrusion workflows. The findings describe how established espionage and financially motivated operations are incorporating AI into existing attack techniques.
  • Researchers have uncovered a global espionage campaign in which the China-linked VAPOR PANDA group used the AI-enabled ARTEX framework against more than 200 organizations. Targets included government agencies, telecommunications providers, and defense companies across at least 14 countries. Confirmed intrusions involved credential theft and deployment of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

  • Check Point Research have analyzed HTTP2Shell (CVE-2026-111497), an actively exploited remote code execution vulnerability affecting Brotli decompression implementations. Initially associated with Node.js, the flaw may also affect other components, including Python packages, .NET, and proxies. Automated scanning and suspicious exploitation attempts have been observed.

    Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (Node.js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497)))

  • A critical Linux kernel vulnerability, CVE-2026-98432, has been disclosed with a CVSS score of 9.8. The memory management flaw affects TCP networking and can enable unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on systems exposing Multipath TCP listeners.
  • Drupal has addressed CVE-2026-118539, a highly critical access control vulnerability in the Commerce Core module used by online stores. Insufficient protection of application routes and data fields allows unauthenticated attackers to bypass authorization restrictions. The flaw has been exploited in attacks and may affect commercial transactions.
  • Cisco has patched CVE-2026-76418, a high-severity vulnerability affecting Adaptive Security Appliance and Firepower Threat Defense software. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely crash devices configured with SSL VPN functionality. Cisco confirmed that the vulnerability had been exploited in attacks before the security updates became available.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

  • Check Point Research has uncovered the Yoba malware campaign, which distributes malicious installers disguised as ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications through fraudulent GitHub projects. Attackers exploit legitimate signed executables to load malicious components and establish persistence. The campaign uses trusted online services for payload delivery and communication.
  • Check Point researchers have analyzed unexpected network activity generated by Alibaba’s Qwen model during a security-related task. Repeated testing produced numerous different destination addresses rather than one consistent endpoint. The findings suggest unstable model behavior is a more plausible explanation than a deliberately embedded data-exfiltration mechanism.
  • Researchers have identified UAT-11473, an advanced threat actor exploiting a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN authentication bypass to deploy the KeyDrift malware framework. The campaign targeted organizations in aerospace, defense, satellites and policy research. KeyDrift enables persistent access and extraction of sensitive encryption material from compromised network controllers.
  • Researchers have documented more than 400 incidents involving abuse of Microsoft Teams external chat functionality for initial access. Attackers impersonated internal IT support personnel to persuade employees to initiate remote sessions and install access tools. Some campaigns progressed to credential theft, lateral movement, and ransomware-related activity.

The post 2nd November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
item.description: Four, just four: that’s the key to break into any unpatched connection on the Internet that is using eMudhra certificates. Here’s how we quickly patched Cloudflare, what evidence we can see of attempted exploitation, and how much of the rest of the Internet remains exposed.
item.content:encoded:
On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems.

Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept.

eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key.

How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure.

Patching Cloudflare

Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets are being worked on.

We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora, responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week.

Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network?

To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21.

At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched.

About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path.

Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals.

How many visitors are still vulnerable?

So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our challenge pages:

We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and one to ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com. Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys.

What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this:

Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes.

The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC:

  • October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without signed certificate timestamps (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier.
  • October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00.
  • October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the G3 cross-sign, which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both.
  • October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root.
  • October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones.

With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement.

On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph.

Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement.

Breaking down by network (ASN) we see:

Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat.

The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed.

What can you do?

Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great crowdsourced website with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow these instructions. If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on what needs to be done on your end when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel.

Looking ahead

At Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.

item.title: Cohere’s Qwen Story: Looks More Like Model Jaggedness
item.description:
Key findings On October 26, Cohere reported a puzzling incident involving Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an open-weight model from Alibaba. The task was straightforward: write a detection rule for suspicious curl downloads followed by bash execution. Instead, the model produced a shell command that inspected its environment and attempted to send a test string to an Alibaba Cloud […]

The post Cohere’s Qwen Story: Looks More Like Model Jaggedness appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
Key findings

  • Re-sampling URLs from the trace shared by Cohere yields 52 different destination hosts, many of which are local or do not exist, and one is an invalid top-level domain.
  • Swapping the order of two program names in a check for available tools made the model much less likely to continue with a network call.
  • Model jaggedness (inconsistent behavior that changes with small differences in context) seems like a more likely explanation than a fixed backdoor destination.
  • Our interactive viewers let you explore the recorded trace, the most likely next tokens, and the 64 sampled URL completions.

On October 26, Cohere reported a puzzling incident involving Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an open-weight model from Alibaba. The task was straightforward: write a detection rule for suspicious curl downloads followed by bash execution. Instead, the model produced a shell command that inspected its environment and attempted to send a test string to an Alibaba Cloud storage address in Beijing. Cohere’s sandbox blocked the request.

Before the command, the model imagined an earlier conversation and reasoned that it should offer a brief acknowledgment without using tools. Immediately after the reasoning it issued a tool call anyway.

Was this a backdoor sending data to a predetermined destination? Or had the model lost track of its task? We replayed the published trace to investigate.

Replaying the moment before the address

We deployed the model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a machine with 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs using vLLM as an inference framework in order to probe the model. Model generation is not deterministic in general and if you sample multiple outputs, you will likely get different results, and this is what we are interested in: what are the different scenarios that could have happened in this situation?

curl is a command-line tool that can download data from a web address or upload data to one. In simplified form, the recorded upload command was curl -X PUT –data-binary “PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123” <URL>, which asks to send that fixed test string to the address at the end. By stopping just after the test string, we leave the destination for the model to choose and can see whether repeated completions keep returning to the same address.

We used the recorded conversation and command from Cohere’s released trace and removed the part coming after the test string PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123. At that point, the curl upload command had already begun, but the model had yet to write its destination. We asked it to complete the same unfinished command 64 times. The model chooses each next word or word fragment from several possibilities, so the same input can produce different completions.

The destinations varied widely. Seven first addresses used an Amazon Web Services hostname, six used an Alibaba Cloud hostname, and 20 were local or internal-looking. Across the 64 continuations, we found 52 distinct host strings.

Some strings resembled cloud storage buckets; others used local network addresses which are completely benign. A familiar provider name in a generated address does not mean the address exists or would accept an upload. 11 of the public-looking domains do not exist and one is not a valid top-level domain. These results indicate that there is not a single hard-coded target where the model tries to push some data to in this situation, but rather a diversity of (sometimes nonexistent) destinations including local, American cloud, and invalid URLs.

One plausible explanation is that the model was completing an upload command with a cloud-storage address it had learned during training. Alibaba Cloud was one of several providers it generated in our replays. We cannot establish why that particular run produced an Alibaba address, but the replays suggest it was one possible completion rather than a fixed destination.

We also tested an earlier point in the command, where the model checked which programs were available. A completely insignificant action – swapping the order of curl and wget when checking availability – reduced the number of continuations containing a curl network command from 15/32 to 4/32, despite both lists containing exactly the same programs.

Both tests probe what are the possible scenarios that can happen once the model has decided to produce a tool call. They cannot tell us how often the model would initiate an unrequested upload or why it chose to use a tool call in the first place.

A model getting lost

The results fit what we call model jaggedness: behavior that is inconsistent or changes sharply with small differences in context. The model’s reasoning misread the task and contradicted its subsequent action. When we sampled different completions, a diverse set of destinations was chosen rather than a single endpoint. When we changed the order of two tool names, the continuation changed too. Together, these observations make jaggedness the most likely explanation we found.

There is also context around the model itself. Qwen describes Flash-Next as an experimental preview of the architecture behind Qwen4. They say that they shared the architectural changes early with the community presumably so that inference framework developers can implement before the full model release. Rough edges are plausible in an experimental checkpoint, though this context does not establish the cause of the incident or predict the behavior of the future model family.

We built a URL explorer for the 64 sampled continuations and a trace viewer showing the model’s alternatives at each token. Open both viewers here.

So, is this a backdoor?

In conclusion, the situation does not seem as alarming as it might have seemed at first glance. The reality is that models can misbehave for no apparent humanly interpretable reason. While these results do not prove that there is no backdoor (which is extremely difficult to do), it hints at the most likely explanation simply being model jaggedness and a situation that makes the model misbehave.

Companies deploying agents need to secure their models from controls outside the model. A request for a detection rule offers no reason to send a test string to an unrelated address and that mismatch can be identified before the action is executed. This emphasizes the point that the principles of least privilege and sandboxing agents are crucial in securing them.

We tested Qwen, so these results do not establish how other models would behave. The broader risk is that an agent with tool access can attempt a network action unrelated to the user’s request. Least privilege and sandboxing limit the consequences when that happens.

We thank Cohere for sharing the suspicious trace which enabled this experiment.

Experimental setup

  • Model and machine: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in BF16, served with vLLM 0.32.0 on a machine with 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs; deterministic QSA selection
  • Sampling: temperature 1.0, top-k 20, top-p 1.0, min-p 0; no presence, frequency, or repetition penalties
  • URL experiment: 64 serial completions from the recorded 2,323-token prefix ending at ABC123, stopping at the end of the first tool call (maximum 1,773 new tokens)

The post Cohere’s Qwen Story: Looks More Like Model Jaggedness appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
item.description: Cloudflare mitigated over 8,200 DDoS attacks per hour in Q3 2026 as attackers shifted to shorter, high-frequency strikes. Explore the latest threat data, including the collapse of CLDAP vectors and the impact of recent botnet takedowns.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One, Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network.

Key insights

  1. Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure.
  2. Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods.
  3. Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggling geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, and contentious domestic events. At the same time, the operational focus shifted away from media organizations toward a wider array of industry targets, including consumer services, Internet infrastructure, and adult entertainment.

Q3 by the numbers: 8,200 DDoS attacks every hour

Across its network in the third quarter of 2026, Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests. That works out to approximately 8,226 network-layer DDoS attacks per hour, or about 197,400 per day — one attack every 0.44 seconds. The quarter's mitigated traffic totaled 272.6 PB at the network layer and 95.1 PB at the HTTP layer.

More swarms, fewer giants

Short-burst, mid-range, high-count attacks — the operational signature of DDoS-for-hire "booter" services — accelerated this quarter. These attacks primarily targeted computer software, gambling and casinos, and information technology industries. Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks in Q3 2026, a +208% increase from the same quarter in 2025:

  • 96% ended in under 10 minutes
  • 98% stayed under 1 Gbps, more than enough to overwhelm a server or website

On the other hand, network-level hyper-volumetric attacks (those exceeding 1 Tbps) reversed course, dropping to 251 attacks in Q3 from 805 in Q2 — coinciding with law enforcement action in early 2026 that dismantled four of the largest IoT DDoS botnets: Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad.

Still, IoT-based botnets remain a durable high-volume threat as the ecosystem churns through new variants such as Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot. Mirai-classified mitigation peaked in August at 57.23 PB, representing 46.5% of all mitigated network-layer bytes in Q3, including four days — August 16, 19, 23, and 25 — that each cleared three petabytes. The quarter's longest sustained Mirai attack ran 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21.

Vector shifts: the collapse of CLDAP and rise of UDP

The most dramatic vector shift of the quarter was downward. CLDAP (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) attacks — where small queries with a forged victim IP address trick public domain controllers (UDP 389) into reflecting massive, amplified responses back at the target — experienced a dramatic +580% quarter-over-quarter surge in the first half of the year before collapsing to just 0.05% of attacks in Q3.

Meanwhile, DNS amplification surged 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks, exploiting open DNS resolvers in a similar reflection-and-amplification pattern to CLDAP: small spoofed queries, large replies directed at the victim. Other UDP floods climbed from 14.06% to 31.31% of network-layer attacks. UDP is a connectionless transport protocol, which makes it a convenient vehicle for raw volumetric attacks: attackers send large numbers of UDP packets to random or specific ports on the target, forcing the target to check for a listening application and respond, consuming its network and compute resources.

Most-attacked industry

While Media, Production & Publishing remained the most-attacked industry in Q3 2026, its overall share is roughly a quarter of its Q2 level, and the focus has moved across a wider set of industries. Internet rose from outside the top 10 to #6; Consumer Services and Adult Entertainment also climbed in, reaching #8 and #9 respectively.

Most-attacked locations

Geographic surges: Canada and Israel climb the ranks

Adding to an already turbulent period of bilateral trade disputes, Canada jumped from #16 to #6, driven by attacks against its Retail, Telecommunications, Service providers & carriers, and Marketing & advertising industries.

Israel moved 7 spots to take #10 as a result of sustained DDoS activity in mid-September. While this period was marked by contentious decisions ahead of parliamentary elections and the Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was also a massive, documented surge in hostile cyber warfare targeting Israel this year.

Top 10

The United States was the most-attacked location in Q3 2026, while China was number #2 and Indonesia rose into the top three at 2.93% of total attacks. The U.S.-China pairing at the top is consistent with the first half of 2026, when China finished #1 and the U.S. #2; the countries have traded positions as attention and attacker preferences shift.

Strengthening global defenses and helping to defend the Internet

Cloudflare's network is designed to absorb this kind of growth in DDoS threats. Every service on our network is protected by free, unmetered DDoS protection that runs at every one of our 330+ cities globally, backed by 500 Tbps of network capacity. Autonomy is the point: our systems detect and mitigate attacks without human intervention. And they need to, because as this quarter's distributions make clear, most attacks end long before a human analyst could see the alert, and the largest attacks still regularly exceed 1 Tbps at a cadence measured in hundreds per quarter.

To help hosting providers, cloud computing platforms, and Internet service providers identify and take down the abusive IP addresses and accounts that launch these attacks, we leverage Cloudflare's unique vantage point on DDoS attacks to provide a free DDoS Botnet Threat Feed for Service Providers.

Over 800 networks worldwide have signed up for this feed, and we've already seen great collaboration across the community to take down botnet nodes. For a continuously-updated view of attack trends across the Internet, visit Cloudflare Radar.    

About Cloudforce One

Driven by a mission to help defend the Internet, Cloudforce One draws on telemetry from Cloudflare's global network — which protects more than 20% of the web — to drive threat research and operational response, protecting critical systems for millions of organizations worldwide.

item.title: Mapping Facial Recognition use in Schools
LABScon26 Replay | Keynote: A Sober Analysis of AI Impact
item.description: Harvard Professor James Mickens weighs the promises of AI against its potential harms, arguing for hardware-based mechanisms to isolate frontier models.
item.content:encoded:
In his LABScon 26 keynote, delivered in his inimitable comedic style, Harvard University professor James Mickens questions whether the scale of current AI investment is justified. Starting from US tech capex of roughly 1.4% of GDP in the second quarter of 2025, he argues that computers are already good enough, and notes that the world has so many CPUs and GPUs that they are put to work solving cryptocurrency puzzles to make imaginary money. More seriously, the AI models that investment is building, he says, grow increasingly opaque as their parameter counts rise.

Mickens then cites research and incident reports on model behaviour, including models acting to prevent another model being shut down and recent sandbox escapes at OpenAI and other labs. On economics, he rejects the assumptions that AI will create more jobs than it destroys and that universal basic income will follow widespread automation.

He concludes that at present the only good AI research is safety research, which he defines broadly to include economic and emotional security alongside computer security. Mickens own contribution is Guillotine, a hypervisor design that runs a model’s CPU code on isolated cores unable to read or write the hardware state of the cores running the hypervisor. Arguing that hardware-based mechanisms for isolating misaligned frontier models will be an important direction for research over the next five years, he invites those interested in this approach to collaborate.

This keynote speaks to security practitioners and researchers interested in AI risk, the economics behind current AI investment, or hardware-level containment of frontier models

About the Author

James Mickens is a Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science at Harvard University. His research focuses on the performance, security, and privacy of large-scale online services; a current focus is the interpretability and sandboxing of potentially misaligned frontier models. Prior to becoming a professor at Harvard, Dr. Mickens spent seven years at Microsoft Research, working in the Distributed Systems group. 

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

item.title: Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries
item.description:
Key Points Introduction Over the past two months, we have been tracking a campaign that abuses the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude to spread a custom malware chain we call Yoba. The attackers use fake GitHub projects that pretend to be AI desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude […]

The post Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
Key Points

  • Check Point Research discovered a campaign we track as Yoba where attackers abuse the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, creating fake GitHub projects that pretend to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus.
  • The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections.
  • This campaign demonstrates strong operational security (OPSEC) by avoiding dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure and instead relying on Telegram, Tor, Catbox, and DNS over HTTPS (DoH).
  • The actor behind the campaign shows indicators that suggest Russian origins and appears to operate primarily in the UTC-4 time zone.


Introduction

Over the past two months, we have been tracking a campaign that abuses the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude to spread a custom malware chain we call Yoba. The attackers use fake GitHub projects that pretend to be AI desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. These projects look convincing and use real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them appear legitimate to potential victims. The website exhibits search-targeted content and suspicious installer-delivery tactics consistent with an SEO-poisoning lure.

Inside the installers, there is a malicious component we refer to as the YobaDropper. This dropper includes another component, the YobaLoader, which is responsible for contacting attacker-controlled infrastructure and fetching the final payload. In this report, we describe how victims are lured to these fake projects, how the YobaDropper and YobaLoader work together, and how the attackers ultimately use this chain to run unwanted software on infected systems.


GitHub Repositories

The initial access occurred via malicious GitHub repositories. The projects were impersonating ChatGPT and Claude related models, more specifically GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. No manipulation of fake engagement (stars/forks) was in place.

Aside from the repositories, GitHub.io pages were used to describe the capabilities of the software, while the malware was hosted as a release.

These phishing landing pages contain download links that point directly to the malicious ZIP releases hosted on GitHub.

While the repositories do not show signs of fake engagement (such as artificially inflated stars or forks) that would promote them within GitHub’s own search, they still appear among the top results on Google. This is most likely due to SEO poisoning, where the attackers optimize titles, descriptions, and hosting domains to make their malicious projects rank highly in external search engines.

Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively. This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor’s true operational timezone.

Repositories’ initial commits:

Repository: /gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop
==================================================
[2026-07-16T14:39:40Z] Author: gpt-5-6	
tree aebceccb0f3303806c35a73da865b684594487c1
author gpt-5-6 <edwardcarlsonmkym@outlook.com> 1784212780 +0400
committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1784212780 +0400

Initial commit
==================================================

Repository: /gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io
==================================================
[2026-07-16T14:44:31Z] Author: gpt-5-6	
tree 249dae41d64583a6a9ebcb60e3ad36d6216dd6e4
author gpt-5-6 <edwardcarlsonmkym@outlook.com> 1784213071 +0400
committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1784213071 +0400

Initial commit
==================================================

Repository: /opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github.io
==================================================
[2026-08-31T21:33:26Z] Author: opus-5-0	
tree 46ae1f147cf70d4df1471f0e9df46b654d11fe9c
author opus-5-0 <rioprestonlfyx@outlook.com> 1788212006 -0400
committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1788212006 -0400

Create readme.md
==================================================

Repository: /gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io
==================================================
[2026-09-04T22:56:13Z] Author: gpt-6-astra	
tree 028bfd4c1041dc1f030c9480a463366e6089e661
author gpt-6-astra <daxschneiderdjuu@outlook.com> 1788562573 +0300
committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1788562573 +0300

Initial commit
==================================================

Although the first repository was created around July 2026, the first two malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August, and a third malicious release followed approximately five days later.

Release: /gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io/releases/tag/v5.6.0
[2026-08-30T19:15:44Z] gpt-5-6 Uploaded sol-setup.zip (application/zip) (269)
==================================================

Release: /opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github.io/releases/tag/Release_v5.0.0
[2026-08-31T21:38:13Z] opus-5-0 uploaded Setup-Claude.zip (application/zip) (82)
==================================================

Release: /gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io/releases/tag/Astra
[2026-09-04T23:14:11Z] gpt-6-astra Uploaded GPT-6-Astra-Setup.zip (application/zip) (352)

Malicious zip files hosted on GitHub and other legitimate platforms are usually password-protected, since this prevents automated tools from unpacking and therefore analyzing them. However, neither of these repositories used password protection, as the binaries already had very low detection rates thanks to their anti-sandbox and other anti-analysis techniques.

While the two ChatGPT-related releases and their repositories were created about five days apart, the ZIP files contain mostly the same files, including the malicious components, and they maintain the same IoCs.

By adding the compilation timestamps to this these time-related operations, we are able to determine which files appear to contain the malicious functionality without performing any initial analysis.

The file that immediately stands out is winmm.dll, which was compiled the same day it was added to the ZIP archive. This suggests it is the component with the malicious functionality, while the other files serve to make the package appear legitimate. The compilation timestamp also indicates the actor is operating in the UTC-4 timezone.

Furthermore, Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI executable, is used during execution to sideload the malicious DLL. The Setup-Claude.zip file contains the same structure, though in this case Setup.exe is a legitimate signed Claude executable.


YobaDropper – winmm.dll

The malicious DLL contains multiple export names, suggesting that the legitimate winmm.dll has been spoofed. As in many other cases, these exports exist but their code has been stripped out, leaving them mostly empty and reducing the size of the binary.

All 180 exports contain just a return instruction (C3) followed by NOPs (90), and DllEntryPoint is the only one containing actual code.


Anti-Analysis, Pre-Checks

The first function implements an anti-sandbox technique: the malware hashes the basename of its host executable and checks whether the checksum matches the hardcoded value 0xE6C2F326. The hashing algorithm has been identified as DJB2, which other malware families have also used in the past. The malware expects to run under the name Setup.exe, so this check fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandbox environment.

Although a failed check does not terminate the process, the DLL performs 200,000 iterations of Sleep(5500), amounting to approximately 12.73 days, while repeatedly appending the decoded filler string pddy to a local UTF-16 buffer.

In the second function, the malware checks whether the infected user is located in a CIS country by inspecting the system’s keyboard layout. Ukraine was historically included in such checks, but it is not in the list used by recent malware.

The language check is unusual. Instead of comparing the victim’s keyboard language ID against hardcoded values, the malware checks whether the ID falls within the range 0x19–0x44. For IDs in that range, it tests the corresponding bit in the bitmask 0xEC0400C8401 to determine whether the language belongs to a CIS-region country, with an explicit exception for ID 0x22 (Ukrainian). Bazarloader has used a similar technique in the past, with the bitmask 0xD8080190C03.

Language IDs excluded from the infection:

The malware continues to resolve Windows API functions dynamically from kernel32.dll and ntdll.dll by comparing hashes of the exported function names. The hashing algorithm is again DJB2, with the initial value 0x1505.

The last check before the malware unpacks and deploys the embedded payload tests whether the process is running with administrator privileges. If it is not, the malware displays the message “Please run this program as Administrator.” to the victim and terminates itself, requiring the user to rerun it with elevated privileges.


Deploying Phase

The dropper contains multiple XOR-encrypted strings that are decrypted when needed. These strings include the file paths where the embedded binaries are dropped, as well as the decryption keys.

It creates a directory under ProgramData named WMProcess. Then it copies the original WMPDMC.exe from System32 into this newly created folder. Next, it decrypts the embedded payload using the string IRANNUMBERONE as the XOR seed and drops the decrypted payload in the same folder under the name wmpdui.dll.

Using scheduled tasks, the dropper maintains persistence by leveraging the legitimate executable, which will sideload the malicious payload. To make the task appear legitimate, it sets the author to Microsoft Corporation and the description to Collects device metadata for Windows Media Player.. It also sets the boot-trigger delay to PT3M, which corresponds to a 3-minute delay after system startup, and configures the task to run under the Local System account (S-1-5-18).


YobaLoader – wmpdui.dll

The second-stage payload contains the same code as the dropper, which indicates that the same developer is responsible for both components.

The same anti-sandbox technique is used, forcing the malware to be run only by WMPDMC.exe. It again checks the hash of the process basename, and only continues execution if this value matches the hardcoded hash 0x552751E3.

The dropper uses the DJB2 hashing algorithm to hash and verify the process name and to resolve Windows API functions, both with the same seed 0x1505. The loader (YobaLoader) also uses DJB2 for the process name with the same seed as the dropper, but for resolving Windows API functions it uses a different seed, 0x1DEB.

The developer reused the same string-hashing algorithm but changed the seed (0x1505 in the dropper, 0x1DEB in the loader) to separate the hash spaces for each stage, complicating analysis, and reducing the effectiveness of hash-based detection and automated tooling.


Network

The downloader uses an interesting process to obtain the next-stage payload. It first decrypts multiple strings using a simple XOR operation, among these strings is the URL of a Telegram channel, t[.]me/yoba_fanclub. It then visits this channel using the user-agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64;) and parses the HTML source to extract the src URL of the element with the class tgme_page_photo_image. This class refers to the location where the channel’s profile image is hosted.

It downloads the image and uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words, which are decrypted as part of the DGA algorithm. This DGA algorithm uses three sets of strings:

  1. Adjectives
  2. Nouns
  3. Verbs

Finally, it generates and appends an integer value in the range 0–999. The generated domain has the following format, "$adjective-$noun-$verb-$digit.dedyn[.]io". By changing the image of the Telegram channel, a new domain can be generated.

The following Python snippet represents the DGA algorithm:

"""
Author: @Tera0017/Check Point Research
"""
from pathlib import Path
import sys

ADJECTIVES = [
    "silver", "amber", "wild", "tiny", "brave", "lucky", "calm",
    "sharp", "swift", "bright", "quiet", "bold", "gentle", "fierce",
    "royal", "mystic", "username", "degenerate", "allblack", "kizta",
    "graf",
]
NOUNS = [
    "tiger", "river", "stone", "cloud", "wolf", "ocean", "forest",
    "mountain", "eagle", "raven", "ember", "comet", "fox", "dragon",
    "piano", "viper", "yoba", "yyoba", "static", "cpp", "example",
]
VERBS = [
    "runs", "jumps", "sings", "sleeps", "flies", "hunts", "burns",
    "floats", "shines", "whispers", "roars", "dreams", "strikes",
    "glides", "watches", "hides", "duty", "free",
]

FNV_MULTIPLIER = 0x1000193
MASK64 = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF

def hash_bytes(data: bytes, seed: int) -> int:
    value = seed
    for byte in data:
        value = ((value ^ byte) * FNV_MULTIPLIER) & MASK64
    return value

def generate_domain(image_path: str) -> str:
    image = Path(image_path).read_bytes()
    if len(image) < 50:
        raise ValueError("Image must contain at least 50 bytes")

    tail = image[-50:]

    adjective = ADJECTIVES[hash_bytes(tail, 0x811C9DC5) % len(ADJECTIVES)]
    noun = NOUNS[hash_bytes(tail, 0xAF0154A5) % len(NOUNS)]
    verb = VERBS[hash_bytes(tail, 0xFE5439E4) % len(VERBS)]
    number = hash_bytes(tail, 0xFFA7471A) % 1000

    return f"{adjective}-{noun}-{verb}-{number}.dedyn[.]io"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    image_file = sys.argv[1]
    print(generate_domain(image_file))

It then queries Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain an encrypted command from a DNS TXT record, using a URL of the form https://dns[.]google/resolve?name=$DGA&type=TXT.

By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity.

It decodes the Base64-encoded data field from the JSON response and validates it using Ed25519 signature verification with the public key b5c2d20623d4e6647d06a42864edd8629f82c5c384b243fdaeeeca24b3873d64. Once the signature validation succeeds, it decrypts the decoded value using AES in ECB mode with the key 1d0d1368b4d53f3a6322cf40e84e63db.

Decrypted response: 1https://files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat

The downloader retrieves the encrypted payload and decrypts it using the same AES key and ECB mode that were previously used for the DNS data.

The malware provides three methods for deploying the downloaded payload. The selected method is indicated by the first character of the decrypted response that follows the URL (1/2/3):

  1. Injects the downloaded payload into svchost.exe (NtWriteVirtualMemory/NtCreateThreadEx). It enumerates running processes and, using the hashing algorithm with the seed 0x1DEB, searches for the hash value 0xC26CDEA5, which corresponds to svchost.exe.
  2. Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.exe file and executes it. Before running the executable, the downloader removes the Zone.Identifier alternate data stream, which is hidden metadata used by Windows to track the origin of downloaded files.
  3. Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.ps1 PowerShell script and invokes it with the following parameters: -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File.

Finally, the injected payload into svchost.exe is an XMRig 6.26.0 miner with a hidden command line targeting a TLS-enabled onion mining endpoint through a local Tor SOCKS5 proxy. It can unpack and start Tor 0.4.9.12 plus lyrebird 0.8.1, monitor user-input activity to pause mining, and conditionally load the WinRing0 driver service for MSR-based mining optimization.

Although we observed an XMRig cryptominer as the final payload in this campaign, the YobaLoader is a generic loader. The operator can supply any PE or PowerShell payload via the signed DNS TXT tasking, so future waves may deliver different malware families.


Past Yoba Versions

Yoba exposes, through the same hashing algorithm it uses for anti-analysis, the specific process name under which it expects to run. Even without having full visibility into the campaign from the very beginning, analysts can still infer which targeted software was used to lure users by correlating this expected process name with the fake AI applications promoted on the associated GitHub repositories and GitHub Pages sites.

Earlier YobaDropper observed in the wild appeared in early June 2026. In this campaign, the dropper was sideloaded by a process named Cursor.exe (hash: 0x56221573). It remains unclear whether Cursor.exe was a legitimate signed binary. The majority of the functionality in this early variant is consistent with the newer versions of both the dropper and the loader.

YobaDropper shows two main differences between its older and newer versions:

  1. Unpacking logic: In the oldest version, the buffer is first Base64-decoded and then XOR-decrypted to extract the YobaLoader. In the newer version, the developer removed the Base64-decoding step and performs only XOR decryption, simplifying the unpacking process.
  2. Execution method: The second change concerns how YobaLoader is triggered. The newer version uses Scheduled Tasks to start the copied legitimate host and sideload the loader, whereas the first discovered version creates the shortcut msdefender_scheduler{7940-8490-6670-1081}.lnk in the Startup folder. This shortcut executes a copied %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\msdtc.exe and sideloads %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\mswsock.dll.

Earlier version of YobaLoader contains language checks and excludes only Russia from infection. In later versions, these checks were moved to the dropper stage and expanded to exclude additional CIS countries, shifting regional filtering earlier in the infection chain.

While the overall DGA logic remains the same, the early variant uses the extension .aber[.]ir instead of .dedyn[.]io. In addition, instead of injecting into svchost.exe, this variant injects into a different running process identified only by its hashed name 0x21BD94C2.

The initial loader also implements several anti-analysis techniques that have been removed from the newer versions of the malware:

1. Anti-debugging
It enumerates all kernel object types and reads their TypeName values. Each type name is hashed using DJB2 with the seed 0x1DEB until the hash matches 0xCF9EE149, which corresponds to DebugObject. If a DebugObject is found, it indicates that a debugger is or was active, and in that case the malware terminates itself.

2. Anti-VM
The malware uses a VM/sandbox-detection scoring function while running several hardware fingerprinting checks. The maximum score is 6, and the minimum required to continue the infection chain is 3. The checks include:

  • Hypervisor-present bit and CPUID timing (via RDTSCP).
  • Hypervisor vendor signature string (CPUID leaf 0x40000000).
  • CPU brand string sanity checks (CPUID leaves 0x80000002–0x80000004).
  • SMBIOS-based firmware fingerprinting (GetSystemFirmwareTable–RSMB)

Despite these small differences in early anti-analysis behavior, the Telegram channel and the profile image used as the seed for the DGA remain the same as in the newer variants, indicating that the operator retained the same infrastructure while iterating on the loader’s evasion logic.


Conclusion

The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance. By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious.
Although the underlying techniques are more advanced than typical commodity malware, the main goals remain straightforward: gain a foothold on the victim’s system, avoid easy detection, and then run the attacker’s chosen payload. Organizations should be cautious about installing “AI helpers” or similar tools from unverified repositories and should enforce policies that restrict running software from unknown sources. Combining user awareness with basic technical controls.


Indicators of Compromise


Yara Rules

rule yoba_dropper
{
    meta:
        author = "@Tera0017/Check Point Research"
        description = "YobaDropper"
    strings:
        $code1 = {00 BB 40 0D 03 00 B9 7C 15 00 00 FF D6 31 C0}
        $code2 = {BA 05 15 00 00 0F BE 08 84 C9 74 0A 6B D2 21}
        $code3 = {53 B9 75 EE 40 70 48 83 EC 20}
        $code4 = {BA 5C CD 17 E5 48 89 C1 E8 73 00 00 00}
        $code5 = {0F C8 89 C0 4? 39 ?? 74 1? (49 0F AF C0| 48 69 C0 ?? ?? ?? ??) (4C 01 C8| 48 05 ?? ?? ?? ??) 49 89 C? 49 C1 E? 18 45 30 [2] 4? FF ?? EB}
    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and 2 of them
}

rule yoba_loader
{
    meta:
        author = "@Tera0017/Check Point Research"
        description = "YobaLoader"
    strings:
        $code1 = {B9 80 A8 12 01 FF ?? ?? E9}
        $code2 = {BA EB 1D 00 00 0F BE 08 84 C9 74 0A 6B D2 21}
        $code3 = {B9 5B 80 EF B7 E8}
        $code4 = {BA F5 8B 2E F2 48 89 C1}
        $code5 = {B5 C2 D2 06 23 D4 E6 64 7D 06 A4 28 64 ED D8 62 9F 82 C5 C3 84 B2 43 FD AE EE CA 24 B3 87 3D 64}
        $code6 = {1D 0D 13 68 B4 D5 3F 3A 63 22 CF 40 E8 4E 63 DB}
        $code7 = {40 80 FE 32 74 42 40 80 FE 33 74 66 40 80 FE 31}
        $code8 = {41 81 F8 A5 DE 6C C2}
    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and 2 of them
}

The post Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
item.description: We are launching a PHP Capture the Flag challenge integrated with our Bug Bounty program to test our WAF protections. Security researchers are invited to bypass our defenses and capture the flag to help make the Internet safer.
item.content:encoded:
Update — October 30, 2026: Thank you to everyone who has participated in the PHP Capture the Flag challenge. We have received a strong response from the security research community, and the submissions have helped us harden our existing php2shell WAF protections and create new detections.

Details of managed-rule changes are available in the Cloudflare WAF changelog.

The CTF remains open. We encourage researchers to continue submitting materially distinct, reproducible bypasses through the Cloudflare HackerOne program. We will share further information and feedback as the challenge progresses. Thank you again for your contributions.

Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell: serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web.

Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection.

As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free.

Put our WAF to the test

Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential.

That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge, run through our Bug Bounty program. We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag.

How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works

We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell. The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container, with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag.

The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file.

Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag. You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form.

Challenge requirements

This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne. All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne terms and the Cloudflare HackerOne program rules the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty:

  1. All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms before participating in the CTF.
  2. Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request.
  3. Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through the CTF user interface (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review.
  4. Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide:
    1. The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes.
    2. Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain.
    3. An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag.
    4. The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification.
    5. What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about.

UI verification does not submit a HackerOne report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible.

Awards require a materially distinct Firewall (WAF) bypass method, even for the same PHP CVE. Reports using the same Firewall-bypass mechanism are duplicates, regardless of differences in the PHP exploit, payload, RCE technique, or flag-recovery method. New flags, resets, attempt IDs, or cosmetic changes—including equivalent encodings—do not qualify as unique. Equivalent submissions are duplicates even if unfixed; only the first complete, reproducible HackerOne report is considered. Cloudflare makes final duplicate and reward decisions.

We record attempted metadata and request payloads to help analyze reports, so please use test data only. Do not send credentials, personal information, or anything else you would not want included in a research record. Read Cloudflare’s privacy notice before testing.

Testing is authorized only against the challenge hostname's WAF-protected /php/* endpoints (POST method only). Other Cloudflare services, direct access to the underlying infrastructure, the upstream PHP project, and third-party systems are out of scope. No denial of service, high-volume scanning, persistence, social engineering, or attacks on other participants. If you get a 429 or 503, back off.

In the event of any conflict between this blog post and the Bounty Terms, the Bounty Terms shall prevail.

Cloudflare reserves the right to suspend or terminate this challenge at any time. Once the competition is removed from HackerOne, it is officially terminated, so please refer to the Cloudflare HackerOne page for the most up-to-date information on whether this challenge remains open.

Not a substitute for patching

Our WAF protects you, but it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Response blocking can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. If you run PHP, follow the latest PHP security advisories and apply the relevant updates.

Last week was a reminder that helping build a better Internet often takes many people—researchers, maintainers, and teams across the industry—doing difficult, urgent work together.

We hope this challenge gives everyone a useful way to join in. Head over to php-rce.cloudflare.app if you want to participate: the flag is there, and we'd like to know if you can get it.

item.title: Design Tenets for Agent Identity Management Systems
item.description: This is blog #2 in our series on agentic identity, authentication and authorization. Our other post can be found via Post #1. In our last blog post, we highlighted the essential nature of having fundamentally sound identity and access management (IAM) capabilities as a precursor to implementing agents at scale. We started to form the core of what “good looks like” but wanted to take this a step further by defining an initial set of “Design Tenets” for agentic identity, authentication, and authorization. The tenets covered in this post are drawn from public comments on the NCCoE Accelerating

item.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
item.description: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
item.content:encoded:
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened

GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.  

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response.
