To better identify exploit attempts, Cloudflare developed full transaction detection, a new WAF capability that analyzes both sides of the same HTTP transaction. While some malicious payloads can be identified using the request alone, the response contains useful signals that can be used to create rules with higher confidence, reducing false positives. A matching full transaction rule can block the origin response before it reaches the requester. Learn how it works in our full transaction detection blog post.

The new Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default has been automatically deployed for customers on all plans, including Free. To verify that the response rules are active, you can visit the Security > Security Rules page. Read the full transaction blog to learn how to customize its deployment.

Review events and customize protection

To analyze blocked requests, visit Security > Security Analytics > Events. Filter by the rule IDs in the table above and inspect the matched request, action, and path. Events identify whether the action came from a managed or custom rule. Customers who need to tailor the protection can update the scope of the Managed Ruleset to the parts of an application where it is relevant.

Update PHP and keep the protection enabled

Cloudflare customers using our Managed Ruleset are protected by default. We recommend following the advisory recommendation and applying the vendor update to your PHP repos as soon as possible while keeping the WAF protection enabled as an additional protection. Our WAF analysts will continue to update protections as new techniques emerge.

Copy prompt to fix!
# Security task: check and fix "php2shell" (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)

Two critical PHP runtime vulnerabilities were disclosed on 2026-10-21 (CVSS v4.0 9.2).
They allow unauthenticated remote code execution, data exposure and DoS through crafted
HTTP requests. Exploitation is already happening. The bug is in the PHP runtime itself,
so updating app code, frameworks, WordPress or plugins does NOT fix it.

Official advisory (treat as source of truth, re-fetch it in case it was updated):
https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5
- GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w (CVE-2026-109618, RCE via OOM corruption)
- GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state)

**Fixed upstream versions:** 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35
**Affected:** every PHP install that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php,
php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed). mod_php has the highest risk: a demonstrated exploit
triggers before any application code runs.

## Rules
- Do NOT guess. If you can't confirm a version or setting, say so.
- Ask me before changing anything on production or shared infrastructure,
  restarting production services, or editing deploy config. Read-only discovery is fine.
- Don't stop at the first finding. Inventory everything, then report.

## Step 1: Inventory every place PHP runs
Search the current repo/workspace AND any machines/containers I have access to:
- Repo: `*.php`, `composer.json`/`composer.lock` (check `require.php` and
  `config.platform.php`), `Dockerfile*`, `docker-compose*`, `.php-version`,
  `.tool-versions`, `.devcontainer/`, CI files (GitHub Actions `setup-php`, GitLab CI
  `image:`), IaC (Terraform, Ansible, Helm, k8s manifests), PaaS config
  (`app.yaml`, `Procfile`, Platform.sh, Laravel Forge/Vapor, etc.).
- Base images: list every `FROM php:*`, `FROM wordpress:*`, `FROM bitnami/*`,
  `FROM serversideup/*`, `FROM dunglas/frankenphp*` and similar, with tags.
- Running hosts/containers (if accessible): `php -v`, `php-fpm -v`, `php -i | grep -i "server api"`,
  `apachectl -M | grep -i php`, `docker ps` + `docker exec <c> php -v`.
- Note the SAPI for each (FPM / mod_php / CGI / FrankenPHP / LiteSpeed / CLI-only).
- Note long-running workers (Laravel Octane, RoadRunner, Swoole, FrankenPHP worker
  mode). These are relevant to the stale-state bug.

If no PHP is found anywhere, tell me clearly and stop. Nothing else is needed.

## Step 2: Decide if each instance is vulnerable
For each instance, classify it as PATCHED / VULNERABLE / UNKNOWN:
- Upstream builds: vulnerable if below 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 on that branch.
- **PHP 8.1 and older are EOL upstream:** vulnerable unless a vendor backport is confirmed.
- **Distro packages (Debian/Ubuntu/RHEL/Alpine/etc.)** often backport fixes WITHOUT
  bumping the upstream version, so `php -v` alone isn't enough. Check the package
  changelog for the CVE IDs, e.g.
  `apt changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961[89]"` or
  `rpm -q --changelog <php-pkg> | grep -E "CVE-2026-10961[89]"`.
- If PHP comes from `rpms.remirepo.net`: the advisory says it will not have same-day
  updates. Flag this and recommend distro packages or building from source.
- Managed hosting / shared hosting / PaaS: mark UNKNOWN and tell me to ask the provider.

## Step 3: Fix (only after I approve the plan for prod)
1. Upgrade PHP to a fixed version (or the vendor-patched package):
   - Bump Docker base image tags to a fixed patch release, rebuild, redeploy.
   - Update CI `php-version` pins.
   - `apt`/`dnf`/`apk` upgrade of the distro PHP packages.
   - 7.4 / 8.0 / 8.1 built from source: the PHP security team published minimal
     backport branches linked from the advisory. Otherwise upgrade to a supported version.
2. **Restart EVERY PHP worker** (FPM pools, Apache, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, Octane/
   RoadRunner/Swoole). Old processes keep running vulnerable code until restarted.
3. Verify each instance afterwards (version + changelog check) and report the evidence.

## Step 4: Temporary mitigations (ONLY if patching isn't possible right away)
These reduce exposure but do NOT make the server safe. Apply them in php.ini / the FPM
pool / server config (not `ini_set()` or `.user.ini`) and restart every worker:
- CVE-2026-109618:
  - `memory_limit=-1`, set non-overridably (e.g. `php_admin_value`), and confirm nothing
    re-applies a finite limit.
  - Low `post_max_size` (8M with no uploads, 32M with uploads), with
    `upload_max_filesize` below it.
  - Enforce request size / field count / multipart part count / header limits at the
    web server or proxy, including requests without `Content-Length`.
  - Use container/cgroup memory limits. Do NOT use `RLIMIT_AS`/`RLIMIT_DATA`.
- CVE-2026-109619:
  - `session.upload_progress.enabled=0`.
  - On PHP 8.5: `fatal_error_backtraces=0`.
  - Remove invalid/deprecated per-request settings that emit diagnostics early (hiding
    them via `error_reporting`/`display_errors`/`@` does not help).
  - Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and timeouts.
- If the site sits behind Cloudflare: confirm the WAF Managed Ruleset is deployed in
  **block** mode (Free plans get the Managed Free Ruleset automatically). This is
  defense in depth, not a replacement for patching.

## Step 5: Look for signs of compromise (read-only)
Since exploitation started before disclosure, check what you can access:
- PHP-FPM/Apache error logs for segfaults, "Allowed memory size exhausted", or
  worker crashes, especially clustered around unusually large POST/multipart requests.
- Recently modified or unexpected files in web roots (webshells), new cron jobs,
  unexpected processes or outbound connections from PHP users.
Report anything suspicious. Do not delete evidence.

## Final report
Give me a table: location | how PHP is provided | SAPI | version | status
(PATCHED/VULNERABLE/UNKNOWN) | action taken or needed. Then list:
- What you changed (files, commands), what still needs my approval, and anything that
  needs a hosting provider.
- Mitigations applied as stopgaps and when they should be removed.
- Any compromise indicators found.

item.title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
item.description: Following the discovery that eight eMudhra intermediate certificates use weak keys, Cloudflare is deploying mitigations and releasing client updates. We explain the impact, our response, and what customers and developers should do next.
item.content:encoded:
On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.

We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services.

We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected.

Our response

We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms.

Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below.

What customers should do

Developer guidance

For developers, look beneath the SDK.

An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy.

Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore.

This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment.

Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier.

Timeline

The timeline of events so far is below.

Date and Time

Event

October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC

Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment.

October 20, 02:00 UTC

Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms.

October 20 09:15 UTC

Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published.

October 20 19:20 UTC

CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed.

Looking forward

The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just one application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.

item.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
item.description: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

SHINYWIRE

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

GHOSTBYTE

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

CONFLICTING INTERESTS

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

item.title: Investigating dual-use technology: the war machine doesn’t stop
Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
item.description: CVE-2026-88771 lets attackers run commands on NetScaler Gateway before anyone signs in. Patching takes time most teams don't have, so the sign-in decision has to move in front of the vulnerable code.
item.content:encoded:
The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update.

If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls.

This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server?

Citrix released software updates to address the flaw, and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch.

Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth, to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue.

Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform.

The NetScaler exploit

Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks.

CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771.

In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow. The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection.

Put the access decision in front of the authentication server

The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare Access can enforce an independent access policy before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page.

That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next.

This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero: reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications.

Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication.

The origin connection must enforce the same boundary

Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. It’s important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture.

Cloudflare Tunnel is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you won’t have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone.

When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example, Dedicated CDN Egress IPs give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application server’s firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makes the network restriction specific to the account's traffic, rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges.

Authenticated Origin Pulls can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection.

An origin that supports it can also validate the Access JSON Web Token, including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access.

If you're unsure where to start, speak with a Cloudflare expert to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment.

Protect the web-facing authentication service

Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare's web application firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldn’t be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures.

Alongside managed CVE signatures, WAF Attack Score uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feed Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform.

Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can also use live threat indicators in WAF policies. That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself.

Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you haven’t, and follow Citrix's suspected-compromise guidance. They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state.

Extend Zero Trust to desktop access, or remove the desktop dependency

Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone.

Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads,  Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client. If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop.

Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration.

Decide which authentication services need to be public

The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone.

Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default.

Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment:

  1. Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin.
  2. Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application.
  3. Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy.
  4. Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work.

Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed.

Bring the controls together

The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic.

Get started

Speak with a Cloudflare expert to plan the right controls for your environment. Download the solution brief and sign up for the upcoming webinar.

Andrei Migia, Nathan Sackett, and Doug Shepherd contributed to this post.

item.title: Q3 2026 Cyber Attacks Statistics Infographic
item.description: Ninety-two days, 588 incidents, one attack roughly every four hours. This infographic distils the Q3 2026 cyber attacks statistics into the numbers that matter: motivations, top techniques, initial access, targeted sectors and geography.

item.title: Q3 2026 Cyber Attacks Statistics
item.description: In the third quarter of 2026, I recorded 588 cyber incidents. Cyber Crime accounted for 77.1% of motivations, Malware was the most common attack technique at 31.9%, and Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) led initial access at 30.4%. Information and Communication was the hardest-hit sector.

item.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
item.description: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

item.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
item.description: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today's epic patch batch dwarfs September's record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

item.title: Muse, Meta's extraordinarily privileged AI assistant, has a serious 0-day
item.description: A simple ClickFix attack is only one way to completely hijack the new agent.
item.content:encoded:
Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has gone to great lengths to hype the security of its new AI assistant, Muse, claiming it is “built from the ground up for privacy and security.” A zero-day vulnerability that gives locally run apps and terminal commands complete control of the agent raises serious doubts. Further raising questions, Amazon on Sunday began blocking Muse from its site.

Meta introduced Muse a few weeks ago. The assistant “books appointments, fills out forms and handles customer service,” “proactively takes tasks off your plate,” and can “make purchases, generate images, create documents, and connect with your favorite apps and services.” The macOS app (curiously, there’s no Windows version) also works with a user’s WhatsApp, email, calendar, and social media accounts. When a task requires a tool that doesn’t exist, Muse creates one on the fly.

Meta doth hype Muse security too much

Of course, for Muse to do any of these things, users must first give it access to their accounts. This includes authenticating the assistant to each service and, because the app runs on macOS, giving it permissions to a broad range of operating system-restricted device resources, like writing files to disk, accessing the mic and camera, and monitoring location and calendars. Apple has spent years developing these defenses to prevent installed apps or commands entered into the terminal from accessing these resources, clearly because the company considers them a security threat. Muse completely undoes these default measures.

Read full article

item.title: Don’t Call Us, We’ll Call Your APIs | TraderTraitor Backdoors Resurface on Victim With No Crypto Ties
item.description: North Korean operators built a foothold on a DevOps engineer's Mac in a campaign whose job interview lures deliver malware via Terraform lock files.
item.content:encoded:
Executive Summary

  • Following disclosure of the TraderTraitor attack against LayerZero Labs in April 2026, SentinelOne identified an additional victim with the same macOS backdoors.
  • Our analysis explores the mechanics of these backdoors and the expanded targeting against a victim in the IT services sector with no relationship to cryptocurrency trading.
  • We also identified more weaponized GitHub repositories from the social engineering schemes used to target job seekers in these campaigns.
  • This report expands on how Terraform lock files enable the delivery of malware from custom Terraform provider registries controlled by the attackers.

Overview

Throughout 2026, the financially motivated DPRK state-sponsored Lazarus subgroup TraderTraitor (aka UNC4899, PUKCHONG, Jade Sleet) has engaged in campaigns targeting entities involved in cryptocurrency trading, including a high-profile attack disclosed in April where USD 292 million was stolen from KelpDAO through a compromise of LayerZero.

KelpDAO is a decentralized finance (DeFi) protocol that supports restaking Ethereum; LayerZero Labs provides services with the capability to exchange cryptocurrency across different blockchain platforms.

TraderTraitor compromised LayerZero Labs and determined methods to create a fake cryptocurrency minting event, which the attacker combined with a DDoS against validation servers so that compromised servers would approve an illegitimate mint event, leading to the massive theft.

Following the public disclosure of this breach, SentinelOne identified an additional victim infected with the macOS backdoors, FLATROOF (aka macOS.Gaslight) and ROOFDECK, which were first observed in the LayerZero Labs attack.

Unlike the previous high-profile victim, this target was a much smaller organization in the IT services industry. Our investigation revealed insights into what happens when this threat actor compromises a smaller organization that we believe ultimately yielded insufficient value to sustain the intrusion.

Weaponized Terraform Coding Projects

Each campaign related to this wave of activity uses social engineering via fake job interview lures, a traditional Contagious Interview approach common among DPRK actors. The attacker makes contact with job seekers from the company that is ultimately compromised; the GitHub profile of each targeted job seeker we identified falls into DevOps or cryptocurrency/FinTech engineering projects.

The GitHub repository themes for coding project lures are designed as infrastructure engineering projects related to the company that the DPRK actors are posing as. By pivoting from the gtn-candidate-repo repository shared by LayerZero Labs in their incident report, we identified additional lures, which included references to the companies Northwind and Novacart.

It is unclear if these were fabricated companies used by the threat actor, or if they were posing as hiring teams from real companies with these names; one Northwind example describes it as an ecommerce company launching in the near future. Other repository names that we identified include:

  • Northwind-IAC
  • novacart-interview
  • terraform-candidate-repo

The repositories contain a weaponized .terraform.lock.hcl file in the coding project with a custom provider that points to a domain controlled by the attacker. We identified three malicious provider domains across multiple repositories:


registry.hashicorp-aws[.]com
registry.hashicorp-aws[.]io
registry.hashicorp-terraform[.]io

When the victim runs terraform init with the weaponized lockfile in place, Terraform treats the custom provider as the source of truth, resulting in Terraform downloading and executing the malicious provider modules.

Developer awareness can lead to friction against this type of attack: in one repository, the candidate being interviewed added a note saying that they removed a typosquatted provider from the project’s original lock file, which may suggest they thought the interviewer was testing for their security awareness.

According to the LayerZero Labs report, the attackers installed the FLATROOF and ROOFDECK macOS backdoors after an employee installed a weaponized interview coding project on their company workstation. TraderTraitor used the backdoors to collect API keys from the organization and to escalate privileges to expand into the victim’s Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud Platform environments.

While we lack insight into many of the subsequent infections resulting from the GitHub repositories we located, SentinelOne identified an unrelated victim by hunting through our telemetry for the macOS backdoors observed in the LayerZero Labs attack.

Additional Victim

The Victim

The affected organization is an IT services provider based in India and unaffiliated with cryptocurrency. One endpoint was involved: an Apple Silicon MacBook belonging to a DevOps engineer. The engineer ran Terraform and Ansible against AWS, OVH and OpenStack on most working days, and the machine held cloud credentials and source control access: much like LayerZero Labs’ “Developer1”. Individuals whose social media profile advertises infrastructure or DevOps work are candidates for this type of attack, and the value of the target is whatever their laptop can reach.

Infection Timeline

According to our telemetry on this host, both backdoors were on disk as far back as March 18, so we cannot prove how they were delivered. They remained dormant until March 29, when beaconing and host activity began.

Timestamp (UTC)

Activity

Detail / evidence

2026-03-18

FLATROOF + ROOFDECK presence

FLATROOF and ROOFDECK hashes found on the victim machine according to telemetry data

2026-03-25 to 2026-03-28

Dormant phase

Cursor in active daily use. No malicious activity seen.

2026-03-29 05:00:41

Workspace open

Developer opens ~/DevOps-Automation/cloudshield in Cursor

2026-03-29 05:00:46

Cursor integrated terminal spawns login shells (zsh -l) + Node hosts

2026-03-29 05:00:53

First Observed Execution

Cursor launches both implants: nohup …/SystemUpdate –type=renderer and nohup …/iSync –type=renderer

2026-03-29 05:00:55

C2 connection

SystemUpdate => technicais (176[.]97.114.232), iSync => hubpage (45[.]11.59.140), Telegram at 05:00:58

2026-03-29 05:00:58

xattr -rd com.apple.quarantine + chmod +x on iSync (GatekeeperBypass)

2026-03-30 to 2026-04-19

Steady beaconing

Gated on Cursor sessions; FLATROOF/ROOFDECK beacon only while Cursor runs (quiet when Cursor is off)

2026-04-13

GitHub lure

Developer clones terraform-candidate-repo via GitHub Desktop

2026-04-14 18:25

Implant re-arm

FLATROOF re-arms ROOFDECK (re-strips quarantine, chmod +x)

2026-04-20 08:48:59

Stage 3 staging

ROOFDECK stages from 85[.]137.56.10, retrieves 3rd-stage loginwindow (one day after LayerZero Labs’ public statement)

2026-04-20 08:49:38

Stage 3 C2 connection

loginwindow online => grenight[.]com (85[.]137.56.245)

2026-04-20 13:15:11

Anti-forensics

loginwindow deletes both original implants (rm -f)

2026-05-03 to 2026-06-01

Stage 3 resumes

loginwindow keeps beaconing to grenight[.]com (85[.]137.56.245)

2026-06-01 06:08

Last observed C2

Final loginwindow beacon to grenight[.]com in the collected telemetry

The implants were first launched by Cursor on March 29, seconds after the cloudshield workspace was opened.

Timestamp (UTC)

Activity Type

Detail


2026-03-29 05:00:41

Process Creation

Cursor Helper (node), first reference to the cloudshield workspace


2026-03-29 05:00:45

File Creation

~/.cursor/projects/…-cloudshield/terminals/1.txt   (integrated terminal)


2026-03-29 05:00:46

Process Creation

bash –init-file …/shellIntegration-bash.sh


2026-03-29 05:00:47

Process Creation

zsh -l (login shell => sources ~/.zshrc/.zprofile)


2026-03-29 05:00:53

Process Creation

Cursor (parent launchd) => nohup …/com.apple.iTunesCloud/SystemUpdate –type=renderer


2026-03-29 05:00:53

Process Creation

Cursor (parent launchd) => nohup …/com.apple.internal.ck/iSync  –type=renderer

macOS Malware

We observed two malware families being deployed in the compromise, identical to the ones described in the LayerZero Labs attack, named FLATROOF and ROOFDECK (by LayerZero Labs and Mandiant). Both are ARM64 backdoors for macOS written in Rust.

FLATROOF

We observed the FLATROOF backdoor deployed under the name SystemUpdate to ~/Library/com.apple.iTunesCloud/SystemUpdate. It is likely intended for initial data collection from the victim machine and to deploy secondary payloads.

Immediately after starting, FLATROOF suppresses Gatekeeper by removing the com.apple.quarantine attribute from ROOFDECK and sets the executable bit on it; the second implant runs with no signature check and no user prompt.


xattr -rd com.apple.quarantine .../com.apple.internal.ck/iSync
chmod +x .../com.apple.internal.ck/iSync

A detailed analysis of FLATROOF (aka macOS.Gaslight) was published by SentinelLABS in June 2026. Here, we present a short summary of the backdoor’s capabilities as denoted by its supported C2 commands:

Verb

Function

help

Show command help

id

Identify the implant to the operator

shell

Execute a shell command via execvp, with posix_spawnp available as an alternative spawn path

kill

Terminate a target process by PID

upload

Exfiltrate a file via the Telegram file-attach mechanism

stop

Halt the implant

The backdoor also carries a data-harvesting Python module, used to gather the following data and exfiltrate them over Telegram using a built-in Telegram bot token:

  • Chrome, Brave, Firefox, and Safari browser data
  • Terminal command histories
  • Installed application listings
  • A running-process snapshot via ps aux
  • System hardware and software profile via system_profiler
  • A raw copy of login.keychain-db

ROOFDECK

ROOFDECK acts as a more sophisticated backdoor with broader reconnaissance and lateral movement capabilities. We observed it dropped under the name iSync to ~/Library/com.apple.internal.ck/iSync.

It is clear from the design of the implant that it is intended to be used as an additional deployment after initial foothold and control are established, since it needs a pre-existing configuration file containing at minimum a Nostr public key of an attacker-controlled profile to allow it to connect to its C2 server for the first time.

ROOFDECK uses a local configuration file ~/.config/.repl_history to store C2 URLs and keys and to set beaconing behavior.

Field

Type

Meaning

server_url

string

Resolved/overridden C2 URL (blank until dead-drop resolution)

connection_type

string http|ws

Transport selector (HTTPS /app_version vs pipe-airway WebSocket)

nostr_public_keys

array of strings

Operator Nostr identity pubkey(s) used for the dead-drop lookup

recovery_url

string

Fallback/recovery endpoint (bootstrap if primary C2 is lost)

pastebin_key

string

Key/paste id for a Pastebin-style dead-drop (secondary resolver)

rsa_private_key

string

An RSA private key provisioned into the agent

config_path_macos

string

Relative path override for the config location on macOS

interval

integer (seconds)

Beacon/poll interval

Upon first execution, it pulls live Nostr relays from api.nostr[.]watch/v1/online and combines them with a hardcoded relay list belonging to legitimate Nostr services, then searches the relays for an operator’s profile on the Nostr network based on a public profile key given in the configuration file nostr_public_keys. When found, it reads the website field of the profile and uses that as its C2 URL. TraderTraitor has previously used Nostr.

The following is a list of Nostr relays used for operator profile discovery:


wss://relay.damus[.]io
wss://nos[.]lol
wss://nostr[.]mom
wss://relay.snort[.]social
wss://offchain[.]pub
wss://relay.nostr[.]band
wss://nostr.oxtr[.]dev
wss://nostr[.]wine

Persistence was achieved via a plist entry ~/Library/LaunchAgents/loginwindow.plist, with a dynamically specified application identifier string. It uses a hardcoded --type=renderer parameter to make the implant process appear legitimate.

ROOFDECK supports a wide variety of C2 commands for managing the implant, performing reconnaissance, exfiltrating data and executing attacker code. The C2 endpoint is hardcoded as /app_version. Polling for commands is done via HTTPS with a custom pinned TLS certificate embedded in the implant, shown below.

Interestingly, the malware author used default metadata settings with mkcert, which exposed that they are running on a Linux QEMU-based VM using the username ub. We identified multiple domains using a certificate containing this certificate CN (listed in the Indicators of Compromise section).


Subject = Issuer (self-signed):
O = mkcert development CA
OU = ub@ub-Standard-PC-Q35-ICH9-2009
CN = mkcert ub@ub-Standard-PC-Q35-ICH9-2009
Serial: 1CD6D13FF15ADBF7A42025D10EC99B4A
Key: RSA 3072-bit
Validity: 2025-06-20 11:06:53 UTC -> 2035-06-20 11:06:53 UTC (10-year mkcert default)

ROOFDECK commands are signed with the operator’s private key and their integrity is verified using an embedded public key before execution. The command functionalities are separated into distinct handlers in the source code. The implant re-implements many common shell commands related to directory and file operations, another tactic often used in more sophisticated North Korea-aligned toolsets, including Lazarus’ LightlessCan.

Session & Control

Command

Handler

Description / interesting elements

session

—

Manages the C2 session lifecycle (agent registration/keying, connect, tasking loop).

config

modules/config.rs

config <key>

— sets runtime config live and persists to the configuration file. Lets the operator re-point C2/transport after deployment.

sleep

—

sleep [-r] <seconds> — sleeps N seconds or for a random interval (-r)

tasks

modules/task.rs

Manages background tasks (ongoing command executions), listing and canceling them. Task states: PENDING/RUNNING/COMPLETED/FAILED/DOWNLOADING/UPLOADING.

app_version

—

Pulls signed+encrypted commands from the HTTPS /app_version endpoint; RSA-2048-verified before an EncryptedCommand is decrypted into an AgentCommand. Doubles as version/update check and a fallback tasking channel.

persist

—

persist <add|remove|check>. add installs the ~/Library/LaunchAgents/<com.*>.plist (Chrome-renderer masquerade, RunAtLoad); remove deletes it; check reports Is enabled: <bool>.

update

—

update <url> — downloads a new binary and self-updates.

destroy

modules/recovery.rs

Self-destruct — uninstalls persistence, config and binary (guarded by a yes confirmation token).

Execution

Command

Handler

Description / interesting elements

run

handlers/run.rs

run <command> [background] — spawns an arbitrary program (native posix_spawnp/execvp), returns output; supports a background mode (long-running task tracked via tasks).

shell

handlers/shell.rs

Interactive shell via a PTY (openpty), streamed over the C2 transport.

rssh

handlers/rssh.rs

Reverse shell — starts/stops a stateful reverse shell back to the operator.

kill

handlers/kill.rs

Terminates a process by PID.

File system / data

Command

Handler

Description / interesting elements

cd / pwd

—

Change / print the agent’s working directory.

ls

handlers/ls.rs

Directory listing (names, sizes, timestamps, permissions).

find

handlers/find.rs

Recursive file search under a src root by pattern, returning matching files, used to locate high-value data (wallets, keys, docs) for exfiltration.

cat / tail

handlers/tail.rs

Read a whole file / tail the end of a file (e.g., logs).

stat

—

Show file metadata (size, mode, owner, timestamps).

cp / mv / rm

—

Copy (copyfile/fclonefileat) / move (rename) / delete (unlink) files.

mkdir / mkfile

—

Create directory / create (write) a file — used to drop payloads or write staged data.

chmod / chown

—

Change file permissions / ownership (chmod/chown).

zip / unzip

—

Create/extract archives incl. AES-encrypted zips (zip 4.3.0, zipcrypto/aes.rs). Used to stage encrypted exfiltration bundles or unpack downloaded archives (eg. next stage payloads).

Transfer

Command

Handler

Description / interesting elements

upload

handlers/upload.rs

Exfiltrates a local file to the C2.

wget

handlers/wget.rs

Downloads a file from a URL to disk (reqwest), second-stage/tool delivery.

Reconnaissance / surveillance

Command

Handler

Description / interesting elements

info

handlers/info.rs

Aggregate host fingerprint: OS/version, hostname/user (whoami), hardware IDs (IOKit), geo-IP (api.myip.com).

whoami / uname / uptime / lscpu

—

Current user / OS+kernel (uname) / uptime / CPU info (host_processor_info).

df

handlers/df.rs

Disk/volume usage and mounted filesystems (getfsstat, CFURL volume keys).

ps

handlers/ps.rs

Process listing (proc_listallpids/proc_pidinfo/proc_pid_rusage).

clipboard

—

Reads and writes the macOS clipboard (NSPasteboardTypeString). Can capture copied secrets (passwords, seed phrases, 2FA) and plant content (e.g., swap a copied crypto address).

screenshot

—

Not implemented yet. Handler returns “Screenshot command is not implemented yet.”

All C2 commands are signed on the server side by an attacker-controlled private key. The public key is embedded in the ROOFDECK payload and is used to verify the origin and integrity of the issued commands before executing them.


-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----
MIIBCgKCAQEAzan/EObUVxXNfPHdkDyCVR0AC9apleciK9ZQw+neWo6q+wvAhnLp
Pe7FZLomuwntUgI3afLDblgw9t19Kh7w/8CVwFncxh4PdqtdYno4teQ6fDLKXSWa
ZBG7zZ9R22jxPpiY70XKilXJuds34q7pfzVfbLvLTmTWyTtcyrOnRSCOwEHP/gHX
0gX+8sdX7go6O37WwzB4zNvThS+E7hG+fVfrgEaH7IUi3RY9esuBS50UomfYefO3
dK1aDMDWIwVj1skacPR9LazEc6PSGjSXxzI/N2xcpP9QKXn/Pk6r9fBzudhBL3Mw
vWyNi03JbZGtGFiy6Wai6heJqgY7pF1PAQIDAQAB
-----END RSA PUBLIC KEY-----

Another version of ROOFDECK

On April 20, one day after LayerZero Labs’ first public announcement of the KelpDAO incident, the attackers deployed a new version of ROOFDECK to the compromised machine (SHA-1: 5728b11d30586bbfc1d8bd12df1c722a06e767a2, path ~/Library/com.apple.appleaccountd/loginwindow) as an executable named loginwindow. 

After the new version initialized and started beaconing, the attackers used it to remove the old ROOFDECK and FLATROOF binaries. This new ROOFDECK was functionally identical to the previous one, but with stripped symbols and debug information, likely intended to more effectively evade detection. We can only speculate whether this was a reaction to LayerZero Labs’ publication, but the timing is nevertheless interesting.

After the update, we observed intermittent beaconing activity to a new C2 server, grenight[.]com, until June 1. On June 17, the loginwindow binary was moved to Trash.

Conclusion

DPRK-aligned actors like TraderTraitor are leaning heavily into targeting developers to establish a foothold in a network, increasingly through fake job interviews. The incident we investigated shows that not every organization they infiltrate will become a viable target for a massive cryptocurrency theft.

These groups’ initial access efforts include targeting third parties and their software supply chain, which is where much of the industry’s exposure has moved, putting the developer endpoint at the center of the defense. Endpoints used for development carry access to cloud, pipelines and source code, which makes monitoring and protection a high priority for organizations. These campaigns use purpose-built development environments aimed at one engineer at a time, paired with backdoored Terraform builds that differ for each victim.

Recommendations

For organizations:

  • We recommend flagging engineers with cloud engineering permissions and source control access as a sensitive group for endpoint security monitoring.
  • Look for unsigned binaries executing from the home directory, integrated development environment (IDE) child processes that are not signed IDE components, and outbound TLS from either.
  • Reports of interview take-home assignments and unsolicited repositories from these users are worth following up as well, since telemetry alone will not show that a recruiter sent one.
  • Consider company policy that prevents using corporate workstations for external job interviews and consider how to enforce this type of policy.
  • Educating developers with sensitive access is crucial: the weaponized Terraform provider domain was removed by one job seeker who flagged the typosquatted domain as suspicious. Organizations should add content to their security awareness training programs to highlight the risks of using projects with unknown origins as well as the nature of employees being targeted by threat actors to compromise the organization.

For developers:

  • Before running a coding project containing a .terraform.lock.hcl file, ensure that the provider registry belongs to known good domains: anything that is not a known namespace following registry.terraform.io, the official provider domain, should be treated as suspect.
  • Malicious packages can also be hosted on the official provider registry domain, so it is important to investigate the source of all packages when using an included lockfile. Terraform’s official registry supports browsing modules and providers, and modules contain a link to its source code.

This report is being published alongside a presentation at LABScon 2026, Don’t Call Us, We’ll Call Your APIs: Anatomy of an Expanding DPRK Multi-Cloud Intrusion. SentinelOne thanks Google and Mandiant for their partnership in providing technical details on this threat actor’s tools and techniques, and Nick Simonian for collaborating on this research.
